canonical.summary: Lesions first develop on lower leaves as small brownish-black spots that expand to 1/4-1/2 inch with characteristic concentric rings producing a 'bull's eye' or 'target-spot' appearance; surrounding tissue may yellow and entire leaves may become chlorotic, with dark sunken fruit lesions also showing concentric rings.
diagnostic_features: Characteristic concentric rings in the darkened lesion area giving a 'bull's eye' or 'target-spot' appearance on lower leaves; on fruit, lesions are sunken, leathery, dark brown to black with concentric rings, often entering through the calyx around the stem attachment; potato tuber lesions are dark, sunken, circular, often bordered by purple to gray raised tissue with dry, leathery, brown underlying flesh.
treatments: Maintain plant vigor through adequate fertilization to reduce host susceptibility
Remove volunteer weeds and volunteer tomatoes that serve as an inoculum source
Rotate every 2-3 years away from tomato to reduce inoculum density

Use resistant or tolerant cultivars (e.g., 'Mountain Magic', 'Mountain Fresh Plus F1', 'Bush Celebrity Hybrid', 'Big Beef Hybrid', 'Celebrity Hybrid', 'Rutgers', 'Juliet F1', 'Tommy Toe', 'Old Brooks', 'Cabernet F1')
Start with disease-free seed, transplants, and seed tubers
Control susceptible weeds (e.g., horsenettle) and eliminate cull piles
Plow under plant debris after harvest
Time irrigation to avoid late afternoon or evening; use proper plant spacing to reduce leaf wetness duration
Stake or trellis plants to improve air circulation and reduce soil contact; use mulch to prevent spore splash
Avoid working plants when they are wet; prune the bottom-most leaves as the plant grows

Apply fungicides preventatively (7-14 day intervals) — e.g., azoxystrobin + chlorothalonil (Quadris Opti), azoxystrobin + difenoconazole (Quadris Top), boscalid (Endura), chlorothalonil (Bravo), cyprodinil + fludioxinil (Switch), difenoconazole + benzovindiflupyr (Aprovia Top), difenoconazole + cyprodinil (Inspire Super), fenamidone (Reason), flutriafol (Rhyme), fluopyram + trifloxystrobin (Luna Sensation), fluopyram + pyrimethanil (Luna Tranquility), fluxaypyroxad + pyraclostrobin (Priaxor), mandipropamid + difenoconazole (Revus Top), penthiopyrad (Fontelis), pydiflumetofen + fludioxonil (Miravis Prime), pyrimethanil (Scala), strobilurin products (Quadris, Cabrio, Gem, Evito)
Schedule spray applications using spore trapping or forecasting systems (TOM-CAST)

Organic options: Bacillus amyloliquefaciens strain D747 (Double Nickel 55), Bacillus mycoides isolate J (LifeGard WG), Bacillus pumilus strain QST 2808 (Sonata), Bacillus subtilis strain IAB/BS03 (AVIV), Bacillus subtilis strain QST 713 (Cease, Serenade ASO, Serenade Opti), extract of Reynoutria sachalinensis (Regalia), fixed copper, polyoxin D zinc salt (OSO 5%SC), potassium bicarbonate (Carb-O-Nator), Streptomyces lydicus WYEC 108 (Actinovate AG)

treatments.quote: Maintain plant vigor. Maintaining adequate fertilization and improving host vigor can reduce susceptibility to early blight. Remove volunteer weeds. Removing volunteer tomatoes can reduce disease as they can serve as an inoculum source. Rotate every 2-3 years. Rotating away from tomato can reduce inoculum density in a field. Apply fungicides preventatively. Plant tolerant varieties.

canonical.summary: A brown to black lesion develops on the lower stem near the soil line and can completely girdle the stem, causing a sudden and permanent wilt of all above-ground parts; early infections show pale green leaves that cluster and cup upwards, and under moist conditions a white mycelial mat with tan to reddish-brown spherical sclerotia develops at the stem base and on infected fruit.
diagnostic_features: White mycelium at the base of the stem bearing spherical sclerotia (0.5 to 2 mm in diameter) that are initially white to tan, then yellow, maturing to dark brown; brown/tan round sclerotia on the stem just above the soil line are conclusive for southern blight.
look_alikes: other diseases that cause lower stem and crown rots
treatments: Avoid planting in fields with a history of southern blight; avoid movement of infested soil to clean fields.
Rotate host crops with corn, wheat, barley, or other non-host (graminaceous) crops for 2-3 years to reduce soil inoculum.
Modify planting dates to avoid conditions that favor disease development.
Reduce inoculum by burying infected plant debris and sclerotia via deep plowing (>4 inches) to invert the soil.
Ensure the previous crop is decomposed prior to planting (may require disking the field several times in fall and spring).
Scout to detect infections and remove/destroy symptomatic plants; reduce or eliminate weed populations.
Manage soil pH: keep soils from becoming acidic (germination of sclerotia is inhibited at pH 7 or greater); maintain adequate pH for plant growth.
Use well-composted mulch, avoid overwatering, and time irrigation by taking rainfall into account.
Use certified, pathogen-free seed.
Graft tomato varieties onto rootstocks 'Maxifort', 'Big Power', and 'Beaufort', shown to maintain yields in southern-blight-infested fields.
Soil solarization to reduce sclerotia viability (temperatures of 50°C to 55°C / 122°F to 131°F for up to 6 hours); anaerobic soil disinfestation; steam infected soils to a depth of 3-4 inches.
Biological control agents such as Trichoderma harzianum, Trichoderma viride, and certain mycorrhizal fungi.
Soil fumigants: chloropicrin, metam-sodium (sodium metam sodium), and allyl isothiocyanate, applied days to weeks before planting (limited by economic considerations).

Fungicides: pre-plant PCNB (pentachloronitrobenzene) and flutolanil; azoxystrobin (2.08F) or Terraclor 75WP applied to transplant water; strobilurins (pyraclostrobin, azoxystrobin, fluoxastrobin); SDHIs (fluxapyroxad + pyraclostrobin, penthiopyrad); triazoles (tebuconazole, prothioconazole). canonical.summary: A brown-to-black lesion develops on the lower stem at the soil line and can girdle the stem, causing sudden permanent wilt of above-ground parts; under moist conditions a white mycelial mat (often fan-shaped) appears at the stem base, followed by tan to reddish-brown spherical sclerotia (1-2 mm); fruit in contact with soil develop sunken, water-soaked, star-shaped lesions that collapse within 3-4 days.
diagnostic_features: White mycelial mat with a distinct fan-shaped pattern plus tan to reddish-brown spherical sclerotia (1-2 mm / 0.04-0.08 inch) at the stem base near the soil line; fruit lesions are sunken, water-soaked, soft, and star-shaped with no offensive odor, distinguishing it from other soilborne wilt diseases.
treatments: Avoid planting in fields with a history of southern blight
Crop rotation with non-host plants such as corn, wheat, barley, and other small grains/grasses; wait 5-6 years before returning with the same crop family
Deep plowing (>4-8 inches) to bury infected plant debris and sclerotia (pathogen is highly aerobic)
Ensure the previous crop residue is fully decomposed prior to planting
Sanitation: early detection and removal of symptomatic plants, crop residues, and weeds; use protective gloves, boots, and disinfectants
Use certified, pathogen-free seed and transplants
Modify planting dates to avoid wet/warm conditions favorable to disease (77-95°F)
Wider plant spacing to improve airflow
Maintain or raise soil pH by liming (lower pH encourages disease)
Avoid injuring plants during cultivation
Use physical barriers (aluminum foil or plastic bags around the stem at the soil line for home gardeners; plastic mulch in commercial fields/tunnels)
Apply straw mulch to the soil
Use grafted tomato rootstocks tolerant to southern blight ('Maxifort', 'Big Power', 'Beaufort')
Use ammonium-source nitrogen instead of nitrate
Soil solarization (raise soil temperatures to 50-55°C / 122-131°F for up to 6 hours)
Anaerobic soil disinfestation
Biological control: Trichoderma harzianum, Trichoderma viride, certain mycorrhizal fungi, Penicillium spp., Gliocladium virens, Bacillus subtilis (often combined with soil solarization)
Soil fumigants: chloropicrin, metam-sodium (sodium metam), allyl isothiocyanate
Pre-plant fungicide: pentachloronitrobenzene (PCNB / Terraclor) applied as a transplant solution or in-furrow soil spray; flutolanil
Strobilurin fungicides: pyraclostrobin (Cabrio EG), azoxystrobin, fluoxastrobin (Aftershock, Evito 480 SC)
SDHI fungicides: fluxapyroxad + pyraclostrobin (Priaxor 500 SC), penthiopyrad (Fontelis)
Triazole fungicides: tebuconazole, prothioconazole
Difenoconazole + benzovindiflupyr (Aprovia Top)

canonical.summary: Signs include coarse white fan-shaped mycelial strands on lower stems, pods, and soil, along with tan to brown round sclerotia; symptoms begin as wilting or yellowing of branches or the main stem, followed by rapid decline and death from an extensive lower stem rot, with brown paper-bag colored canker-like stem lesions near the crown, dark brown brittle shredded stems and crowns, and rotted pods.
diagnostic_features: Coarse white fan-shaped mycelium on lower stems and spherical tan to brown sclerotia 0.5 to 1.5 mm in diameter on mycelium, lesions, or soil; stem lesions the color of a brown paper bag with a canker-like appearance; colonized stems and crowns are dark brown, brittle, and shredded.
treatments: Rotate two years or more to a non-host crop (e.g. corn) to prevent inoculum build-up; longer rotations are needed to reduce established high inoculum, and rotations with soybean, tobacco, melons, and vegetables should be avoided.
Maintain weed control during rotations to prevent increase on susceptible species.
Use cultivars with good partial resistance and avoid highly susceptible cultivars.
Avoid excess canopy development and over-irrigation, which promote disease.
Avoid cultivation during the season (it uncovers buried sclerotia and throws infested soil onto plants); use deep plowing to bury debris and sclerotia.

Apply fungicides with good to excellent activity against stem rot (e.g. azoxystrobin, flutolanil, flutolanil + thiophanate-methyl, tebuconazole, PCNB): first application 45 to 75 days after planting (commonly 45 to 60), at least one more 14 to 28 days later, up to four applications at 2 to 4 week intervals in severe areas.
Apply fungicides in-furrow or in banded sprays within 3 to 4 weeks after emergence to enhance stem rot control.
Spray plants at night when leaves are folded to expose stems and crowns.
Purchase only pathogen-free plants, cuttings, or seeds from a reputable dealer, and select areas with no history of S. rolfsii.
Promptly remove and destroy infected/whole plants to prevent adding fungal inoculum to the soil.
Perform localized soil removal and replacement where feasible.
Treat soil with heat, solarization (clear plastic 0.025-0.4 mm for 4-8 weeks), or aerated steam (160-180 degrees F for 30 minutes).
Use soil fungicides/fumigants such as pentachloronitrobenzene (PCNB), metam sodium, or dazomet.
Keep soil pH at about 6.5 by adding lime.
Add organic amendments such as compost, oat or corn straw, or cotton gin trash.
Use biological control agents (Bacillus subtilis, actinomycetes, a mycorrhizal fungus, or certain Trichoderma species).
Practice aerification and thatch removal.

canonical.summary: Leaf lesions are small, irregular to circular, gray with reddish-brown borders, occurring most commonly on the upper leaf surface; lesions start as dark, water-soaked spots (generally 1-5 mm) and as they age the central area becomes gray to light brown with dark, red-brown margins; in severe cases the disease causes premature leaf drop and spreads to stems and pods.
diagnostic_features: Reddish-purple margins surround the gray centers on mature lesions; on some varieties, lesions may have light green to yellow halos; fuzzy, gray sporulation (conidia) can occur in lesions on the leaf underside; small black dots that resemble fine ground pepper (fungal spores) may be visible in the middle of lesions. Stem lesions are elongated gray with purple margins; pod lesions are circular, gray with purple margins.
treatments: Plant resistant soybean varieties (varieties with resistance to all known races are available)
Rotate to non-host crops (e.g., corn, sorghum, wheat, alfalfa, small grains) to reduce survival of C. sojina
Tillage / deep tillage to encourage breakdown of crop debris and reduce fungal overwintering
Plant certified, disease-free seed to reduce seedborne infections
Apply foliar fungicides between R3 and R5 growth stages (late flowering to pod filling)
Avoid strobilurin (QoI) fungicides as solo applications due to widespread fungicide resistance
Rotate fungicide chemistries or use products with multiple modes of action when spraying multiple times per season

treatments.quote: Crop rotation with non-host crops (e.g. corn, sorghum, wheat) is encouraged to limit fungal build-up in the field. Practices that encourage the breakdown of crop debris (tillage, deep tillage) help to reduce fungal overwintering. While seed infections are rare, planting certified, disease-free seed may reduce the potential for seedborne infections. Host resistance is the most economical way to reduce losses from FLS. ... Fungicide applications are most effective between R3 and R5 growth stages. Fungicide resistant FLS populations have been identified broadly in North Carolina, and strobilurin fungicides should be avoided as solo applications. To reduce losses of control, rotate fungicide chemistries when spraying multiple times within a season or use a fungicide with multiple modes of action.

profiles.disease: Bacterial Canker And Wilt Of Tomato

canonical.summary: Symptoms include small white raised spots and yellow-to-tan interveinal patches on leaves with brown burned-looking margins, one-sided wilting of lower leaves, brown streaks in the vascular system with stem cankers that may exude yellow sticky fluid, and 'bird's eye' spots (small ~1/4 inch raised white spots with tan/brown centers and cream-colored halos) on fruit.
diagnostic_features: Bird's eye spot on fruit (small ~1/4 inch raised white spots with tan/brown centers surrounded by a light yellow or cream-colored halo); brown streaks in the vascular system visible when stem is cut, with mealy pith; yellow sticky fluid exuding from squeezed cut stem; one-sided wilting of lower leaves; marginal leaf browning that looks burned on the edges; dark sunken leaf veins on young greenhouse plants.
treatments: Remove leaves with symptoms
Crop rotation to a non-host crop for 3-4 years (no tomato, potato, pepper, or eggplant); UMN also notes a shorter 2-3 year option
Plant certified pathogen-free seed from a reputable supplier; do not save seeds from infected plants
Treat saved seed before planting: soak in 1 part germicidal bleach to 4 parts water for 1 minute, then rinse in water for 5 minutes
Hot water seed treatment: soak seeds in 122°F water for 25 minutes
Seed may also be treated with dilute solutions of sodium hypochlorite
Purchase healthy transplants from a reputable grower; inspect and avoid transplants with spots, discoloration, or that have been pruned or cut back
Keep tomato leaves as dry as possible — water with drip irrigation or a soaker hose, in the morning so leaves dry quickly
Use filtered and/or treated irrigation water
Space plants so that air flows between them
Stake or cage plants, and clean and sanitize stakes/cages each year
Dispose of wooden stakes from an infested field; discard strings and wooden stakes
Disinfect tools and equipment between seasons with a commercial greenhouse sanitizer or a 1:9 bleach:water solution for 1-5 minutes
Regularly clean pruning tools; alternate between two pruners between plants to allow proper soaking time
Wash re-used pots and trays to remove crop debris, then sanitize; use new potting media stored in a sanitary environment
Wash hands, exposed clothing, and boots regularly; designate specific boots and clothes for each greenhouse or bay; wash hands before and after moving between greenhouses
Eliminate or reduce weeds (especially Solanaceae such as nightshades) and volunteer tomato/pepper plants during rotation
Avoid working in fields when the foliage is wet with rain, irrigation, or dew
Immediately remove and destroy all diseased material; in greenhouse/high tunnel production, bag and remove infected plants including roots, plus adjacent plants even if they appear healthy
Remove symptomatic plants and adjacent plants during transplant production
Remove or plow in remaining plant debris immediately after harvest to encourage decomposition
Switch to hydroponic tomato production where the pathogen has built up in the soil and rotation is a challenge
Regular, preventative spraying of copper compounds provides some protection from bacterial canker
Sprays during transplant production are more effective in prevention than sprays post-transplanting or once symptoms appear in the field

canonical.summary: Plants wilt in the field, often recovering overnight but continuing to wilt each day; wilt progresses down the vine until the entire vine wilts or dies, with leaves yellowing and browning at the margins before completely withering.
diagnostic_features: Sever an infected vine close to the crown, press the cross-sections together briefly, then slowly pull them apart; thread-like sticky strands of bacterial ooze connecting the cut surfaces confirm the pathogen.
treatments: Manage cucumber beetles with appropriate insecticide programs (the most effective way to prevent bacterial wilt)
Rogue and bury (or otherwise remove) infected plants to prevent further spread and to keep beetles from moving the bacteria to other cucurbits
Use floating/spunbonded row covers as seedlings emerge; remove them when flowers appear to allow pollination
Use insect exclusion screens (e.g., 0.8 x 1.0 mm screen size) in hoop houses or greenhouses to keep beetles out while allowing ventilation
Plant a sprayed perimeter trap crop of Blue Hubbard squash to protect more susceptible crops
Remove or destroy crop residue to reduce overwintering sites for cucumber beetles
Use crop rotation to reduce beetle numbers in adjacent areas
Apply Surround (kaolin clay) to reduce beetle numbers
Plant cucurbit cultivars with resistance to bacterial wilt; resistant cucumber cultivars are being developed
Do not rely on copper sprays or bactericides: because the bacterium is transmitted systemically, copper sprays and direct bactericide applications are of no value

canonical.summary: The first symptoms are swollen or puffy portions on newly expanding leaves, shoots, buds or flowers, which turn into galls ranging in color from green, silvery white, to pink or red; as the galls age they develop a white surface growth of spores, then turn brown and shrivel into hard galls.
diagnostic_features: Galls ranging in color from green, silvery white, to pink or red that develop a white surface growth consisting of a layer of reproductive spores as they age; galling is generally most abundant on the lower portions of the plant.
treatments: Hand pick or clip off and dispose of galled tissue before it develops a covering of white, spore-forming structures.
Prune hosts or hand pick galls only when conditions and foliage are dry.
Avoid overhead watering; instead irrigate using drip emitters or by flooding soil.
Avoid crowding plants and provide good air circulation; consider removing some crowded plants to improve air circulation.
Reduce greenhouse humidity.
Avoid planting highly susceptible cultivars and consider replacing them with less susceptible cultivars.

Preventive copper fungicides (e.g., Bordeaux mixture, Captan 80 WDG, Bonide Copper, Nu-Cop 50 DF, Fore 80WP Rainshield, Protect DF) applied before budbreak in spring with a second spray 2 to 3 weeks later may reduce the extent of new infections.

canonical.summary: Pale green or yellowish spots without well defined margins appear on the upper leaf surface and turn a distinctive yellow, with an olive-green mold visible on the lower leaf surface; lesions coalesce when disease is severe, foliage curls, withers, and may drop; symptoms appear first on lower leaves and progress upward, and olive-green asexual conidia eventually emerge as spots become necrotic.
diagnostic_features: An olive-green mold on the lower leaf surface paired with distinctive yellow spots on the upper leaf surface; fruit symptoms consist of a dark, leathery rot at the stem ends; spots are more discrete than those caused by nutrient deficiency, and disease progresses from the bottom to the top of plants.
treatments: Plant resistant varieties (Determinant: Red Mountain, Primo Red, Mountain Spring, Florida 97; Indeterminant: Geronimo, Trust, Boa; Heirloom: Cherokee Purple, Amish Paste, Prudens Purple)
Remove diseased plants and surrounding plants to prevent pathogen spread
Remove and destroy crop residue after harvest
Dispose of infected plant material and sterilize all equipment used in the greenhouse
Sanitize greenhouse thoroughly between crop cycles
Rotate crops and move high tunnels regularly
Start with certified, disease-free seed from a reputable source, or treat seed with hot water
Minimize long periods of leaf wetness by avoiding wetting the foliage and using fans to circulate air
Stake and prune to increase ventilation and reduce disease spread
Maintain night temperatures in the greenhouse higher than outside temperatures
Apply Champ 30 WG or Zonix for organic control
Apply Quadris Top (azoxystrobin and difenoconazole) for conventional control
Apply Bravo Weather Stik (chlorothalonil) for conventional control

canonical.summary: Infected plants are wilted and stunted with small leaflets that turn brown; brown to dark spots appear on cotyledons at seedling stage, reddish-brown to black lesions on unifoliate leaves, and light brown to grey superficial lesions on stems mid to late season, with reddish-brown discoloration in the pith and vascular tissues.
diagnostic_features: Small black specks (microsclerotia) form beneath the epidermis and inside the lower stem and taproot, giving them a charcoal-sprinkled, marbled appearance; microsclerotia also present in vascular tissue, pith, and mature and dry pods.
treatments: Manage fields to reduce or avoid drought stress (drought-stress mitigation through irrigation when needed)
Crop rotation with non-hosts or crops with relatively low susceptibility (such as cereal grains) to limit fungal survival in soils
Reduced tillage may reduce charcoal rot, perhaps due to cooler soils and less moisture stress
Reduced seeding rates may reduce drought stress and charcoal rot
Soybean cultivars may exhibit different levels of susceptibility, but none are fully resistant

canonical.summary: Symptoms begin on leaves in the lower plant canopy with gray-green, tan to dark-brown, or reddish-brown angular lesions (2-5 mm diameter) developing first on the underside of leaves; small pustules form in the lesions and break open to release masses of tan spores; lesions may also appear on petioles, pods, and stems.
diagnostic_features: Angular lesions 2-5 mm in diameter that are gray-green, tan to dark-brown, or reddish-brown, with small pustules (blisters) that develop in the lesions and break open to release masses of tan spores; lesions and pustules can be seen with a 20X hand lens.
look_alikes: other common leaf diseases on soybean
treatments: The primary management of rust is through the use of fungicide applications.
Fungicide applications made between R3 and R5 may provide the most yield protection for soybeans.
Different modes of action should be used if more than one fungicide is needed in a growing season.
Fungicides are likely not needed if soybean rust is not within 100 miles of a field.
Regularly scouting fields throughout the growing season is important to monitor for foliar diseases like rust.
Scout the lower canopy of fields weekly, especially during wet weather after soybeans begin to flower.
Soybean rust must be diagnosed at an early stage to be successfully managed.
Soybean varieties that are resistant to soybean rust are in development.

canonical.summary: Lesions begin as circular to elliptical purple spots (initially indistinguishable from common leaf spot or leaf scorch) that develop dark brown centers as they enlarge; some leaves show large V-shaped lesions with the widest part at the leaf edge, and heavily infected leaves turn purple or red and may die. Dark lesions can also occur on stems and berry caps.
diagnostic_features: Older lesions develop a characteristic pattern of three color zones (a pale brown or tan center surrounded by a brown ring surrounded by a ring of dark brown, red, or purple), enlarge to become V-shaped and delineated by major leaf veins, and bear numerous tiny black pycnidia in the center.
treatments: Obtain certified disease-free strawberry plants from a reputable, commercial supplier.
Plant strawberries in a sunny, open location on a shallow berm or raised mound; avoid crowding plants and control nearby weeds.
Select a field with excellent soil drainage and good air circulation, allowing enough space between plants.
Use drip or furrow irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers; if irrigating overhead, apply water in the early morning so foliage dries rapidly, and avoid prolonged waterlogging.
At the end of the season remove and dispose of (or till in) strawberry debris away from where strawberries will be grown next season, since overwintered fungus in debris is a source of new inoculum.
Consider growing strawberries as an annual instead of a perennial.

Broad spectrum fungicides (captan, thiram) offer some control, and fungicides with a specific mode of action (e.g. Rally, possibly the QoI/strobilurins) also offer control; in matted row systems, post-harvest applications followed by mowing/removal of older leaves reduce inoculum.
Potassium silicate and calcium silicate applied separately as a soil treatment combined with foliar spray.
Fungicides are generally not effective or warranted for Phomopsis leaf blight of strawberry in home gardens; integrated disease management is the most effective way to avoid P. obscurans infection.

canonical.summary: The most common symptoms on peppers are crown rot and fruit rot; under wet conditions plants wilt then die, crown lesions become dark brown and girdle the stem, and fruit develops water-soaked areas covered with white powdery to cottony mold.
diagnostic_features: On peppers, a dry, corky canker on the main stem at the soil line, chocolate brown rotting roots, blackened stem branch points, and diseased fruit covered with a thin, dense layer of white mold.
treatments: Plant resistant/moderately resistant varieties (e.g., bell pepper cultivars Vanguard, Paladin, Revolution, Declaration); some bell, sweet, and hot peppers have moderate resistance to P. capsici.

Improve soil drainage; plant in fields with good drainage and even terrain; do not plant in low areas; use raised beds and plastic mulch; cut water furrows across plastic-mulched raised beds; subsoil.
Use irrigation water from wells, not surface water (ponds, creeks, streams, rivers) which may be infested; irrigate moderately via drip; avoid overhead irrigation once fruit is present.
Rotate to nonhost crops (e.g., cereals) after any susceptible vegetable; do not plant a fall susceptible crop in the same field after a spring susceptible crop.
Monitor/scout fields for disease.
Remove diseased and rotting fruit or plants away from the field; do not leave culls in the field or near surface irrigation water sources; harvest fruit as soon as possible from problem fields.
Sanitize/power-wash soil from farm equipment after working infested fields; enter noninfested fields before entering infested fields.
Use plastic or organic mulches to prevent infested soil splashing onto fruit.

Apply fungicides preventively: soil applications at transplant followed by drip applications; foliar sprays with good coverage to protect fruit; rotate and tank-mix at least two recommended products to avoid resistance. Example products: Cyazofamid (Ranman 400 SC), Ametoctradin + dimethomorph (Zampro), Fluopicolide (Presidio), Mandipropamid (Revus), Mefenoxam + copper (Ridomil Gold/Copper), Famoxadone + cymoxanil (Tanos 50WG), Fluazinam (Omega 500 F), Orondis Gold, Orondis Ultra.

Only OMRI-labeled active ingredients with some efficacy are fixed copper formulations; home gardeners have no effective chemical control options and must rely on host resistance and cultural strategies.

canonical.summary: Leaves develop large dark brown blotches with a green-gray edge (not confined by major leaf veins); irregularly shaped water-soaked lesions often with a lighter halo appear on younger leaves at the top of the canopy; stems show firm dark brown infections; tomato fruits develop firm, dark brown, greasy-to-leathery circular spots. In high humidity, thin powdery white fungal growth (sporangia) appears on infected tissue, especially the leaf underside.
diagnostic_features: Lesions occur on new growth at the top of the canopy (unlike early blight which starts on lower leaves), are light brown or tan (vs. dark brown with concentric rings for early blight); large dark brown leaf blotches have a green-gray edge that is not confined by major leaf veins; produces white cottony/powdery sporulation on the leaf underside under high humidity.
treatments: Plant tomatoes where no tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or eggplants have been for the past 3-4 years
Plant early in the season to escape high disease pressure later in the season
Keep leaves as dry as possible; water with drip irrigation or a soaker hose; water in the morning so leaves dry quickly
Stake or cage plants and space plants so that air flows between them
Remove or bury plants at the end of the season; manage cull piles so culls break down over winter
Scout plants often and remove infected plants, infected fruit, volunteers and weeds
Destroy potato cull piles before the growing season begins by burying, incorporating into fields, or feeding to livestock
Control volunteer potato plants, as infected plants can grow from infected tubers
Plant certified potato seed
Inspect tomato transplants for late blight symptoms prior to purchase and/or planting
If infection is found in only a few plants within a field, remove, disc-under, kill with herbicide or flame-kill infected plants to avoid spreading
Sign up to receive alerts at the USAblight website
Plant resistant varieties when possible (will still show some symptoms under highly favorable conditions)

summary.value: Leaves develop large dark brown blotches with a green-gray edge (not confined by major leaf veins); irregularly shaped water-soaked lesions often with a lighter halo appear on younger leaves at the top of the canopy; stems show firm dark brown infections; tomato fruits develop firm, dark brown, greasy-to-leathery circular spots. In high humidity, thin powdery white fungal growth (sporangia) appears on infected tissue, especially the leaf underside.
summary.quote: Leaves have large, dark brown blotches with a green gray edge; not confined by major leaf veins. Infections progress through leaflets and petioles, resulting in large sections of dry brown foliage. Stem infections are firm and dark brown with a rounded edge. In cool, wet weather, entire fields turn brown and wilted as if hit by frost. In tomatoes, firm, dark brown, circular spots grow to cover large parts of fruits. Spots may become mushy as secondary bacteria invade. In high humidity, thin powdery white fungal growth appears on infected leaves, tomato fruit and stems.

diagnostic_features.value: Lesions occur on new growth at the top of the canopy (unlike early blight which starts on lower leaves), are light brown or tan (vs. dark brown with concentric rings for early blight); large dark brown leaf blotches have a green-gray edge that is not confined by major leaf veins; produces white cottony/powdery sporulation on the leaf underside under high humidity.
diagnostic_features.quote: Late blight can be differentiated from early blight on tomato and other foliar fungal diseases by where they occur on the plant. Lesions caused by late blight can be found anywhere on the plant, but are mostly found on the new growth whereas early blight typically starts on the lower leaves and slowly moves up the plant. Also, lesions caused by late blight tend to be light brown or tan in color while lesions caused by early blight tend to be dark brown in color with concentric rings.

canonical.summary: Lesions are small (<1/4 inch) and white; diamond to lens-shaped on vines, petioles and leaf veins, and round on fruit and leaves. On fruit it causes white, tan, or silver russeting that can merge into a continuous dry, scabby surface.
diagnostic_features: Small (<1/4 inch) white lesions that are diamond to lens-shaped on vines, petioles and leaf veins and round on fruit and leaves; lesions coalesce until vines and petioles turn white; on fruit, white, tan, or silver russeting merging into a dry, scabby surface. Foliage collapses in a circular pattern early in infection, detectable from a distance.
treatments: Rotate away from summer squash and pumpkins, using nonhost crops, for at least 2-3 years.
Choose sunny, well-drained sites for cucurbit production.
Space plants and orient rows (e.g. with the prevailing wind) to improve air circulation and rapid drying of leaf surfaces.
Scout for disease and apply protectant fungicides when the disease first occurs / beginning at fruit set.
Ensure thorough coverage of foliage, vines, and fruit for good control.
Promptly remove and destroy diseased plant material during the growing season.
Manage weeds and potential alternative hosts.
Avoid movement of infested soil to clean fields.
Promptly destroy crop residues after harvest and deep plow to bury residual inoculum.
Systemic fungicide options include Cabrio, Flint Extra, Merivon, and Quadris/Satori.

canonical.summary: Small black spots (⅛ to ¼ inch) on leaves, often more prominent on the undersides, sometimes developing a yellow halo; on fruit, very small pinpoint-like spots ranging from brown to black, which may be raised, flat or sunken, with darker green haloes on green fruit and subtle yellow haloes on ripe fruit.
diagnostic_features: Small, angular (straight-edged) spots with yellow haloes on leaves; pinpoint-like superficial spots on fruit that do not penetrate deeply into the tissue.
treatments: Start by using high quality, pathogen-free seed or transplants from a reputable seed supplier or garden center
Consider treating the seed in hot water prior to planting to eliminate the pathogen
DO NOT use a sprinkler to water; instead use a soaker or drip hose to water at the bases of plants
Only work with tomato plants when they are dry
Routinely disinfect garden tools with 10% bleach or 70% alcohol (e.g., rubbing alcohol)
Remove contaminated tomato debris from the garden at the end of the growing season (deep bury, burn where allowed, or hot compost)
DO NOT replant tomatoes in the same area the following growing season; practice non-host crop rotation (three-year field rotations)

As a last resort, apply chemical treatments with a copper-based product labeled for tomatoes; apply first treatment before symptoms develop and repeat every 10–14 days while cool, moist conditions continue
Sanitize all greenhouses, equipment, flats and trellising stakes at the end of the season
Practice irrigation control to minimize leaf wetness during cooler periods
Remain vigilant/scout: remove diseased plants and a few of the surrounding plants once symptoms are observed; plow under infected areas/fields
Few resistant varieties are available

profiles.profile_id: St. Augustinegrass::Rhizoctonia Damping-Off, Blight And Rot

canonical.summary: The fungus causes a soft, dark rot at the base of the leaf closest to the soil, so leaves pull easily off the stem and have a rotted odor; the turf shows small patches (about 1 ft) that turn yellow then reddish brown, brown, or straw colored, expanding to several feet, often as rings with apparently healthy turf in the center. Circular patches can range from 3 to 26 ft in diameter and appear in spring and fall, with peripheral leaves turning bright yellow and/or orange.
diagnostic_features: A soft, dark rot at the base of the leaf near the soil with a rotted odor, so leaves pull off easily; roots are not affected; water-soaked, reddish-brown or black lesions occur on the leaf sheaths; patches may form rings with healthy turf in the center and a dark, wilted outer margin. It is diagnostic if one tugs gently on the leaves in the recently discolored perimeter and the blades pull free.
treatments: Establish a turfgrass species best adapted to your geographical area and situation

Regulate moisture levels in the thatch and soil; install drainage tile, modify the soil profile to increase porosity, and/or cultivate soil to reduce compaction and thatch accumulation; provide good surface and subsurface drainage
Control traffic patterns to prevent severe compaction and core aerate to improve drainage and air circulation
Where air movement and sunlight penetration are low, prune or remove surrounding trees and shrubs
Prevent excessive thatch buildup

Avoid excessive/high nitrogen on warm-season grasses in mid-to-late fall or early spring before the lawn fully greens up; avoid fast-release forms of nitrogen; use slow-release nitrogen sources during disease-development periods

Apply a balanced fertilizer with equivalent amounts of potassium and nitrogen based on an updated soil test; do not apply nitrogen before soil temperatures at the 4-in depth are consistently 65 °F and rising

Irrigate only when needed (deeply, no more than once a week, to a depth of 4-6 inches / ~1 inch per week) during early morning hours (between 2:00 and 8:00 a.m.) when dew is already present; do not subject the lawn to drought

Keep mowing height consistent and correct for the variety (e.g., mow centipede at 1½ to 2 inches); mow diseased areas last and wash mower clippings before proceeding; remove clippings if the weather is warm and moist

For professionals/preventatively, apply fungicides in classes: carboxamides, benzimidazoles, carbamates, dicarboximides, DMI fungicides, di-nitro anilines, nitriles, polyoxins, and Qo inhibitors, including several biological fungicides; make the first fall application when thatch temperature drops below ~69.8 °F for several consecutive days (early October) and repeat 2-4 weeks later before dormancy, with a spring application in April; alternate fungicides to prevent resistance buildup

Fungicide active ingredients include azoxystrobin, chlorothalonil, fludioxonil, flutolanil, iprodione, mancozeb, metconazole, myclobutanil, polyoxin D, propiconazole, pyraclostrobin, thiophanate-methyl, thiram, triadimefon, trifloxystrobin, triticonazole, vinclozolin, and combination products (azoxystrobin+propiconazole, pyraclostrobin+triticonazole)

canonical.summary: Foliage suddenly turns an intense bright yellow at or near fruit set, beginning with interveinal yellowing and progressing to whole-vine yellowing; terminal leaves stand erect with curled margins, older leaves develop scorched margins, and plants ultimately wilt and collapse. Vascular tissue (phloem) at the crown turns a characteristic honey-brown rather than translucent green.
diagnostic_features: Honey-brown discoloration of the phloem in the crown and lower stem (visible at stem cross-section) is the key diagnostic; symptoms appear suddenly approximately 2 weeks before fruit maturity; terminal leaves stand erect, fail to expand, with margins curling inwards; unlike bacterial wilt, cut stems do NOT exude sticky ooze; in watermelon, fruit turn yellow as leaves discolor.
treatments: Control the squash bug (Anasa tristis) vector beginning at crop emergence or transplanting - this is the foundation of CYVD management
Target early-season adult squash bugs as they colonize the field; insecticide applications should hit young seedlings (< 3-5 true leaves) as soon as squash bugs are present
Manage the first generation of squash bugs during the nymphal stage to reduce the adult population; foliar sprays targeting newly hatched nymphs are more effective than against later stages
Repeat foliar sprays for extended periods of control
New generation synthetic pyrethroids (e.g., Capture, Brigade) tend to work better than most other materials against squash bug; Thionex may also be effective on squash bug and cucumber beetle
Systemic insecticides used for cucumber beetle management will provide up to 3 weeks of squash bug suppression
Crop rotation with non-cucurbit plants, or at a sufficient distance from previous cucurbit plantings
Remove crop debris and old/unharvested fruit to reduce overwintering squash bug populations

Use Hubbard squash (e.g., 'Blue Hubbard') as a perimeter/trap crop around later-planted pumpkins or other cucurbits; alternatively use early-planted straightneck summer squash ('Lemon Drop', 'Hyrific') as a border trap crop
Time the trap-crop spray just prior to main-crop emergence, with a second application at the first true-leaf stage of the main crop if needed
If infection has occurred, harvest and market fruit from infected pumpkins, winter squash, cantaloupe, or muskmelon vines early to avoid crop loss

canonical.summary: On peppers, foliage forms small brown necrotic spots and/or chlorotic ring spots; heavily infected leaves brown, roll, and wilt, seedlings form a "shepherd's crook" and die, and fruit show yellow ringspots and brown necrotic sunken areas. On tomatoes the uppermost leaves appear bronzed with small brown lesions.
diagnostic_features: Lesions caused by TSWV have blurred margins, whereas lesions of look-alike diseases have definite margins.
treatments: Use virus- and thrips-free transplants (ideally from transplant houses that monitor for thrips and inspect for disease)
Manage thrips populations on transplants if necessary
Practice good weed management in and around fields; control weeds such as dandelions, sow thistle, chickweed, buttercup, and plantain, including on fallow fields, volunteers, and unused land nearby
Avoid planting new fields near older fields, especially those confirmed to have TSWV infection
Monitor fields for the presence of thrips and manage populations
Monitor for TSWV using tests including ELISA, immunostrip tests, and PCR
Consider roguing plants infected at the seedling stage
Sanitation: promptly remove and destroy old crops and volunteers after harvest (plowing and physical removal)
Deploy TSWV-resistant varieties (Sw-5 gene in tomato, Tsw gene in pepper)
Apply insecticides for thrips control; treating transplants with imidacloprid just before setting in the field is one of the most effective approaches to suppress primary spread
Use reflective mulch to disorient thrips and prevent them from landing on plants
Segregate and quarantine externally sourced plant material; inspect transplants for symptoms and discard symptomatic plants
Use biological control: minute pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus) and big-eyed bugs (Geocoris punctipes) prey on thrips
Minimize thrips entry in greenhouses using thrips-proof screening on air intakes and vents and double-door entries
Monitor thrips in the greenhouse with sticky yellow card traps and apply insecticides when populations grow
Avoid growing ornamentals and vegetables in the same greenhouse
For home gardeners: spray early in the season with neem oil or other botanical insecticides; summer oil or insecticidal soap may also be used

summary.value: On peppers, foliage forms small brown necrotic spots and/or chlorotic ring spots; heavily infected leaves brown, roll, and wilt, seedlings form a "shepherd's crook" and die, and fruit show yellow ringspots and brown necrotic sunken areas. On tomatoes the uppermost leaves appear bronzed with small brown lesions.
summary.quote: On tomatoes infected with TSWV, the uppermost leaves appear bronzed with small brown lesions (Figure 1). Infected peppers form small brown necrotic spots and/or chlorotic ring spots on the foliage (Figure 2). Infected foliage on both tomatoes and peppers may become covered with so many spots that the entire leaf browns, rolls, and wilts. Infected seedlings form a “shepherd’s crook” appearance and die (Figure 3).

canonical.summary: Pecan scab manifests as small (1 to 5 mm), circular, black or olive green lesions on leaves, shucks, and twigs; lesions may coalesce into larger blackened areas and, on nut shucks, may be slightly raised.
diagnostic_features: In early infection lesions appear velvety due to production of conidia on their surface, then harden and turn dark grey to silvery-brown; lesions on young shoots appear sunken due to swelling of tissue at the margins.
treatments: Selection of resistant cultivars is the first line of defense.
Commercial growers rely on fungicides to manage pecan scab; fungicides should be applied before conditions favorable for disease development occur.
Fungicides must be rotated by FRAC group to reduce selection pressure for resistant fungi (e.g., mixing/alternating triazoles with organometals).

Spray schedule: begin in early spring at leaf emergence; between bud break and nut set apply every 10 to 14 days; from nut set to shell hardening every 10 to 21 days (extension sources note applications every 2 to 3 weeks over a 5- to 6-month season depending on rainfall).
Organic growers may spray with Bordeaux mixture (copper sulfate and hydrated lime); other options include oils such as neem oil, phosphorous acid (FRAC P07), sulfur (FRAC M02), and ziram (FRAC M04).
Specific fungicides: boscalid (FRAC 7) + pyraclostrobin (FRAC 11), propiconazole (FRAC 3).
Plant trees with adequate spacing/orientation for good sunlight exposure and airflow to keep foliage dry.
Selective pruning of damaged branches during the dormant season to promote sun exposure and air circulation.
Good sanitation practices to limit primary inoculum.

canonical.summary: Infection begins as minute water-soaked spots on the lower leaf and calyx surfaces that enlarge into translucent, angular spots delineated by small veins; lesions may exude a viscous bacterial ooze (drying to a whitish, scaly film) and later coalesce, producing reddish-brown, necrotic spots surrounded by a chlorotic/yellow halo on the upper leaf surface. Caps of the fruit may turn brown or black.
diagnostic_features: Lesions are angular (confined/delineated by leaf veins) rather than round, and are translucent when a leaf is held up to a bright light and viewed from the backside — the "windowpane" effect — while appearing dark green and water-soaked with reflected light.
treatments: Use pathogen-free transplants or certified planting material grown under strict conditions
Minimize overhead sprinklers/irrigation (especially during establishment and freeze protection); use drip irrigation instead when possible
Use protective structures such as high plastic tunnels or floating row covers as an alternative to water for freeze protection
Choose a planting site with good air circulation and sun exposure, and control weeds to promote drying of foliage
Avoid moving equipment/harvesters through wet fields; handle and harvest infested fields after non-infested fields to limit dissemination
Use straw mulch to minimize water-droplet splashing
Rotate crops to avoid infesting fields
Soil-incorporate strawberry debris under serious disease conditions to optimize tissue breakdown
Apply registered copper-based products (e.g., copper hydroxide) preventively at low rates prior to rapid growth, avoiding warm temperatures and repeated sprays due to phytotoxicity risk
Apply Actigard (plant-resistance activator / defense inducer) preventively at the lowest label rate to suppress ALS

canonical.summary: Infected plants in small clusters show foliar interveinal chlorosis followed by necrosis (foliar yellowing and death), with root rot, premature plant death, and stems that break at the crown when pulled; roots remaining attached are embedded with black fungal stroma along the primary root.
diagnostic_features: Black fungal tissue (stroma) along the primary root (and less frequently on lateral roots), white cottony fungal growth (mycelia) within the pith when roots are split longitudinally, and reproductive stromata ("dead man's fingers") on infected soybean debris and at the plant base under humid conditions — white at the tip (sometimes pinkish when young) turning black at maturity.
treatments: Practice crop rotation — rotation to cotton, corn, grain sorghum, rice or sugarcane will likely reduce the incidence and severity of TRD
Till fields after harvest/before planting (reduced or conventional) to facilitate breakdown of soybean debris and reduce inoculum
Use resistant cultivars — some commercially available soybean cultivars have shown resistance in greenhouse and field experiments
Differences in soybean variety susceptibility to TRD have been observed
Follow good sanitation practices — avoid moving soil from infested to non-infested fields, and clean soil and crop debris from machinery, clothes, boots, tools
Certain fungicides applied in-furrow have been observed to be beneficial (no fungicides are currently labeled for management of taproot decline)

treatments: Use a well-designed integrated LDM management plan that includes host resistance, chemicals, and cultural practices

Use irrigation practices such as drip irrigation that minimize leaf wetness or soil moisture
Apply broad-spectrum protectants (sulfur, copper fungicides, mancozeb) and more specific oomycete compounds (translaminar or systemic)
Initiate prophylactic chemical applications when conditions favorable for pathogen infection occur

canonical.summary: On pines, yellow-to-orange spots or bands appear on green needles in spring, needles turn yellow, and tiny raised white tubes form and break open to release powdery orange spores. On asters, yellow leaf spots appear on the upper leaf surface with raised orange spore-filled pustules and powdery yellow-orange spores on the lower leaf surface.
diagnostic_features: Reddish-orange spots on pine needles with swelling pads of fungal tissue that rupture to release flattened white spore-bearing structures (aecia); because the base of the needles remains green, infected needles are often retained in the canopy. On aster and goldenrod hosts, orange spots and blotches appear.
treatments: Pine needle rust is a minor stress on the tree and no management is required.
Increase the vigor of infected trees by watering during dry conditions and mulching to conserve water.

Removal of alternative hosts such as wild or cultivated species of aster (Aster), goldenrod (Solidago) and several other members of the daisy or aster family (Asteraceae) from the immediate area of the trees will reduce infections of pines.
In areas with large numbers of wild asters, plant conifers resistant to needle rusts like spruce, white pine or balsam fir.
Avoid planting members of the Asteraceae (specifically asters and goldenrods) near two- and three-needle pines.
Chemical management to control rust diseases is notoriously difficult and is not recommended.
Provide good air circulation; do not crowd plants.
Practice good weed control so lower needles are not kept moist for extended periods of time.
For high-value trees, remove and destroy fallen needles that collect in branch crotches and on the ground.
Protect trees in late summer when telia are seen on alternate hosts.
Armada 50 WDG at 9 oz/100 gal water. Do not use a silicone-based surfactant. Not for nursery or greenhouse use. Group 3 + 11 fungicide. 12-hr reentry.
Heritage at 1 to 4 oz/100 gal water plus a non-silicone-based wetter sticker. Registered for conifers including Christmas trees. Group 11 fungicide. 4-hr reentry.

canonical.summary: Small, angular lesions develop on leaves and inflorescences, enlarging into irregular yellow to orange necrotic patches with dense sporulation on leaf undersides that gives a gray to purple, downy appearance; systemically infected plants develop black streaking inside stems and heads, and cabbage heads develop sunken black spots.
diagnostic_features: Dense sporulation (grayish-white mycelial growth) on leaf undersides gives a gray to purple downy appearance; on seedlings bright yellow lesions have networks of black spots or lines throughout, looking almost like a web; cabbage heads develop sunken black spots.
look_alikes: cold-damaged tissues with subsequent secondary leaf rot
treatments: Removal of crop debris and weed hosts (including brassica-family weeds and volunteers) may reduce inoculum.
Start with disease-free seed; ask your seed supplier if the lot has been tested for downy mildew, or hot-water treat your seeds.
Scout seedlings in the greenhouse/seedbed and maintain low humidity; check each seedling before transplanting and remove any showing symptoms.
Practice crop rotation with non-brassica crops (a two-year rotation away from brassicas, and rotate out of crucifers for at least two years).
Improve air circulation, avoid overcrowding seedlings, and irrigate early in the day so leaves are wet only for a few hours.
In the field, lower leaf wetness and canopy humidity by increasing spacing, controlling weeds, planting in the direction of prevailing winds, and planting in areas with full sun.
Collect and burn or bury as much of the crop as possible when harvest is complete; remove or bury infected crop debris near new plantings.
Plant resistant or tolerant cultivars (limited resistant varieties of cabbage and Chinese cabbage are available).
If fungicides are needed, spray with systemic metalaxyl/mefenoxam, or protectant mancozeb, copper, or chlorothalonil.

On transplants apply first spray as soon as seedlings appear and repeat until plants are set out in the field; examples include Actigard 50WG, Forum, Revus, Orondis, Presidio, Ranman 400 SC, Zampro, phosphonates (Aliette/Fosphite), Regalia, and biological controls (Cease, Double Nickel LC, LifeGard WG, Sonata, Stargus).

canonical.summary: Infection causes a brown, soft decay that destroys the plant crown tissue; older leaves wilt and eventually the entire plant wilts and collapses. Lower leaves wilt and drop to the soil surface, and where the leaf contacts the soil a white mycelium forms and sclerotia develop.
diagnostic_features: Profuse white mycelia and small (up to 0.125 inch / 3 mm) black, hard sclerotia form on the outside of the decayed crown for S. minor, while S. sclerotiorum forms larger sclerotia (0.25â€“0.50 inch) and produces airborne spores that can infect upper leaves causing a watery soft rot.
treatments: Crop rotation with non-hosts; for S. minor, crop rotations and deep inversion plowing may help reduce incidence.
Deep plowing to keep sclerotia from the soil surface.
Avoid known crop hosts including beans, cauliflower, celery, corn salad, endive, escarole, fennel, pepper, radicchio, and tomato.
Avoid cover crop hosts including Austrian winter pea, mustards, phacelia, and vetch.
Avoid overly wet soils and keep the bed surface as dry as possible with careful irrigation; use drip irrigation below the soil surface.
Level land for even water distribution and good drainage, with beds as high as possible.
Collect and remove infected plants.
Use cultural controls in an organically certified crop.

For S. minor, apply protectant fungicides after thinning, directed to the base of young plants before they become too large; for S. sclerotiorum, apply fungicides beginning at the rosette stage when conditions favor disease.
Before disease appears, apply fungicides on a 14-day interval.
Example products: Iprodione (Rovral 4F), Cyprodinil/Fludioxonil (Switch 62.5WG), Boscalid (Endura), Fludioxonil (Cannonball WG), Dicloran (Botran).

canonical.summary: Early lesions on leaves are small and circular-to-oval, often with a prominent light green to yellow halo; as they mature the fungus erupts through the leaf surface forming light orange to cinnamon-red pustules.

treatments: Resistant varieties are the most cost-effective means to manage southern rust in field corn.

Consult your seed dealer to determine the best hybrids and inbreds for your area.

Intercropping can also reduce the severity of the disease.

The application of quinone outside inhibitor (Qol) or Qol + demethylation inhibitor (DMI) fungicides at tasseling stage were most effective when SCR was present and environmental conditions favored rust development.
A combination of triazole and estrobirulina was feasible to reduce SCR severity.
Avoid late planting.

canonical.summary: Symptoms first appear on fruit as a slight water-soaked, light-tan area on or near the blossom (distal) end that darkens and enlarges in a widening circle; the affected tissue becomes dark/black, shrunken, and dry and leathery. Affected fruit ripen faster than normal.
diagnostic_features: Lesion forms specifically at the blossom (distal, bottom) end of the fruit and can occur on unexposed fruit surfaces; normally dry and leathery, and affected fruit ripen faster than normal.
treatments: Test the soil to determine whether calcium levels fall within the recommended range.

Lime the soil according to soil analysis recommendations (dolomitic or high-calcium limestone), usually to pH 6.5-6.8 (up to 7), applying 2-4 months / several months before planting and mixing thoroughly into the top 8-12 inches.
Use gypsum (land plaster) at 500 to 1000 pounds per acre as a supplement to liming on calcium-deficient soils.

During the growing season, foliar spray fruit with anhydrous calcium chloride (or calcium nitrate / calcium chloride dihydrate plus surfactant) on a weekly schedule beginning when fruit forms or when symptoms first appear.
Regulate and maintain a uniform, even supply of soil moisture through proper/controlled irrigation, wetting the root zone at least every 7 to 10 days.
Provide proper drainage and do not plant where drainage is poor, surface water accumulates, or soil is droughty, to avoid root disorders that reduce water uptake.
Mulch (black plastic or loose organic material) to help maintain even soil moisture.
Fertilize only moderately; avoid excessive nitrogen and side-dress only if needed to maintain green color and moderate growth.
Avoid fertilizer products high in potassium, sodium, magnesium, and ammonium, as they compete with calcium for uptake.
Choose tolerant cultivars; for peppers, shorter/rounder varieties tend to have more tolerance than longer varieties.
If cultivation is necessary, keep it shallow to avoid root pruning.
Ensure good air movement through plant spacing and pruning practices.
Remove affected fruits when symptoms are first observed.
Control root diseases, nematodes, and flooding.
Use polyethylene mulches (black in cool spring, silver or white-on-black in summer/fall) to moderate soil temperature and improve root function and calcium uptake.

canonical.summary: Leaves on or near the soil first develop a dark, water-soaked lesion and turn light brown, then a gray or brown fuzzy growth of fungal spores appears; a soft rot of leaves and stems develops, plants shrivel and the whole head wilts and rots (beginning with the oldest leaves) until the plant collapses, with abundant gray powdery spore masses and black sclerotia forming under rotted parts.

treatments: Plant on well-drained, raised beds, use furrow irrigation whenever possible, and keep the surface of vegetable beds as dry as possible

canonical.summary: Anthracnose fruit rot appears as brown to black, water-soaked spots on green and ripe fruit, developing into firm, sunken brown to black lesions, sometimes with pink, salmon, or orange masses of spores; under dry conditions the entire fruit may dry up and mummify.
diagnostic_features: During wet weather the lesions become covered with sticky, light orange ooze composed of millions of spores (conidia) in a mucilaginous matrix; the combination of signs (spores) and symptoms is diagnostic for this disease.
treatments: Use disease-free plants — the most important management strategy for controlling this disease; obtain transplants from pathogen-free nurseries and control by exclusion
Grow resistant/less-susceptible cultivars (e.g. Sweet Charlie; 'Florida 127', 'Florida Brilliance', 'Florida Ember')
Periodically scout fields, especially during warm and wet weather, for early detection
Remove and destroy (bury or burn) infected plants and surrounding plants (5 to 10 foot radius)
Keep foliage dry and reduce water splash using drip irrigation; avoid excess overhead irrigation and do not over water or over fertilize
Use calcium nitrate (nitrate) sources for nitrogen instead of ammonium
Practice field sanitation: pick the infested area last and avoid moving personnel/equipment from infested to clean areas; do not work plants when wet
Rotate out of strawberries for 2 or 3 years to reduce soil inoculum
Apply preventive/protectant fungicides (e.g. captan) at higher label rates during critical bloom periods; add curative products such as Switch and Miravis Prime when needed
Time fungicide applications using the Strawberry Advisory System (StAS) based on leaf wetness duration and temperature

Biologicals: Bacillus pumilus (Sonata), Bacillus subtilis (Serenade Max)
Narrow range oil (JMS Stylet Oil, Saf-T-Side, etc.)

canonical.summary: Infected plants become stunted, turn yellow, wilt, and may die; they show a characteristic rot of the crown and upper tap root, a soft mushy stem rot that turns dark brown at the base, and root rot with light-colored water-soaked areas that darken, often with white to pink fungal growth at the soil line.
diagnostic_features: A characteristic dark brown necrotic rot of the crown and upper tap root; infected plants break off easily at or just below the soil line; the root cortex sloughs off while the fibrous vascular tissue remains; and in hot, humid weather white to pink mycelial growth appears on the lower stem at the soil line.
treatments: Rotate out of squash and other cucurbits for 4 years (the fungus survives 2–3 years as chlamydospores).
Avoid fields with a history of severe Fusarium disease.
Use laboratory-tested pathogen-free seed.
Plant fungicide-treated seed to reduce disease introduced from infected seed; treat seed with Maxim 4FS (Group 12) at 0.08 to 0.16 fl oz/100 lb seed plus a dye.
Select fields with good water drainage and avoid over-irrigation.
Deficit irrigation (reducing water by no more than 40%) early in the season is associated with less disease incidence; do not limit water when fruit is setting.
Avoid injury of fruit during harvest, packing, and transport.
Actinovate AG at 3 to 12 oz/A as a soil drench at planting.
Bexfond at 7 to 28 fl oz/A.
Double Nickel LC at 1 to 2 quarts/A as a banded soil spray or drench on 4- to 6-week intervals or at 0.5 to 4.5 pints/A on 2- to 4-week intervals.
Rootshield WP at 3 to 8 oz/100 gal water for greenhouse soil drench and field chemigation or at 16 to 32 oz/A as an in-furrow spray.
Stargus at 3 to 4 quarts/A as a soil drench on 10- to 21-day intervals.

canonical.summary: Infected flower parts turn light brown and may develop areas of buff-color (M. fructicola) or gray (M. laxa) spores; blossoms and small twigs collapse, twigs develop elliptical cankers with profuse gumming, leaves on infected shoots turn brown and wither but remain attached, and fruit symptoms begin as small dark spots that enlarge rapidly.
diagnostic_features: Twigs develop elliptical cankers with profuse gumming at the margin between diseased and healthy tissue; beige/buff-color (M. fructicola) or gray (M. laxa) spore masses develop, sometimes in concentric rings, and infected fruit remains fairly firm and dry relative to a watery rot.
look_alikes: watery rot caused by Rhizopus sp.
treatments: Rely on good sanitation and proper timing of protectant fungicides.
Prune blighted (diseased) shoots back to healthy tissue during dry weather.
Remove and destroy infected twigs and branches in summer.
Shorten large trees and prune out shaded limbs in summer for a more open canopy that dries out quickly.
Remove and destroy all mummified fruit in and around the tree, and remove fallen fruit.
Control insects that could wound and injure fruit, and avoid wounding fruit during harvest.
Cool fruit rapidly after harvest; a short (2.5 min) soak in hot water (122°F) has reduced postharvest decay in nectarines and peaches.
Use moderate amounts of nitrogen fertilizer.
Start treatment at the popcorn stage of bloom and spray every 14 days until bloom is completed, shortening the interval to 10 days during continued heavy rainfall.
Apply fungicides during the bloom period at early popcorn, full bloom, and/or petal fall to control the blossom blight phase.
Alternate or tank-mix fungicides from different groups with different modes of action to reduce resistant fungal strains.
Ground sprays are generally more effective than aerial applications.

Fungicide active ingredients include azoxystrobin/difenoconazole, azoxystrobin/propiconazole, tebuconazole, propiconazole, fenbuconazole, myclobutanil, triflumizole, fenarimol, metconazole, iprodione, fenhexamid, thiophanate-methyl, pyraclostrobin/boscalid, captan, and chlorothalonil.
Biological control options: Botector, BotryStop, Howler Evo, Serenade OPTI, Serenade Garden Disease Control Concentrate.

canonical.summary: Infected flower parts turn light brown with buff-colored or gray spores; flowers collapse and adhere to twigs, twigs develop girdling lesions with profuse gumming, and fruit develops small dark spots that enlarge rapidly into a firm rot with masses of buff-colored spores and concentric rings of gray sporulation.
diagnostic_features: Fruit rot starts with a small, round brown spot which expands to eventually rot the entire fruit; infected fruit remains fairly firm and dry (relative to a watery Rhizopus rot), produces masses of buff-colored spores with concentric rings of gray sporulation, and turns into a mummy that stays attached to the tree.
look_alikes: watery rot caused by Rhizopus sp.
treatments: Remove and destroy infected twigs and branches in summer.
Remove and destroy all mummified fruit in and around the tree.
Removing fallen fruit (due to thinning or lack of pollination) can significantly reduce the amount of rot at harvest.
Control insects that could wound and injure fruit.
Avoid wounding fruit during harvest.
Cool fruit rapidly after harvest.
Use moderate amounts of nitrogen fertilizer.
A short (2.5 min) soak in hot water (122°F) has reduced postharvest decay in nectarines and peaches.
Apply fungicides during the blossoming period at early pink bud, full bloom, and/or petal fall to control the blossom blight phase.
Fruit rot sprays can be applied before harvest if wet weather is expected.
Tank-mix and/or alternate products with different modes of action to prevent the build-up of resistant fungi.
Biological control options: Botector, BotryStop, DoubleNickel 55, Howler Evo, Serenade OPTI, Serenade Garden Disease Control Concentrate.
During pruning in winter, remove all cankerous parts of the tree.
Spray during full bloom and two subsequent sprays at 10 to 14-day intervals to prevent infections of flowers and young fruit.
Begin spraying at 7-day intervals (typically three times until harvest) when the fruit turns color from green to yellow and red.
Select a fungicide containing captan that is labeled for use on peaches.
Hobbyist gardeners may use bags to protect the fruit from pests and diseases.

canonical.summary: Blighted flower buds, brown and undersized foliage, wilted shoot tips, and scattered twig and small branch dieback; blossoms and the associated shoots wilt and die, and gum exudes at the base of infected flowers. Fruit infection first appears as small water-soaked lesions that rapidly expand to consume the entire fruit, and discolored decay spots develop on fruit and nuts.
diagnostic_features: Cankers on blighted twigs have tan centers with dark margins, and during foggy, humid, or rainy weather gray to tan velvety spore masses form on diseased blossoms and twig cankers. Shoots killed by brown rot turn mostly brown to tan (versus black for bacterial blast, which produces no visible spores). Diseased shriveled fruit may be held in the canopy as mummies, and stem cankers are accompanied by copious gum production (gummosis).
look_alikes: Bacterial blast, blight, and canker caused by the Pseudomonas syringae bacterium
Citrus brown rot caused by Phytophthora species
treatments: Where available, choose plant varieties that are resistant to brown rot, and keep trees vigorous with appropriate cultural care.
Remove infected leaves, shoots and fruit to reduce inoculum within and around the tree; promptly remove and dispose of diseased shoots during dry weather.
Prune branches (and thin interior branches of young trees) during dry weather to maintain an open canopy for better air circulation and sunlight penetration, which promotes drying.
After working on an infected tree, clean tools and dip or spray them with a 10% bleach solution, 70% isopropyl rubbing alcohol, or a commercial disinfectant.
Use drip or furrow irrigation or low-angle sprinklers to avoid wetting blossoms, foliage, and fruit.
Avoid overfertilizing with nitrogen, and manage other diseases and pests that wound fruit or nuts.
Inspect green fruit at least weekly and remove affected fruit before spores form; cool fruit quickly after harvest and inspect during storage.
Chemical control is based on protection of flower parts; time applications to each cultivar's bloom stage, treating at pink bud (5-10% bloom) and full bloom.
One application at full bloom is sufficient in most orchards in most years with low rainfall; a second or third near full bloom may be needed in severe years or extended wet bloom.

Begin applications just before buds open (pink or white color) and repeat at regular intervals per label; e.g., myclobutanil or thiophanate-methyl at 20-40% bloom, with a second application at 80-100% bloom if high humidity or heavy rainfall follow.

Fungicides labeled for use against Monilinia include: calcium polysulfide, copper hydroxide, copper salts of fatty and rosin acids, fenarimol, iprodione, mancozeb, propiconazole, sulfur, thiophanate-methyl and ziram.

Registered products for almond include pyraclostrobin/fluxapyroxad (Merivon), propiconazole (Bumper, Tilt), fenbuconazole (Indar 2F), difenoconazole/cyprodinil (Inspire Super), difenoconazole (Inspire), fluopyram/trifloxystrobin (Luna Sensation), metconazole (Quash), fluopyram/tebuconazole (Luna Experience), azoxystrobin/propiconazole (Quilt Xcel), azoxystrobin/difenoconazole (Quadris Top), pyraclostrobin/boscalid (Pristine), iprodione (Rovral, Nevado) plus narrow range oil, pyrimethanil (Scala SC), thiophanate-methyl (Topsin M WSB), cyprodinil (Vangard WG), azoxystrobin (Abound), fenhexamid (Elevate 50 WDG), trifloxystrobin (Gem 500SC), myclobutanil (Laredo EW, Rally 40WSP), captan (various 50WP), and tebuconazole (Toledo, Tebucon).

canonical.summary: On tubers, soft rot first appears as small, tannish, water-soaked spots that rapidly enlarge into a soft, blister-like area that oozes a slimy or watery substance; the rot becomes brown to black after exposure to air and progresses to a chalky-white, foul-smelling mass. Foliage shows weak, chlorotic plants with upward-curled leaflet margins and mushy stem rot.
diagnostic_features: Infected tissues are sharply delineated from healthy tissue by dark brown or black margins; rotting tissue is usually odorless in early stages but develops a foul odor as secondary organisms invade. Stem lesions are light brown or colorless but not black, distinguishing it from blackleg.
treatments: Use high quality / pathogen-free seed and minimize bacterial contamination in seed lots.
Split applications of water-soluble calcium applied at 100 to 200 pounds per acre during bulking have been shown to reduce infection and severity of soft rot.
Delay harvest until the skin has set (tubers fully mature, lenticels closed) to reduce tuber injuries and entry points; leave a minimum of seven days after vines are totally dead.
Harvest mature tubers with low pulp temperature and well-set skins, and avoid mechanical injury/bruising.
Do not harvest when pulp temperatures are high.
Avoid excessive soil moisture before harvest to reduce lenticel infection; use clean water to wash potatoes; and avoid water films on tuber surfaces during storage.
Postharvest curing/suberization and proper storage temperatures are critical for wound healing and soft rot management.
Provide adequate air flow to promote drying, particularly when tubers first enter storage; ventilate continually if potatoes are wet.
Avoid packing and storing wet tubers; dry potatoes before shipping.
Eliminate soil before storage, isolate problem lots, and check pile temperature at regular intervals (use hot-spot fans if elevated).
Maintain chlorinated recirculated wash water at 50 to 200 ppm (variety dependent), especially when harvesting warm tubers directly from the field.
Sanitize and disinfest seed-handling equipment; crop rotation and avoiding over-irrigation reduce the disease.
FLUDIOXONIL/MANCOZEB (Maxim MZ) seed treatment.
BACILLUS SUBTILIS (Serenade ASO) in furrow; Serenade Opti at 14 to 20 oz/A on 7- to 10-day intervals.
Firewall at 100 ppm (soak cut seed pieces for several minutes); Bexfond at 7 to 14 fl oz/A; Double Nickel LC at 1 to 6 quarts/A; Ecoswing at 1.5 to 2 pints/A.

canonical.summary: At the field level, symptoms appear as circular clumps of yellowed plants a few to many feet in diameter; on individual plants leaf tissue becomes pale green, then tan to brown or yellow, and finally collapses, with lesions sometimes showing a violet-to-purple color. When leaves are wet or humidity is very high, fine, furry, grayish-white growths appear on the surface of older leaves, and systemically infected plants may be dwarfed, distorted, and pale green.
diagnostic_features: Signs of Peronospora destructor appear on older leaf surfaces as fine, furry, grayish-white (grayish violet) growths when leaves are wet or humidity is very high; spots enlarge and often girdle the leaves, and lesions may turn violet-to-purple.
treatments: Plant only pathogen-free transplants, sets, and seed (use disease-free bulbs, sets, and seed).
Practice a 3-year or longer crop rotation away from Allium crops in fields where the disease has occurred.
Avoid poorly drained soils and select fields that are well drained.
Plant in fields with good air movement and align rows with the prevailing winds; manage plant density/spacing and limit intercropping to reduce humidity.
Avoid overhead/sprinkler irrigation; use drip or sub-surface irrigation, or adjust irrigation to maximize leaf drying.
Change planting date to avoid a full canopy during conditions favorable for downy mildew.
Destroy onion plant refuse, cull piles, residue, volunteer plants, and eradicate wild Allium spp.
Avoid over-application of nitrogen, which promotes succulent leaves and disease.
Avoid entering fields when leaves are wet and avoid injuring the crop with herbicides and other materials.
Use resistant red onion cultivars (e.g., Calred) where available (resistance active in flower stalks, not leaves).
Spray at the first sign of disease and rotate fungicides among different mode-of-action groups; ensure thorough foliar coverage.
Use the DOWNCAST forecast program to optimize field scouting and spray timing.

Seed treatment with a metalaxyl/mefenoxam formulation; foliar fungicides including Actigard (P1), copper (M1), CAA-fungicides/Revus/Forum (40), chlorothalonil (M5: Bravo, Echo 720), mancozeb (M3), Ridomil Gold MZ/Bravo (mefenoxam mixes), Omega 500F/fluazinam (29), phosphonates (P7), Presidio (43), Regalia (P5), Milstop, strobilurins (11), Zampro (ametoctradin/dimethomorph), Orondis Ultra (oxathiapiprolin/mandipropamid), Reason 500 SC (fenamidone).
Biological control: Actinovate AG, Double Nickel LC, Sonata, Stargus.

canonical.summary: Dull to bright yellow spots form on cotyledons and leaves of all ages, later enlarging and becoming tan and dry, with purple downy fungal growth on the leaf underside; heavily infected leaves appear curled, distorted, and blighted.
diagnostic_features: Purplish-gray, fuzzy growth of the pathogen on the underside of leaves is diagnostic; on the top side, opposite the growth, leaf tissue is yellow (initially dull, becoming brighter and larger) and subsequently becomes dry and tan.
treatments: Use resistant cultivars/varieties — the most effective means of control
Minimize leaf wetness: irrigate early in the day so foliage dries before night; use drip irrigation where feasible; do not place row covers over wet plants
Rotate out of land where spinach was grown for at least 2-3 years (plant in soil out of spinach for several years)
Do not grow fall spinach crops in fields adjacent to spring crops or allow volunteer spinach to grow there
Treat seed for 25 min in water at 122°F
Incorporate residues and volunteer spinach into the soil after harvest to reduce overwintering inoculum
Promptly destroy the crop if symptoms continue despite management, or right after final harvest
Apply foliar fungicides preventively/early (protectants) before infection and symptom development, on a weekly/regular schedule
Acibenzolar-S-methyl / Actigard 50WG (Group P1) — induces host-resistance pathways
Mefenoxam / Ridomil Gold (EC/GR/Copper WP)
Fosetyl-Al / Aliette WDG (phosphonate, Group P7)
Fluopicolide / Presidio (Group 43), in combination with a different mode of action
Mandipropamid / Revus (CAA, Group 40)
Fenamidone / Reason 500SC (Group 11)
Phosphorous acid / phosphonate fungicides (ProPhyt, Fosphite)
QoI / strobilurin fungicides (Quadris, Reason, etc.; Group 11)
Cyazofamid / Ranman
Famoxadone + cymoxanil / Tanos
Merivon (fluxapyroxad + pyraclostrobin)
Orondis Ultra / Orondis Gold (Group 49, or 49+40)
Cymoxanil / Curzate 60 DF (Group 27), in combination with a protectant
Mancozeb formulations (Group M3) — seed crops only
MetaStar 2E AG (Group 4)
Copper hydroxide / copper products (Group M1) — not recommended as stand-alone
Potassium bicarbonate products (MilStop SP, Vacres)
Zampro (Group 40 + 45)
Regalia biofungicide (Group P5)
Trilogy (neem)
Biological controls: Actinovate AG, Double Nickel LC, LifeGard WG, Romeo, Sonata, Stargus, Oxidate, Zonix
Check REI and PHI when selecting conventional or organic fungicides
