canonical.summary: Purple to brown, sunken, dry lesions on tuber surfaces that extend inside (turning tissue brown and granular), and brown to gray water-soaked lesions on stems and leaves; leaf lesions begin on the edges, are circular with yellow to pale green borders and may be covered with white sporangia and mycelia on the underside.
diagnostic_features: A yellowish-green halo surrounds the lesions, with a ring or surface of white fungal-like growth (sporangia and mycelia) at the edge of the lesion on the underside of the leaf in cool, wet weather; sporangia are visible in the field with a 20X hand lens, and heavily infected fields have a distinct fetid odor of rapidly dying foliage.
treatments: Use pathogen-free / certified seed free of late blight
Plant early in the season to escape high disease pressure
Do not allow water to remain on leaves for long periods of time
Scout plants often and remove infected plants, infected tubers, volunteers and weeds
Clean tools and equipment after leaving a field
Sign up to receive alerts at the USAblight website
Keep tubers in storage dry and at low temperatures (38°F)
Plant tolerant / resistant varieties when possible
Protect the crop with fungicides; before disease occurs apply at 7-10 day intervals, after disease is detected apply at 5-7 day intervals
Alternate products and tank mix mancozeb or chlorothalonil to avoid generating fungicide-resistant strains
Organic growers: fixed copper formulations are the only OMRI-labeled active ingredients with decent efficacy
Home gardeners: products containing copper or chlorothalonil (e.g. 'Daconil') are the best and only effective products
Eliminate cull piles and volunteer potatoes
Add a seed treatment effective in reducing late blight
Control solanaceous / nightshade weeds
Apply fungicides based on a forecasting scheme
Use early vine killing under some conditions as a control measure
Allow a minimum of two (preferably three) weeks after vine kill before harvest
Minimize bruising and skinning during harvest to reduce tuber-to-tuber transmission

summary.quote: The pathogen causes purple to brown, sunken, dry lesions on the surface of tubers that extend into the tuber ( Figure 1 ). canonical.summary: Initial symptoms are light, roughly-circular, powdery-looking patches (a light-green circular lesion) on young leaves, followed by a subtle white cotton-like growth; severe infection causes leaf curling, puckering, twisting and/or blistering, and circular slightly depressed areas develop on the fruit surface, which becomes covered with white fungal growth.
diagnostic_features: White cotton-like mycelial growth covering the leaf or fruit surface, with small black bodies (chasmothecia/cleistothecia) forming within the white area as leaves age; the disease often initiates on the undersides (abaxial) of leaves and early fruit infections begin where the stem connects to the fruit (the 'bowl' / stem cavity) and radiate outward.
treatments: Manage irrigation: a two-week delay in irrigation delayed disease initiation two weeks with no negative impact on fruit; use irrigation that does not wet leaves/fruit and keep irrigation sets as short as possible.
Prune to promote air flow and leaf drying, reducing humid conditions favorable for disease.
Remove and destroy root sucker shoots to eliminate a source of canopy and fruit infection.
Moderate shoot growth through judicious nitrogen management.
Maintain a consistent fungicide program from shuck fall through harvest, applied protectively rather than reactively.
Rotate/alternate or tank-mix products from different modes of action (MOA); limit applications from any particular group to two or fewer per year.

Apply medium-risk compounds no more than three times per season and no more than twice in sequence; alternate high-risk compounds and limit them to no more than 30% of total sprays; tank-mix with sulfur or other low-risk compounds to limit resistance risk.
Consider post-harvest preventative measures such as sulfur or oil applications, which restrict chasmothecia development and obstruct the fungus from overwintering.
Biological control from shuck fall through harvest at 7- to 10-day intervals.

canonical.summary: White, powdery fungal growth develops on both leaf surfaces, petioles, and stems, usually first appearing on crown leaves, shaded lower leaves, and leaf undersurfaces, with yellow spots forming on upper leaf surfaces opposite the colonies; on watermelon, initial symptoms may appear as a reddish-brown, bronzed appearance on older leaves, and fruit can exhibit white powdery patches on the rind.
diagnostic_features: White, powdery fungal growth (asexual conidia) on both leaf surfaces, petioles, and stems, with yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces opposite the colonies; older plants affected first; dark brown chasmothecia about 0.003 inches in diameter develop late in the season.
treatments: Plant resistant varieties (select varieties with resistance from both parents/homozygous resistance when possible)
Choose planting sites with good air movement and free of shade; ensure adequate plant spacing
Separate successive cucurbit plantings physically (plant up-wind of older plantings) to prevent older plants from serving as an inoculum source
Remove debris, weeds (including citron watermelon), and volunteer plants that may harbor the pathogen
Scout fields routinely (particularly lower leaf surfaces) beginning at the start of crop development; early detection is key
Begin preventative fungicide applications when crops start producing fruit, when first female flowers open, or when powdery mildew is reported in the area
Apply fungicides on a 7 to 10-day interval before disease appears; initiate weekly spray program when symptoms are found
Apply fungicides before the epidemic reaches 10 to 25% severity for best efficacy
Alternate products with different modes of action / FRAC codes to avoid fungicide-resistant strains; apply mobile/systemic fungicides together with a protectant contact fungicide (tank mix)
Use translaminar or systemic fungicides that move to the lower leaf surface
DMI fungicides (FRAC Code 3): Proline, Procure, Luna Experience, Rhyme, Aprovia Top, Inspire Super, Mettle, Rally (Myclobutanil)
Carboxamide / SDHI fungicides (FRAC Code 7): Aprovia Top, Luna fungicides, Miravis Prime
Quinoxyfen (Quintec) and Cyflufenamid (Torino) — apply at most once based on resistance testing

canonical.summary: White, powdery fungal growth develops on both leaf surfaces, petioles, and stems, usually first on crown leaves, shaded lower leaves, and leaf undersurfaces. Yellow spots may form on upper leaf surfaces opposite the powdery mildew colonies, and infected leaves usually wither and die.
diagnostic_features: The first sign is pale yellow leaf spots, followed by white powdery spots on both upper and lower leaf surfaces (asexual conidia) that expand into large blotches covering the entire leaf, petiole and stem; yellow spots form on upper leaf surfaces opposite the colonies, older plants are affected first, and infected leaves wither and die.
treatments: Plant varieties with complete or partial resistance to powdery mildew; select varieties with resistance from both parents (homozygous resistance) when possible.
Provide good air movement around plants through proper spacing, staking of plants and weed control.
Apply fertilizer based on soil test results. Avoid over-applying nitrogen.
Remove debris, weeds, and volunteers that may harbor the pathogen.
Successive cucurbit plantings should be physically separated or at least planted up-wind of older plantings because older plants can serve as a source of conidia.

Monitor through IPM scouting: once a week examine five mature leaves (repeat at 10 locations in large plantings); the action threshold for starting applications is one leaf with symptoms out of 50 older leaves examined.
Initiate a weekly spray program when symptoms are first found; apply fungicides every 7 to 10 days beginning early in disease development.
Alternate among targeted, mobile fungicides and apply them with a protectant (tank mix) using highest labeled rates to manage resistance development.
Apply fungicide to the undersurface of leaves and to leaves low in the canopy using mobile fungicides, because the fungus develops best on these surfaces.
Recommended protectant fungicides include chlorothalonil, sulfur, copper, mineral oil, and several biopesticides.

Fixed copper formulations are the only OMRI-labeled active ingredients with some efficacy for organic production; copper or chlorothalonil products are the best and only effective products available to home gardeners, who should also grow tolerant varieties.
Biopesticides approved for organic production contain natural ingredients such as botanical oils, bicarbonates, hydrogen dioxide, and microbes.

canonical.summary: Downy mildew causes angular, yellow to brown lesions on the upper leaf surface that are restricted by leaf veins; lesions may remain yellow or turn brown and can expand to cover and kill much of the leaf. Under favorable, moist conditions the underside of the leaf below the lesions may be covered in dark gray- to purple-colored 'down' (masses of sporangia).
diagnostic_features: Angular, yellow to brown lesions on the topside of leaves bound/restricted by leaf veins, with dark downy spore (sporangia) growth on the leaf underside; in watermelon and cantaloupe lesions are not always angular, but spores on the underside provide evidence of the pathogen.
look_alikes: Alternaria leaf blight, caused by Alternaria cucumerina
Angular leaf spot, caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans
Powdery mildew, caused by Podosphaera xanthii or Erysiphe cichoracearum
Phytophthora leaf blight, caused by Phytophthora capsici
treatments: Plant early in the season to escape high disease pressure

Plant tolerant/resistant cultivars when possible (e.g., Citadel and Peacemaker pickling cucumbers; SV3462CS and SV4142CL slicing cucumbers; cucumber varieties Calypso, Dasher II, General Lee, and Thunder recommended in Mississippi)

Use cultural practices that promote air flow and reduce leaf wetness (increase plant spacing, grow on a trellis, avoid overhead irrigation; reduce humidity in protected structures); do not allow water to remain on leaves for long periods
Scout plants often and remove infected plants
Sign up for and monitor the Cucurbit Downy Mildew IPM Pipe (ipmPIPE) website for outbreaks and report any outbreaks to alert others

Protect the crop with fungicides, applied before disease develops; before disease appears apply at 7-day intervals for cucumbers and 10-day intervals for other cucurbits, and after detection at 5-day intervals for cucumbers and 7-day intervals for other cucurbits
Use protectant fungicides such as chlorothalonil and mancozeb before onset; once disease develops incorporate systemic fungicides into the spray program
Practice resistance management by alternating fungicides based on FRAC codes and tank-mixing a systemic fungicide with a protectant or a different mode of action (different FRAC group)
For organic growers, fixed copper / OMRI-listed formulations (coppers, neem oil, peroxides, biologicals) are the labeled options with some efficacy
For home gardeners, use products containing copper or chlorothalonil (e.g., 'Daconil')

summary.quote: Downy mildew causes angular, yellow to brown lesions on top of the leaves that are restricted by leaf veins ( Figure 1 ). When conditions are favorable, for example early in the morning when moisture is higher, lesions observed on the underside of the leaf may be covered in dark "down" ( Figure 2 ). This downy growth is masses of pathogen spores called sporangia, which can be seen in the field with a 20X hand lens.

diagnostic_features.value: Angular, yellow to brown lesions on the topside of leaves bound/restricted by leaf veins, with dark downy spore (sporangia) growth on the leaf underside; in watermelon and cantaloupe lesions are not always angular, but spores on the underside provide evidence of the pathogen.
diagnostic_features.quote: Downy mildew causes angular, yellow to brown lesions on top of the leaves that are restricted by leaf veins ( Figure 1 ). ... Identification of downy mildew can be more difficult in watermelon and cantaloupe than in cucumber since lesions do not always have the characteristic angular shape, but spores on the underside of the leaf can provide additional evidence of the pathogen.

Sulfur

canonical.summary: Small orange to yellow raised spots (spermagonia) develop on the upper leaf surface in spring, surrounded by larger yellowish orange pustules (aecia) near the ground; orange to yellow pustules (uredinia) appear on the leaf underside in June and July and later darken to black teliospores.
diagnostic_features: The appearance of aecia on the top of leaves early in the growing season generally distinguishes yellow rust from late leaf rust; season of appearance and which caneberry types are affected help distinguish the rust, though expert spore examination may be required.
treatments: Grow raspberries where they will receive full sun.
Plant them on a raised berm or mound of soil to improve air circulation around the plants.
Remove any wild caneberries near those grown for fruit because they can be alternative hosts from which the pathogen can spread.
Control weeds to improve air circulation and reduce humidity around plants.
Any method of pruning and trellising that improves air circulation around caneberries helps to reduce yellow rust.
The dry conditions in a macrotunnel (hoop house covered with clear plastic) greatly limit yellow rust if the tunnels are constructed before environmental conditions favor rust infections.
After harvest, cultivate to bury debris or dispose of it away from caneberries.
Remove fruiting canes after harvest.
Complete removal of floricanes and the first flush of primocane helps to control this disease because it removes most sources of pathogen inoculum
Stripping leaves from primocanes in the fall will also reduce overwintering inoculum.
spraying Bordeaux mixture or another copper fungicide may be warranted during the delayed dormant season, which is once buds appear and swell before they open
a fixed copper fungicide or myclobutanil can be sprayed during the first bloom

diagnostic_features: Rhizoctonia lesions/cankers are always dry and usually sunken, distinguishing them from the wet, slimy rot of blackleg; irregular black sclerotia (black scurf) form on the tuber surface and do not wash off ('the dirt that doesn't wash off').

treatments: Plant certified seed free of sclerotia; if more than 20 sclerotia are visible on one side of washed tubers, consider a different seed source
Treat seed pieces with fungicides before planting to reduce seed-borne inoculum
Avoid planting in cold, wet soil and favor rapid emergence by warming seed tubers before planting
Cover seed with as little soil as possible (no more than two inches / plant at a shallow depth) to speed emergence
Plant coarse-textured soils first because they warm faster and are less likely to become waterlogged

Harvest soon after vines are killed / when skin is set to minimize black scurf and bruising
Remove or burn vines to reduce overwintering fungus, and separate tubers from crop residues
Increase crop residue decomposition and soil organic matter; chisel plowing can reduce incidence and severity
Do not dump infested tubers on future potato fields; use disease-free soil and avoid fields with a history of the disease
Conduct a soil test prior to planting (low pH is less conducive to disease)
Plant less susceptible cultivars

canonical.summary: Distorted, reddened foliage appears in spring; new leaves and shoots thicken, pucker, and become distorted, turning yellowish then grayish white with velvety spores, and may later die and fall off (defoliation); infected fruit may have raised rough bumps or scabby red lesions.
diagnostic_features: Distorted, reddened foliage in spring that becomes thickened and puckered, turning yellowish then grayish white with a velvety/grayish powdery coating of spores on the leaf surface later in the season.
treatments: Plant resistant varieties (e.g., Frost, Indian Free, Muir, and Q-1-8) where possible.

Peach leaf curl can be controlled with a single fungicide spray, but timing is critical; fungicide application is most effective when the tree is dormant, in the fall after leaves fall or in the spring before buds swell.

Treat susceptible trees with a preventive fungicide every year after leaves fall but before new buds develop in spring; treat just after leaves have fallen, usually late November or December, with a possible second application in late winter before buds swell in high-rainfall areas or wet winters.
The least toxic yet effective fungicides for backyard trees are copper soap (copper octanoate) or copper ammonium (fixed copper); add 1% horticultural oil to increase effectiveness.
Registered fungicides include liquid lime-sulfur, chlorothalonil, and copper products; copper use can be alternated with chlorothalonil.
When spraying, thoroughly cover all branches and twigs until dripping to ensure all spores are killed.
Pruning in fall prior to applying fungicides can reduce overwintering spore numbers and reduce the amount of fungicide needed.
Fungicide applications may be avoided by following good Integrated Pest Management practices.

canonical.summary: Twig symptoms first appear as small, purplish black spots that turn brown as they enlarge, often with a light center and purplish brown margin, with tiny dark brown spore-forming bumps (sporodochia) at the center; affected buds turn dark brown or black and may be covered with exuded gum. Leaf and fruit lesions are small spots, purplish at first, turning light brown in the center, and leaf centers may drop out leaving a "shot hole."
diagnostic_features: Shot hole can be distinguished on peach by the presence of tan twig lesions with dark margins, usually accompanied by profuse gumming; sporodochia form in leaf lesions but not in fruit lesions, and leaf centers often fall out leaving the characteristic "shot hole."
treatments: Manage primarily with fungicide treatments to protect buds and twigs from infection
In orchards where twig infections are prevalent, improve the dormant treatment by pruning out and destroying infected wood
Remove and dispose of any infected buds, leaves, fruit and twigs
If sprinkler irrigated, angle sprinkler heads low enough to keep from wetting the canopy; avoid overhead watering
Bordeaux mixture and some copper formulations are acceptable in organically certified orchards; fixed copper or Bordeaux mixture can be applied in fall
In orchards with a history of the disease, spray at leaf fall or from November 15 to December 1 before winter rains to protect against twig infections
If needed, make a spring application during bloom to prevent fruit and leaf infection
Treat with a product used for both brown rot and shot hole control, such as pyraclostrobin/boscalid, chlorothalonil, or azoxystrobin

canonical.summary: Foliar lesions are small, circular to irregular dark brown to black spots on older lower leaves that enlarge and develop characteristic dark concentric rings alternating with light-tan bands (a target spot appearance); tubers show dark, sunken lesions with a raised dark brown border and dry, corky, dark brown underlying tissue.
diagnostic_features: Dark concentric, target-like rings alternating with bands of light-tan tissue, giving a distinctive target-board / target spot appearance; lesions often surrounded by yellow margins and restricted by leaf veins, giving an angular appearance; early foliar symptoms typically appear on the oldest (lower) leaves.
look_alikes: brown spot (caused by small-spore Alternaria species)
treatments: Rotate away from susceptible solanaceous / nonhost crops for at least three years (3-4 year rotation)
Select a late-season / later-maturing, longer-season cultivar (early-maturing cultivars are more susceptible)
Maintain proper plant nutrition; avoid nitrogen and phosphorus deficiency and maintain appropriate nitrogen fertilization
Time irrigation to minimize leaf wetness duration; avoid over-irrigating and allow leaves to dry before nightfall
Maintain proper spacing between plants to promote airflow
Maximize distance between susceptible fields
Destroy or deep-plow infested plant debris
Eradicate weed hosts such as hairy nightshade to reduce inoculum for future crops
Scout fields regularly (begin after plants reach 12 inches) to identify disease early before significant spread
Monitor physiological days (P-Days) with disease-modeling tools (UW VDIFN; NDAWN Potato Blight app)
Kill vines two to three weeks before harvest to allow adequate skin set
Avoid injury and skinning during harvest
Store tubers under wound-healing conditions (fresh air, 95-99% relative humidity, 55-60 F) for two to three weeks after harvest

Apply foliar fungicides as the primary control, beginning as soon as symptoms appear, with continued protection at 7- to 10-day intervals; fungicide application is justified only when disease is initiated early enough to cause economic loss
Rotate and combine fungicides with differing modes of action and include multisite (group M) fungicides; mancozeb and chlorothalonil are the most frequently used protectant (group M) fungicides

canonical.summary: The earliest symptoms are raised blisters 1–6 mm in diameter appearing on natural openings such as stomata and lenticels of young shoots or near wounds, each usually with a lenticel at its center; these develop into necrotic lesions, sunken lesions that release gum, and abundant gum exudates on stems and branches with limb dieback and cankers.
diagnostic_features: Large amounts of resinous gum exuded from infections at lenticels or entry wounds; raised blisters with a lenticel at their center caused by hyperplasia near lenticels; severely infected limbs have a very coarse periderm layer with a blackish color, whereas non-infected limbs have a generally smooth periderm of a grayish-silver color.
look_alikes: Gummosis from non-pathogenic (abiotic) causes such as physical or chemical injuries
Gumming from larval feeding of lesser peachtree borer (Synanthedon pictipes) and peach tree borer (Synanthedon exitiosa)
treatments: Maintaining tree health with good horticultural practices can help reduce losses due to fungal gummosis.
Monitor for symptoms routinely and manage the fertilization and irrigation system properly to reduce disease-promoting conditions.
Use good pruning practices to remove as much unproductive and diseased wood as possible during winter pruning.
Remove and destroy the pruned wood mechanically (e.g., with a flail mower) to speed decomposition and reduce spore production.
Avoid pruning immediately before or after a rain or irrigation event when the foliage is wet.
Avoid pruning water- and nutrient-stressed trees.
Prune areas of the orchard, specific trees, or varieties with fungal gummosis last.
Disinfect pruning tools periodically with rubbing alcohol, quaternary ammonium solution, or 10% bleach (sodium hypochlorite).
Promote air movement through the canopy by proper pruning and removing suckers from the base of the trunks.
Use peach varieties that are less vigorous and require less pruning.
Prune dead limbs and infected twigs only within a dry period, following with fungicide sprays to protect the fresh wounds.
Establish orchards away from low-lying areas with poor air circulation and soil drainage.
Consider altering irrigation equipment to prevent wetting the trunk during irrigation sets.
Prevent excessive weed growth around peach trunks to increase air movement around the trunk.
Keep trees healthy since the most severely infected trees are water-stressed.
Where gummosis is present, the use of captan or myclobutanil for scab control is the preferred treatment.

treatments.value: Maintaining tree health with good horticultural practices can help reduce losses due to fungal gummosis.; Monitor for symptoms routinely and manage the fertilization and irrigation system properly to reduce disease-promoting conditions.; Use good pruning practices to remove as much unproductive and diseased wood as possible during winter pruning.; Remove and destroy the pruned wood mechanically (e.g., with a flail mower) to speed decomposition and reduce spore production.; Avoid pruning immediately before or after a rain or irrigation event when the foliage is wet.; Avoid pruning water- and nutrient-stressed trees.; Prune areas of the orchard, specific trees, or varieties with fungal gummosis last.; Disinfect pruning tools periodically with rubbing alcohol, quaternary ammonium solution, or 10% bleach (sodium hypochlorite).; Promote air movement through the canopy by proper pruning and removing suckers from the base of the trunks.; Use peach varieties that are less vigorous and require less pruning.; Prune dead limbs and infected twigs only within a dry period, following with fungicide sprays to protect the fresh wounds.; Establish orchards away from low-lying areas with poor air circulation and soil drainage.; Consider altering irrigation equipment to prevent wetting the trunk during irrigation sets.; Prevent excessive weed growth around peach trunks to increase air movement around the trunk.; Keep trees healthy since the most severely infected trees are water-stressed.; Where gummosis is present, the use of captan or myclobutanil for scab control is the preferred treatment.
treatments.quote: Use good pruning practices to remove as much unproductive and diseased wood as possible during winter pruning. Remove and destroy the pruned wood mechanically with powered agricultural equipment, such as a flail mower, to speed decomposition and reduce spore production.

canonical.summary: Infected leaves develop black circular or irregularly shaped spots up to 1/2 inch in diameter with fringed borders, mostly on the upper leaf surface; leaf margins then yellow, the whole leaf yellows, and leaves drop, progressing up the stems until the plant is defoliated. Canes may develop lesions that appear purple at first then progress to black.
diagnostic_features: Lesions are roughly circular, up to 1/2 inch in diameter, dark brown to black, and often have feathery (fringed) margins; older lesions bear black spore-bearing structures (acervuli) producing two-celled conidia.
treatments: Plant black spot-resistant rose cultivars (e.g., HomeRun®, Knock Out®); resistance can be regionally variable.
Practice sanitation: rake and discard/burn fallen leaves and prune out infected canes to reduce inoculum and slow spring infections.
Promote good air circulation and rapid leaf drying by spacing plants far apart and growing in an open, sunny, high-light location.
Avoid wetting foliage: water at the base with a soaker or drip hose, minimize/avoid overhead irrigation, and restrict irrigation during cloudy, humid weather.
Prune diseased branches six to eight inches below obvious infections, only in dry weather.
Disinfest pruning tools between cuts for at least 30 seconds with 70% alcohol or a 10% bleach solution.

Apply labeled fungicide sprays every 7–14 days from bud break/leaf emergence through the fall; fungicides containing chlorothalonil, copper sulfate, and myclobutanil are highly effective, and neem oil is an organic option.
Spray before a rain event and alternate/rotate at least two active ingredients with different modes of action to manage resistance.
Add a spreader to sprays for better coverage given the waxy nature of rose leaves.

canonical.summary: Yellow foliage appears on one or more branches in the outer crown from late spring to midsummer, soon becoming wilted and brown ("flagging"), with yellowing and wilting progressing down the infected branch toward the trunk; fallen leaves may be strewn over the lawn in spring or summer.
diagnostic_features: Wilted and brown foliage on individual branches called "flagging," with brown discoloration/streaking of the sapwood visible when the bark is removed on recently wilted branches.
treatments: Manage by eliminating bark beetle breeding sites: promptly remove dead or dying elm wood with intact bark.
Remove DED-infected branches the same year infection starts, before the disease moves into the main stem, cutting at least 5 feet (preferably 10 feet) below the last sign of streaking in the sapwood.
Properly dispose of elm wood by burying, debarking, burning, or chipping.
Sever root grafts between infected and adjacent elms (e.g., with a vibratory plow or trenching to 3-4 feet deep) before removing the infected tree.
Take down trees with many infected branches.
Choose Dutch elm disease-resistant cultivars for new or replacement plantings.
Preventative fungicide injection treatments (e.g., thiabendazole, propiconazole) can protect highly valuable trees, but are expensive and regarded as a temporary measure.
Without community-wide sanitation, Dutch elm disease is almost impossible to control.

canonical.summary: Leaf symptoms appear as water-soaked spots on the lower surface with a zone of yellow-green tissue (halo) around infection points; severe infection causes generalized systemic chlorosis, and pods show red or brown water-soaked lesions.
diagnostic_features: A zone of yellow-green tissue (halo) around small infection foci, and generalized systemic chlorosis particularly pronounced at 64-73 F (favorable for phaseolotoxin production); mature pod lesions may remain green and exhibit crusty bacterial ooze.
treatments: Crop rotation and clean tillage (for example, plowing) help reduce the risk of disease by reducing the amount of inoculum in the immediate area.
Plant only certified, pathogen-free seed from reputable suppliers and produced in semiarid regions.
Do not enter fields to cultivate or handle plants wet with dew or rain.
Equipment should be sanitized by spraying with a disinfectant before moving from an infected to a blight-free field.
Sprays provide good control of bacterial brown spot and halo blight but only moderate control of common blight.

canonical.summary: White mold first appears as pale, often bleached, water-soaked (watery) rot lesions on stems, leaves, and pods; white threadlike, cottony mycelium is often visible on rotted tissue under moist conditions, after which affected tissue dries and bleaches to a pale tan, beige, or almost white color and black sclerotia develop.
diagnostic_features: The development of black, irregularly shaped (round to oblong) sclerotiaâ€”compact masses of myceliaâ€”within the white cottony fungal growth is the best diagnostic feature; sclerotia are white early in development and turn black when fully developed, formed on plant surfaces and inside pods or stems, while affected tissue dries quickly and bleaches to a pale tan, beige, or almost white color.
treatments: Rotate with non-host crops (small grains, corn, rye, wheat, grasses, cereals) for at least 2-3 years, and up to 3-8 years, to reduce soil inoculum and sclerotia populations.
Use wide row spacing (36 inches recommended) to increase air movement and promote drying of the soil and plant canopy.
Use management practices that reduce heavy canopies and increase air movement.
Avoid heavy applications of nitrogen / over-fertilization, which can produce excessive, dense, lush canopies.

Plant erect, upright, open-canopy (open-base) varieties that hold pods off the ground and do not produce excessive foliage near ground level; resistant bean varieties (including dry bean types) are available.
Orient bean rows in the direction of the prevailing winds to promote air drainage and drying of plant and soil surfaces.
Avoid planting the most susceptible crops in fields surrounded by dense woods that restrict air circulation.
Time irrigations to allow drying of the plant canopy before nightfall and avoid excessive irrigation after petal fall.
Plant garbanzo beans later (December through early February) rather than early (early November) to avoid heavy canopies that increase humidity.
Scout and inspect plants for symptoms beginning at emergence/bloom, keeping written notes and photographic records of occurrence and severity.
Practice good weed control, removing susceptible weeds (in particular ragweed) from the field.
Avoid wounds and remove affected plants.
Incorporate debris promptly after harvest and use deep plowing to bury sclerotia and reduce sclerotia production.
Field flooding during warm temperatures destroys sclerotia.
Use a timely harvest with rapid cooling and pod storage at 45Â°F to 50Â°F for effective postharvest control.

Apply foliar fungicides starting at early bloom (1% to 10% bloom) in fields with a history of white mold, obtaining thorough coverage with high water volume (50 gallons per acre minimum) and high pressure (100 to 200 psi).
Conventional fungicides in FRAC groups 1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 12 and 29 are labeled for white mold, in addition to contact fungicides copper and chlorothalonil.
BOSCALID (Endura) at 8 to 11 oz/A at the beginning of flowering and again at full bloom.
THIOPHANATE METHYL (Topsin M WSB at 1 to 1.5 lb/A; T-Methyl 4.5F AG / Topsin 4.5 FL at 30 to 40 fl oz/A).
Blocker 4F (Group 14) at 4 pints/A at planting and again on 2- to 3-week intervals when disease is severe.
Botran 75W (Group 14) at 2 2/3 lb/A on 7-day intervals.
Cannonball WG (Group 12) at 7 oz/A when 10% of plants have at least one open blossom.
Fontelis at 16 to 30 fl oz/A at the beginning of flowering and again at full bloom.
Luna Privilege at 6.84 fl oz/A on 14-day intervals.
Rovral 4 Flowable at 1.5 to 2 pints/A when 10% of plants have at least one open bloom.
Omega 500F (Group 29) at 0.5 to 0.85 pint/A when 10% to 30% of plants have at least one open blossom.
Switch 62.5WG (Group 12 + 9) at 11 to 14 oz/A.
Jet-Ag at 0.75 to 3.9 fl oz/5 gal water as a weekly preventative treatment.
Biological/soil treatments: Contans WG (a parasitic fungus that attacks sclerotia) at 1 to 4 lb/A as a preplant or postharvest treatment.
Regalia Biofungicide (Group P5) at 1 to 4 quarts/A on 7- to 10-day intervals.
Double Nickel LC at 1 to 6 quarts/A at planting and again at cultivation.
Serenade Opti at 14 to 20 oz/A on 7- to 10-day intervals.
Stargus at 2 to 4 quarts/A plus a nonionic surfactant on 7- to 10-day intervals.

canonical.summary: In peach and nectarine, symptoms include delays in leaf emergence, bud necrosis or doubling, leaf mottling and deformation, and fruit deformation; leaves show chlorotic patterns ranging from tiny spots and flecks to large blotches and are smaller, narrower and often asymmetrical, while fruits can be severely deformed with an irregular, bumpy surface. Blossoms show streaking and color break in spring, and limbs/shoots are slow to form and misshapen with short internodes.
diagnostic_features: Leaves show a variety of chlorotic patterns ranging from tiny spots and flecks to large blotches, are smaller, narrower, frequently deformed and asymmetrical; fruit surface can be irregular and bumpy with the suture area particularly affected; flower colour-breaking is observed especially in cultivars with large pink flowers. Chlorotic (mottled) leaf tissue may disappear once temperatures climb, with short internodes, lateral bud break and whorled terminal twigs.

Avoid injury to trees and provide good cultural care

canonical.summary: Symptoms begin as small yellow or white slightly raised spots on leaf surfaces that enlarge into reddish-brown pustules (uredinia) about 1/8 inch or smaller; pustules may be surrounded by a yellow border and release rusty spores, and severe infection causes leaves to curl, dry, turn brown, and drop prematurely.
diagnostic_features: Rust can be distinguished from other foliar diseases because the rust-colored spores will rub off, while with other foliar diseases, nothing rubs off.
treatments: Rotate bean with non-host crops / rotate away from any bean for two years to remove sources of inoculum.
Plow under or bury infected crop residues and bean debris right after harvest.
Eliminate volunteer bean plants.
Plant within recommended planting periods (e.g. May 15 to June 15) to reduce late-season exposure to the pathogen.
Select planting dates and schedule irrigation to avoid long periods of leaf wetness when temperatures are warm (e.g. avoid foliage staying wet at night for more than 10 hours).
Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available for many market classes including pinto, great northern, small white, red kidney, and black beans), recognizing many races of the fungus exist.
Avoid over-application of nitrogen and ensure adequate potassium fertilization.
Disinfect poles used in pole-bean production.
Scout fields frequently during late vegetative to early pod development for initial rust pustules.

Apply protectant and/or systemic fungicides such as Maneb/Manex (30-day phi), Endura, Headline, Priaxor, or Vertisan (21-day phi), Bravo/Terranil, Folicur or Quadris (14-day phi), Proline (7-day phi), or Fontelis (0-day phi); consult Cooperative Extension or the latest New England Vegetable Management Guide for current chemical recommendations.

canonical.summary: Early foliar symptoms are small, angular, light green, water-soaked or translucent spots that enlarge and merge, with centers becoming dry and brown surrounded by a narrow zone of yellow tissue; pods develop circular, slightly sunken, dark red-brown lesions.
diagnostic_features: Lesion centers become dry and brown, surrounded by a distinct, narrow zone of yellow tissue; in highly susceptible varieties leaves appear scorched, ragged, and torn; pod lesions are generally circular, slightly sunken, and dark red-brown.
treatments: Crop rotation and clean tillage (for example, plowing) help reduce the risk of disease by reducing the amount of inoculum in the immediate area.
Plant only certified, pathogen-free seed from reputable suppliers and produced in semiarid regions.
Do not enter fields to cultivate or handle plants wet with dew or rain.
Equipment should be sanitized by spraying with a disinfectant before moving from an infected to a blight-free field.
Sprays provide good control of bacterial brown spot and halo blight but only moderate control of common blight.

canonical.summary: Brown spots appear on leaves, which enlarge and coalesce causing leaves to drop, with concentric lines of darker and lighter brown; infected leaves range from tan to bronze, and black streaks or lesions occur on stems, leading to extensive defoliation and rapid total leaf loss within days.
diagnostic_features: Concentric lines of darker and lighter shades of brown develop on the leaf spots as they enlarge; dark brown to black sunken streaks or lesions occur on stems from top to soil line leading to branch dieback; root infection does not occur; and the most striking symptom is extensive defoliation with total leaf loss possible within days of symptom onset.
treatments: Remove and destroy any affected shrubs (roots and all), along with any fallen leaves or branches, by burning (where allowed), deep burying (at least two feet deep), or double bagging then landfilling; if confirmed, also remove symptomatic plants and those within 10 feet
DO NOT compost any parts of infected shrubs
Thoroughly decontaminate tools used in removal for at least 30 seconds in 70% alcohol or (as a last resort) 10% bleach
Plant only disease-free new boxwood and host plants purchased from reputable suppliers who have inspected for boxwood blight; buy plants free of leaf spots or stem lesions
Quarantine/isolate new boxwoods away from established plants for at least one month (several weeks) to observe for symptoms before planting
Choose boxwood blight resistant varieties where possible, and do not plant boxwoods where boxwood blight has been a problem in the past; replant removed areas with non-host plants
Space plants far enough apart that branches on adjacent shrubs do not overlap
Avoid overhead/sprinkler watering; use a soaker or drip hose
Avoid holiday decorations that contain boxwood whenever possible

Apply protective fungicides prior to symptom development, especially when conditions favor infection; active ingredients include chlorothalonil (alone or with thiophanate-methyl or tebuconazole), fludioxonil, metconazole, tebuconazole, and mancozeb, with thorough coverage sprayed until runoff
Treat every seven to 14 days throughout the growing season and alternate active ingredients to manage resistance
Routinely (e.g., weekly) check boxwood plants for boxwood blight

treatments.value: Rotate with nonsolanaceous crops (e.g., corn, beans, cover crop) at least every other year; 3-4 years recommended to reduce fungal buildup in soil; Use drip irrigation and avoid overhead/sprinkler irrigation, especially when fruit begin to ripen; Grow tomatoes in a covered structure; Avoid harvesting or pruning wet plants; Stake plants upright and mulch underneath to improve air circulation and minimize soil splash contact; Hot water seed treatment (122 °F for 25 minutes) to reduce early disease pressure; Apply fungicides according to a disease forecasting system; azoxystrobin plus difenoconazole (Quadris Top) Groups 11 & 3; chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stik) Group M05; mancozeb (Dithane F45) Group M03; polyoxin D zinc salt (OSO 5%SC OG / Veggie Turbo 5 SC OG) Group 19 — organic-approved; hydrogen dioxide plus peroxyacetic acid (Zerotol OG) Group NC — organic-approved; Resistant varieties: Chef's Choice FI (orange) and Chef's Choice (red); Fungicides labeled for black mold are effective against anthracnose fruit rot
treatments.quote: There are two slicer-type tomato varieties that are resistant to anthracnose: Chef's Choice FI (orange) and Chef's Choice (red). Cultural: Use drip irrigation and avoid overhead irrigation Grow tomatoes in a covered structure Avoid harvesting or pruning wet plants Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (e.g., corn, beans, or cover crop) for 3-4 years to reduce fungal buildup in soil Stake plants upright and mulch underneath to help improve air circulation and minimize soil splash contact Hot water seed treatment (122 °F for 25 minutes) can help reduce early disease pressure. Chemical: Apply fungicides according to a disease forecasting system. Here are some examples of fungicides you can use: azoxystrobin plus difenoconazole (Quadris Top) Groups 11 & 3, chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stik) Group M05, and mancozeb (Dithane F45), Group M03 . Additional fungicides labeled for organic production are polyoxin D zinc salt (OSO 5%SC OG , AKA Veggie Turbo 5 SC OG ) Group 19 and hydrogen dioxide plus peroxyacetic acid (Zerotol OG ) Group NC.

canonical.summary: A white, very thin, dry growth (mycelium) develops on the leaves; leaf surfaces can become completely covered with the thin mycelia of powdery mildew on both upper and lower surfaces.
diagnostic_features: The first symptom is often yellow patchy areas on a leaf that become necrotic, followed by a white, very thin, dry growth (mycelium) somewhat similar to a very dense covering of plant hair on the lower leaf surface directly below affected leaf spots; during late summer and early fall a peppered speckling (chasmothecia) may develop on the white to light gray growth.
treatments: Plant disease-resistant cultivars: C. florida cultivars Karen's Appalachian Blush, Jean's Appalachian Snow, Kay's Appalachian Mist, and Appalachian Joy; the C. kousa x florida hybrids 'Aurora', 'Constellation', 'Galaxy', 'Stardust', and 'Stellar Pink' are highly resistant
Improve air circulation to reduce relative humidity and accelerate drying of foliage; space plants well and plant in more exposed areas, avoiding heavily shaded areas
Irrigate with microjet sprinklers or soaker hoses to avoid wetting foliage
If practical, prune out and destroy infected tissue as it appears early in the year
In the fall, rake up and destroy fallen leaves

Use an active scouting program and begin fungicides at the first sign of disease (best used preventively, before symptoms develop), at 7-14 day intervals (shorter intervals when conditions favor disease)

canonical.summary: Infected shoots fail to flush new leaves in late winter or spring; leaves turn red then brown and finally tan or yellowish, bend upwards and lay close to their stems, and remain attached for a long time. Stems show discolored, sunken cankers, and in high humidity pinkish orange waxy fruiting structures (sporodochia) develop on discolored leaves and cankered stems.
diagnostic_features: During periods of high humidity (fog, overhead irrigation, or rain) the fungus develops pinkish orange fruiting structures (sporodochia) with a waxy surface on discolored leaves and cankered stems; the dead leaves remain attached for a prolonged period, and these spore masses distinguish Volutella blight from winter injury and boxwood blight.
treatments: Provide boxwoods with a good growing environment and appropriate cultural care; alleviate drought stress with adequate irrigation during the dry season
Avoid excess watering (soggy soil) and excess fertilization; provide proper nutrition based on soil test results
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip or flood irrigation and direct hand watering to the soil while keeping foliage dry
Thin plants (instead of shearing) and remove dense inner stems to improve air circulation and light penetration; do not overcrowd and establish new plants in well-drained soil

Prune out diseased and dead branches several inches below the transition zone, only when foliage is dry, using a sharp tool cutting just outside the branch collar; do not remove more than one-third of healthy branches in a single year
Sanitize pruning tools after each plant (10% bleach solution, 70% isopropyl alcohol, or a commercial disinfectant)
Shake plants periodically to knock down dead leaves lodged in branch crotches, and rake up and remove fallen/diseased leaves away from boxwoods to avoid spreading spores
Dig out and destroy severely infected plants

Preventively spray foliage and stems in late winter/early spring with Bordeaux mixture, another copper fungicide, chlorothalonil, or mancozeb (every 7 to 10 days until new growth is completed), with thorough coverage of the branches

canonical.summary: Circular, tan to gray lesions develop on the lower leaves and stems of the plant, typically small (<1/8 in), with a dark-brown perimeter and often a yellow halo; small dark pycnidia may appear in the center of the lesion. Disease begins on lower leaves and progresses upward.
diagnostic_features: Small (<1/8 in) circular tan-to-gray lesions with a dark-brown perimeter and yellow halo, containing small dark raised pycnidia in the center; on the underside of the leaves, spots may appear as a darker green or water-soaked color. Disease progresses from older (lower) growth to younger (upper) growth.
treatments: Rotate away from tomato (or susceptible solanaceous crops) for 1-2 or more years
Control presence of horsenettle and other host weeds
Remove crop debris from planting areas (particularly tomato crop debris); destroy infested plant debris
Reduce the amount of time plants are wet, when possible; avoid over-irrigating
Stake or trellis plants to improve air circulation and drying of leaves
Use mulches or plastic to reduce contact between leaves and soil; mulch the garden to prevent watersplash
Avoid working in fields when leaves are wet
Scout plants often and remove infected plants/leaves
Clean tools and equipment after leaving a field; disinfect stakes and cages
Maintain proper spacing between plants
Plant resistant varieties
Remove 'suckers' or lowest lateral tomato plant growth
Use raised beds and rotate which bed has tomatoes from year to year

Organic fungicides: fixed copper, potassium bicarbonate (Carb-O-Nator)

treatments.value: Rotate away from tomato (or susceptible solanaceous crops) for 1-2 or more years; Control presence of horsenettle and other host weeds; Remove crop debris from planting areas (particularly tomato crop debris); destroy infested plant debris; Reduce the amount of time plants are wet, when possible; avoid over-irrigating; Stake or trellis plants to improve air circulation and drying of leaves; Use mulches or plastic to reduce contact between leaves and soil; mulch the garden to prevent watersplash; Avoid working in fields when leaves are wet; Scout plants often and remove infected plants/leaves; Clean tools and equipment after leaving a field; disinfect stakes and cages; Maintain proper spacing between plants; Plant resistant varieties; Remove 'suckers' or lowest lateral tomato plant growth; Use raised beds and rotate which bed has tomatoes from year to year; Conventional fungicides applied preventively: azoxystrobin (Quadris), chlorothalonil (Bravo), chlorothalonil + cymoxanil (Ariston), difenoconazole + cyprodinil (Inspire Super), penthiopyrad (Fontelis), famoxadone + cymoxanil (Tanos), fluopyram + trifloxystrobin (Luna Sensation), fluxapyroxad + pyraclostrobin (Priaxor), fixed copper (Kocide), mancozeb (Penncozeb), mancozeb + fixed copper (ManKocide), mancozeb + zoxamide (Gavel), mandipropamid + difenoconazole (Revus Top), zinc dimethyldithiocarbamate (Ziram); Organic fungicides: fixed copper, potassium bicarbonate (Carb-O-Nator); Preventative applications of fungicides containing copper or chlorothalonil are useful in areas with chronic Septoria lycopersici infections; they only provide preventative protection and must be applied before disease occurs

canonical.summary: Lesions appear on leaves and fruit as light green circular spots that become olive green and velvety, later darkening and becoming scabby; severe infection causes leaf curling, puckering, and premature drop, and deformed cracked fruit.
diagnostic_features: Small, velvety, olive green lesions with unclear margins on the lower leaf surface that age into darker spots with more distinct margins; lesions may appear more numerous closer to the mid-vein of the leaf; on some crabapples, infections may be reddish in color.
treatments: Plant resistant or scab-immune apple varieties (e.g., Redfree, Prima, Liberty, Freedom, Jonafree, Macfree, Sir Prize, William's Pride, Enterprise, Gold Rush, Pristine) as the ideal method for managing scab.
Rake and destroy fallen leaves below apple and crabapple trees in the fall (or chop leaves with a mulching/flail mower).
Couple leaf chopping with two or three applications of 5 percent urea to fall foliage to speed leaf decomposition.
For new plantings, select a site with at least eight hours of direct sun and space trees so air moves easily through the canopies and orchard.
Prune trees yearly to open the canopy, increase air movement and sunlight penetration, and promote leaf drying.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
Where resistance is absent, apply protectant fungicides starting at green tip (first susceptible tissue) and continue on a 7- to 10-day schedule through petal fall and fruit development.
Use curative-action fungicides when a weather monitoring system identifies that an infection period has occurred.
Apply cover sprays during the summer only if primary-season scab control was inadequate.
Organic and backyard growers can use biocontrol products to suppress disease development, combined with resistant varieties for maximum control.

canonical.summary: Early symptoms are water-soaked lesions on leaves that quickly change from green to dark brown and enlarge into spots up to 1/4 inch in diameter with slightly raised margins; in less humid weather spots dry and the damaged tissue falls off, giving a tattered appearance. On tomato, leaf lesions are initially circular and water-soaked, sometimes surrounded by a faint yellow halo, and rarely exceed 3 mm. Fruit develops raised, scab-like spots.
diagnostic_features: When Xanthomonas is present, bacteria ooze (bacterial streaming) from infected tissue and can be observed under a light microscope; bacterial streaming is absent from lesions caused by fungal pathogens. Leaf spots have irregular, somewhat angular margins; fruit shows raised, scab-like spots.
treatments: Use pathogen-free certified seeds and disease-free transplants; inspect and reject infected transplants (including your own)
Use resistant varieties
Seed treatment: wash 40 minutes in diluted Clorox (two parts Clorox to eight parts water), hot-water soak 30 minutes at 125 F/51 C, or treat with dilute bleach, hydrochloric acid, or hot water
Remove and destroy symptomatic transplants (or treat with streptomycin only at the very early stage); in the greenhouse discard trays adjacent to an outbreak
Minimize overwatering and handling of wet seedlings; wash and sanitize trays, benches, tools, and greenhouse structures between crops
Crop rotation to a non-solanaceous crop (at least a three-year rotation); avoid fields planted with pepper or tomato within one year, especially with a prior bacterial spot history
Eliminate solanaceous weeds (nightshade, horsenettle, jimsonweed) in and around production areas; keep cull piles away from field operations
Do not spray, tie, harvest, or handle wet plants; replace overhead irrigation with drip irrigation

Preventative copper sprays, optionally combined with a plant resistance inducer (Regalia or Actigard); Mancozeb + copper hydroxide (ManKocide); streptomycin sulfate (Agri-mycin 17, Harbour); bacteriophage (AgriPhage); acibenzolar-S-methyl (Actigard 50WG)

Biological/organic products: Serenade, Sonata, Serifel (Bacillus amyloliquefaciens MBI 600), LifeGard (Bacillus mycoides isolate J); organic growers should use copper + Regalia instead of copper + Actigard
Use an integrated strategy — all products work best applied preventatively; there are no curative products

canonical.summary: Water-soaked, oily areas with yellow halos on cotyledons that become dark angular necrotic patches; small dark angled lesions on mature leaves; and a dark green stain or blotch on the upper surface of developing fruit that rapidly expands to cover the entire fruit and causes rind rupture.
diagnostic_features: The diagnostic symptom of BFB is a dark green stain or blotch on the upper surface of the developing fruit that may be 0.5 inch in diameter at first but will rapidly expand to cover the entire fruit surface within a week.
look_alikes: other less harmful bacteria that can produce identical symptoms on seedling plants
treatments: Practice good greenhouse sanitation: Use a 10 percent bleach solution or Physan 20 to dip all tools, recycled planting trays, and containers for at least 10 minutes.
Spray benches and the interior with the same solution.
Remove any weeds growing in the greenhouse.
Water plants evenly in early morning or by afternoon.
Bottom watering of transplants will help control BFB.
Purchase watermelon seed that has been tested negative for bacterial fruit blotch in a seedling grow-out test.
Monitor transplants for symptoms.
Try to segregate triploid seedless varieties and seed lots from diploid seeded varieties in the greenhouse.
Reduce physical contact with the seedlings.
If suspicious symptoms are observed, remove infected plants and have them diagnosed immediately for bacterial fruit blotch.
If transplants are confirmed to have BFB, destroy all transplants from that seed lot.
A greenhouse with infected transplants can be decontaminated and planted the following season.
If infected plants or potentially infected plants have been transplanted in the field, begin copper spray applications to suppress BFB.
Copper hydroxide fungicides can be tank mixed with most fungicides used to control fungal diseases.
If symptoms are observed, copper hydroxide should be applied immediately after planting on a 7- to 10-day schedule.
If no symptoms are observed but BFB is suspected, copper hydroxide should be applied when the first male flowers appear.
Continue spray applications until all fruit have reached maturity.
Fields should not be cultivated or sprayed when the foliage is wet.
If BFB has occurred, follow a strict three-year rotation, deep plow after harvest and control all volunteer melons and cucurbit weeds.

canonical.summary: Dark-colored, irregularly-shaped, angular spots or blotches occur primarily along the midrib, primary veins and leaf margins; lesions may enlarge and coalesce, killing large areas of leaves, and in severe cases defoliation and twig dieback can occur.
diagnostic_features: Lesions on Norway maple tend to be narrow, purplish-black streaks along leaf veins; on sugar maple, large brown blotches along primary veins; on Japanese maple, tan or black lesions along primary veins and leaf margins. The fungus can be distinguished microscopically by one-celled, colorless conidia in groups of four to eight on the tips of short, broad conidiophores.
look_alikes: leaf scorch caused by drought and heat injury
treatments: Rake/remove and destroy fallen infected leaves (primary inoculum source) to reduce the pathogen and prevent overwintering
Avoid overhead irrigation and splashing water to reduce free moisture on foliage and limit spread
If disease is severe, prune out infected shoots
Maintain tree vigor through adequate fertilization, watering during drought, mulching and pruning
Apply lime if soil pH is too low

Apply labeled fungicides to protect susceptible/nursery trees (e.g. copper hydroxide + mancozeb, thiabendazole, mancozeb, propiconazole), with the first application at or just before bud break and continued through spring

canonical.summary: Early leaf spots are tan colored and expand to 1-3mm in diameter; adjacent spots may coalesce into irregular lesions, and velvety dark green-brown sporulation develops within the lesions as the disease progresses, killing older infected leaves in severe cases.
diagnostic_features: The presence of dark green sporulation in the centers of the spots distinguishes it from anthracnose and Stemphylium leaf spot, both of which also form circular lesions.
treatments: Fungicides can be used to manage Cladosporium leaf spot in conventional spinach crops.

Use seed that has been tested for Cladosporium and treat seed by hot water treatment or chlorine/bleach (soak seed 10 minutes in a 1.2% sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) solution) to eliminate the pathogen from seed.
Till under crop residues promptly after harvest to speed decomposition, and use crop rotation since Cladosporium survives in crop residue.
Avoid overhead irrigation (it may increase disease severity); use drip irrigation or overhead irrigate early on sunny days so foliage dries quickly.
Control weeds within the crop and around the outside edges of high tunnels to increase air flow and eliminate possible weed hosts.
Copper products are effective protectant sprays; apply at 10-14 day intervals, using a suitable agricultural spray oil with some copper formulations.

QoI fungicides / strobilurins (FRAC Group 11) such as Quadris, Reason, and Cabrio, and combination products including Merivon (groups 7 & 11) and Tanos (groups 27 & 11) effectively control the disease.
Add a Bacillus subtilis (e.g. Serenade) or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens (e.g. Double Nickel, Stargus, Taegro, Triathlon) product to copper for a synergistic effect.
Hydrogen dioxide products (e.g. OxiDate) will kill spores on contact.
The Northeast Vegetable Guide lists Lifegard applied at first true leaf stage or after thinning.

canonical.summary: Diseased blossoms become water-soaked, wilt and turn brown; blighted twigs bend at the growing point resembling a shepherd's crook; cankers form on bark with reddish brown sapwood beneath; fruit turn brown to black with bacterial ooze. Scorched appearance of leaves, blossoms, and young terminal shoots, with infected tissue turning black on pear and brown on apple.
diagnostic_features: Blighted shoots wilt and the twigs bend at the growing point and resemble a shepherd's crook or an upside down "J"; during warm and humid weather infected shoots ooze droplets of creamy white to amber bacterial ooze; sapwood beneath a canker has a reddish brown appearance; infected tissue turns black on pear and brown on apple.
treatments: Select and plant resistant varieties
Prune out fire blight cankers and blighted twigs (cut 8-12 inches below visible infection)
Minimize summer pruning of blighted shoots; avoid heavy pruning in early summer
Follow proper pruning and fertilization practices; avoid excessive nitrogen and late-season fertilization
Make an early season application of copper
Spray streptomycin at bloom
Apply the plant growth regulator Apogee (prohexadione-calcium)
Control sucking insects
Sanitize tools with 10% bleach solution (1 part bleach : 9 parts water) between cuts
Use biological control product Serenade Garden Defense (Bacillus subtilis) as an alternative to streptomycin
Use hands to break out small blighted twigs rather than pruners
Remove cankers, blighted tissue, suckers, and root sprouts during the dormant season
Eradicate nearby fire blight hosts such as pyracantha, hawthorn, cotoneaster, and crabapple
Avoid excessive irrigation and avoid wetting foliage with sprinkler irrigation
Protect open blossoms during high-risk warm/wet weather

canonical.summary: Characteristic foliar symptoms include chlorosis and necrosis between leaf veins, followed by leaf curling and leaf death; externally infected stems look healthy but split stems show internal browning of vascular tissue and pith, especially at nodes and in the lower stem.
diagnostic_features: When stems are split lengthwise, internal browning of vascular tissue and pith is evident, especially at nodes and in the lower stem (pith is white in healthy stems); pith color in the lower stem differentiates BSR from sudden death syndrome (SDS).
treatments: Use resistant soybean varieties (the most efficient way to manage BSR)
Crop rotation to non-host crops such as corn, small grains, and forage legumes will reduce pathogen levels
Many soybean varieties with PI 88788-derived SCN resistance also have BSR resistance, so SCN resistance may also help reduce BSR

canonical.summary: Pear scab first appears as small yellow or chlorotic spots, often on the undersides of leaves, with larger more obvious patches on fruit; lesions start as olive-colored circular spots that turn dark brown or black and become soft, and infected fruit often cracks open.
diagnostic_features: All lesions start as olive-colored circular spots that transition to dark brown as the infection progresses; on leaves lesions are more visible on the bottom of the leaf, shoot lesions are usually easily visible (and can be walled-off or sloughed off), and infected fruit often cracks open from the skin lesions.
treatments: Break up leaf and branch residues from previous seasons (mowing or other mechanical means) to reduce inoculum
Apply urea or other nitrogen-based fertilizer to leaves in late fall to break down leaves more quickly and reduce inoculum
Apply lime prior to leaf fall to reduce overwintering inoculum
Plant pear varieties with reduced susceptibility (Barnett Perry, Batjarka, Brandy, Erabasma)
Apply protective fungicides ahead of estimated rain events between delayed green tip and petal fall (Propiconazole, Myclobutanil, Tebuconazole)
Organic options: copper octanoate (copper soap), sulfur, Bordeaux mixtures, mineral oil or neem oil
Do not apply copper and Bordeaux after bloom (russeting risk); apply only between green tip and full bloom

canonical.summary: Fruit symptoms develop from the blossom end as a soft, wet rot; infected fruit are mushy, brown, and covered in fuzzy black growth, with profuse fuzzy growth under wet conditions eventually forming large masses of black spores that resemble a pincushion.
diagnostic_features: White, then purplish-black fluffy fungal growth covering the flowers and the soft, rotted blossom end; dark hairy rots on fruit, flowers and leaves that develop very quickly, with spores borne on long stalks giving the affected parts a hairy look. Usually the fruit nearest the soil is infected.
look_alikes: Rotting of small summer squash fruit as a result of poor pollination
treatments: Space plants far enough apart to provide air movement so fruit, leaves and flowers dry quickly after rain and dew.
Promptly remove and destroy infected/diseased fruit and plant material during the growing season to prevent spread.
Rotate crops so two or more years pass before planting any member of the squash family in the same location.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers where possible, and manage excess moisture (drainage, irrigation).

canonical.summary: Early yellowing/browning of leaf margins (chlorosis) with light- to dark-brown circular necrotic spots that progress from the margins toward the leaf center and appear on cotyledons; tan stem lesions near the crown that can girdle the plant, crack open, and exude gummy amber-to-red ooze; and fruit lesions that start water-soaked and turn brownish-black and leathery.
diagnostic_features: A gummy, amber-to-red exudate in the center of diseased spots and cracked stem lesions, together with black, raised, spore-producing fruiting bodies (pycnidia, perithecia/pseudothecia) on leaves, stems, and fruit; pycnidia swell and release tendrils of spores when wetted. Gumminess alone is not definitive because other causes can produce it.
treatments: Use pathogen-free seed purchased from reputable companies with a good history of GSB-free seed production; if saving seed, do not collect from infected plants.
Seed treatment if not previously treated — disinfectant solutions are more effective than dry-dust treatments.
Rotate out of cucurbits for at least 2 years (a two- to three-year rotation with non-hosts effectively reduces incidence).
Plant GSB/black-rot resistant varieties where available (e.g., watermelon, pumpkin, buttercup, and canary melons).
Regularly inspect/scout transplant seedlings in greenhouses; avoid using healthy-looking seedlings from trays containing infected plants.
Eradicate wild citrons, balsam pear, and volunteer cucurbits, which are alternate sources of inoculum, before planting.
Remove and destroy infected fruit and vines at the end of the season in small plots; in large fields, disk/deep-plow infected debris into the soil to speed decomposition.
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation when possible.
Use IPM to control cucumber beetles, other insect pests, and powdery mildew.

Apply fungicides preventatively and alternate chemistries to prevent resistance: Chlorothalonil (Group M5) and Mancozeb contact fungicides; Carboxamide (Group 7, no more than two sequential applications); DMI (Group 3, alternate/tank-mix with a non-Group 3); Strobilurin (Group 11, no more than one application before alternating). Copper products (Group M1) are not recommended as stand-alone materials.
Double Nickel LC at 1 to 6 quarts/A on 3- to 10-day intervals.
LifeGard WG at 1 to 4.5 oz/A on 7- to 14-day intervals for activating plant resistance.
Avoid wounding fruit during harvest; store only healthy fruit, cure squash 2 weeks at 75°F to 85°F, and store at 45°F–50°F (slightly below 50°F) to prevent postharvest black rot.
Commercial growers should refer to the Midwest Vegetable Production Guide for specific fungicide recommendations.

canonical.summary: Infection initially causes small, brown, irregularly shaped blotches in petals that enlarge rapidly until the entire flower is brown and dead, with blossoms dropping prematurely to the ground often as intact flowers.
diagnostic_features: Petal blight is most easily diagnosed by looking at the base of symptomatic flowers, where after removal of the calyx a ring of white or gray mycelium and a flattened dark sclerotium can be seen; infected veins may give petals a netted appearance and infected flowers retain their shape for many days after falling.
look_alikes: injury due to chemicals, rough handling, or wind
treatments: Prevention/sanitation is the best control: pull off and destroy infected flowers as they appear, and collect and dispose of fallen blossoms in a covered location away from camellias; do not compost, as sclerotia survive composting.
Rake and destroy old leaves, flowers, and debris beneath plants, including spent flowers in the canopy.
Remove the top layer of potting soil on new plants and replace with pathogen-free soil; import bare-root plants to avoid bringing in inoculum.
Remove the top 3-4 inches of soil / raked mulch from beneath plants to eliminate sclerotia in heavily infested soil.
Maintain a fresh 1-4 inch layer of pathogen-free organic mulch under plants during dormancy to suppress spore production; keep mulch thin near the trunk.
Plant camellias in a well-ventilated location, avoid overhead irrigation, and prune lower branches to increase air flow.
Plant autumn- or very early-flowering cultivars/species (e.g., Camellia sasanqua) to avoid the main spring spore crop; hybrids derived from C. lutchuensis are most resistant.

Apply an appropriate fungicide during bloom (soil drench in fall/early winter and/or protective sprays to open flowers when buds show color), reapplying at the labeled interval; e.g., Captan and mancozeb-based products, Terraclor, Ziram, Banner MAXX, Concert, Daconil, and similar labeled fungicides.
Use fungicides only in conjunction with recommended sanitation and cultural practices.

canonical.summary: The pathogen causes seedling damping-off, leaf spots, foliar blight, root and crown rot, stem lesions, and fruit rot; affected tissue initially appears water-soaked, turns brown, and collapses, and a white, yeast-like growth of sporangia often develops on affected fruit.
diagnostic_features: A white, yeast-like growth made up mostly of sporangia develops on affected tissue; seeing these sporangia is diagnostic for Phytophthora capsici.
treatments: Use long rotations between susceptible crops and select fields where Phytophthora blight has never occurred.
Select well-drained fields; minimize hardpans and plowpans by subsoiling or chisel plowing before planting, and use deep-zone reduced tillage.
Physically separate plantings of susceptible crops (cucurbits, pepper, eggplant, and tomato).
Grow a mustard biofumigant cover crop before a susceptible crop, preferably in spring rather than the previous fall.
Prepare raised dome-shaped beds for bush-type crops and cover raised and flat beds with plastic mulch.
Improve drainage by subsoiling between rows after planting and before vining, and seed driveways between vining crops like pumpkin.
Avoid over-irrigating; do not irrigate at night when temperatures are above 70F, and lay drip tape a few inches from crowns to avoid crown rot.
When growing small-fruited pumpkins, select varieties producing hard, gourd-like rinds (such as Lil' Ironsides).
Use targeted fungicides and biopesticides in a preventive spray program, and manage resistance by alternating/combining a diversity of FRAC-code chemistries.
Scout fields routinely for symptoms, especially after major rain storms.
Clean farm equipment, shoes, etc. of soil between fields.
Do not discard cull fruit in the field, and do not save seed from a field where Phytophthora blight occurred.

canonical.summary: Yellowing/chlorosis of leaf margins followed by light- to dark-brown necrotic spots on cotyledons and leaves; ovate stem and vine cankers near nodes that crack and exude a characteristic brown/amber gummy fluid; fruit lesions begin as water-soaked spots that develop into large brown to black depressed spots (black rot).
diagnostic_features: Black fungal fruiting bodies (pycnidia, perithecia, or pseudothecia) on infected leaves, stems, and fruits; pycnidia swell and release tendrils of spores when wetted; stem and vine lesions near nodes that exude a characteristic brown/amber gummy substance; raised, black, pimple-like spore-producing structures within the black areas of fruit rot.
treatments: Purchase seeds or seedlings free of pathogens from a reputable company with a good history of GSB-free seed production
Use treated seed; disinfectant solutions are more effective than dry-dust seed treatments
Plant resistant varieties where available (watermelon, pumpkin, buttercup, and canary melons have resistant cultivars)
Routinely inspect transplant seedlings in greenhouses and dispose of all seedlings near infected plants; do not use healthy-looking seedlings from trays containing infected plants
Rotate crops with non-host plants such as small grains or corn for at least 2-4 years, removing all volunteer cucurbits
Eradicate wild citrons, balsam pear, and other volunteer cucurbits/weeds before planting
Decaying crop debris should be disked and deep-plowed into the soil post-harvest to speed decomposition and reduce overwintering inoculum
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers; if watering by hand, water at the base of the stem
In small gardens, remove and destroy infected fruit and vines at the end of the season
Use integrated pest management to control cucumber beetles and other insect pests, as well as powdery mildew
Avoid wounding fruits during harvest, and store fruits at 45 F-50 F to prevent postharvest black rot
Apply fungicides preventatively; effective contact fungicides include chlorothalonil and mancozeb, and there are many effective systemic fungicides
Alternate fungicide chemistries during the spray program to prevent fungicide resistance

canonical.summary: Foliar symptoms include wilting and yellowing/chlorosis with an erect, upright posture, and systemic infection causes yellow vein banding that may turn necrotic; root symptoms include light brown discoloration of the central stele, stunted taproots with masses of secondary roots ('bearded' appearance), or a constricted 'wineglass' appearance.
diagnostic_features: Constricted taproot with proliferation of small feeder roots (bearding) after early infection, a "wineglass" shape with late infection, and necrosis of vascular elements in cross-section; the necrotic yellowing along leaf veins for which the virus was named is seldom seen in the field.
treatments: Use of resistant cultivars (most effective and least expensive/most cost-effective tool for managing this disease)
Planting early into cool soils
Avoiding overuse of irrigation / avoiding soil moisture wetter than -40 centibars
Crop rotation (minimum 3-4 year rotation)
Soil fumigation and/or solarization where allowed or cost-effective
Water management early in the season, including restraining from irrigation for up to six weeks after first germination, and managing water runoff
Roguing of infected plants based on surveillance, and isolating infected fields
Clean anything that moves soil (farm equipment, people, irrigation water, tare dirt, livestock) and clean footwear/machinery at the infected site; use disposable or rubber footwear
Plant varieties with multi-source rhizomania resistance adapted to the region to minimize increase in soil inoculum
Maintain good weed control in rotation crops
Prevent soil compaction and maintain good drainage

summary.quote: Foliar symptoms of rhizomania in the field consist of wilting (Figure 1) and varying degrees of yellowing or chlorosis with an erect, upright posture (Figure 2) . ... Systemic infection results in foliar symptoms consisting of yellow vein banding (Figure 3) which may later turn necrotic (Figure 4) . ... Classical root symptoms following early infection include small, severely stunted taproots with masses of secondary roots, giving the roots a “bearded” appearance (Figure 5) . ... Infections occurring later in the season often cause roots to be constricted, resulting in a wineglass appearance (Figure 6).

The necrotic yellowing along leaf veins, for which the virus was named, is seldom seen in the field.

summary.quote: Powdery mildew is characterized by a powdery white to gray fungal growth on leaves, stems and heads ( Fig. 1 ). The fluffy white pustules are first detected on the lowest leaves of plants in early- to mid-April. As the plant matures, the white powdery growth changes to a grey-brown color. The leaf tissue on the opposite side of the leaf from the white mold growth becomes yellow, later turning tan or brown.

Deep tillage to relieve initial inoculum pressure
Planting sugar beet far away from previously infested fields
Field monitoring and epidemic forecasting models
Protective and curative fungicides such as dithiocarbamates, benzimidazoles and amines
Alternation of different fungicides to avoid resistant strains
Mineral elements (e.g., CuSO4, S and H3BO3) sprayed mixed with fungicides
Biological control with Trichoderma strains
Inoculation with Bacillus, Emericella and Epicoccum strains
Biocontrol agents Paenibacillus and Pseudomonas
Resistant varieties / genetic resistance breeding
Integrated management combining resistant varieties and repeated fungicide treatments

canonical.summary: Yellowing of leaves and unthrifty growth, with affected bines wilting rapidly and suddenly (often at flowering or in hot weather); the bine base is typically swollen and may have a longitudinal split, and bines detach easily from the crown.
diagnostic_features: Swollen bine base with a narrow, tapered/rounded point of attachment to the crown (only a few central vascular elements connect bine to crown), bines that break off with a gentle tug, sometimes a longitudinal split in the cortical area, and an absence of vascular discoloration.
treatments: Avoid injury to hop plants.
Chemical pruning in the spring reduced canker disease severity compared to mechanical pruning, but no difference was detected in Oregon field studies.
Hilling up the plants enhances adventitious root growth above cankered bine portions, which can help maintain bine vigor and cone yield.
Reduce crown wetness by hilling higher relative to rill irrigation ditches, by removing sucker growth that could shade the crown, and by reducing mulch.
Lime to increase soil pH above 7.
Maintain the higher pH by using less ammonium-based nitrogen fertilizer; use nitrate-based fertilizer instead.
Mefenoxam applications are not an effective chemical treatment for Fusarium canker based on studies by OSU.
Asperello at 1.5 to 10.7 oz/A on 7- to 10-day intervals as a foliar spray or at 0.1 to 0.7 oz/100 gal water on 8- to 12-week intervals for chemigation at 2,000 to 5,000 gal/A.
Bio-Tam 2 at 2.5 to 3 lb/A as a banded ground spray or at 2.5 to 5 lb/A on 14- to 21-day intervals for chemigation.
Bexfond at 7 to 14 fl oz/A for soil applications via drenches, in-furrow applications, drip irrigation, or sprays, followed by irrigation, reapply on 4-week intervals.
Theia at 1 to 5 lb/A for soil applications via drenches, in-furrow applications, drip irrigation, or sprays, followed by irrigation.
