canonical.summary: Yellowish-green blotches appear near leaf tips on older leaves, enlarging and changing to shades of red to purple in oats, yellow to red in wheat, and bright yellow in barley, often with dwarfing and stunting.
diagnostic_features: Reddish-purple or yellowish discoloration of the flag leaf is the most characteristic symptom; symptoms appear patchy in a field due to aphid vector movement and are most apparent when days are cool and light intensity is high; does not produce a distinct mosaic pattern.
treatments: Plant BYDV-resistant or tolerant cultivars (resistance is more available in oats than in wheat and barley); grow diverse varieties.
Delay fall seeding of winter wheat until aphid populations decline; plant winter wheat after the Hessian fly-free date; plant spring oats as early as possible.
Control grassy weeds and volunteer cereals (wheat, barley, oats) within and near production fields to eliminate the green bridge for aphids.
Avoid planting small grains in midsummer as cover or companion crops in wheat-producing areas.
Seed treatments with imidacloprid (Gaucho) or thiamethoxam (Cruiser) can reduce fall aphid populations and primary infections.
Foliar contact or systemic insecticides may be used against aphids in the fall, though insecticide use is generally not economically beneficial due to sporadic aphid movement.
Maintain proper fertilization for good crop growth.

canonical.summary: On leaves, the disease first appears as small, tan to brown lens or diamond-shaped spots that develop into elliptical to elongate tan spots with a dark brown spot near the center and a yellow border; lesions coalesce into larger irregular dead areas and heavy infection can give the field an overall yellow cast.
diagnostic_features: Elliptical to elongate tan spots with a dark brown spot near the center surrounded by a yellow border; pseudothecia visible on stubble by mid-August feel like coarse sandpaper to the touch and are diagnostic of tan spot.
treatments: Three-year conservation tillage rotation system called ecofarming (ecofallow) can be used to reduce the threat of tan spot
In this system, corn or sorghum is seeded directly into winter wheat stubble in a winter wheat-grain sorghum or corn-fallow rotation
Crop rotation-fallow system effectively breaks disease cycles involving host-specific pathogens such as the tan spot fungus that survive in crop residue
Foliar fungicides can be applied to control tan spot if the disease becomes serious during the crucial post-boot stage of wheat development
Begin crop scouting early in the growing season and continue on a regular basis until disease is detected or a decision to spray is made based on the observed disease level

canonical.summary: Many tiny yellow spots appear on both upper and lower surfaces of current-season needles in late summer to autumn, most abundant near the needle apex; spots enlarge and darken over winter, and by spring coalesce into characteristic dark reddish-brown (deep red-brown, mottled) blotches, causing needle browning and premature defoliation, with diseased needles typically cast by late June.
diagnostic_features: Fruiting bodies (apothecia) appear on each side of the midrib on the needle's lower surface; the needle's epidermis lifts up as a patch and splits open, exposing an orange to orange-brown fungus structure. The disease often initiates and is most severe in the lower canopy, and diseased needles are typically cast (dropped) by late June.
treatments: Thoroughly scout trees for disease symptoms from autumn through early spring, prior to bud break
On small trees, prune and destroy diseased branches; prune out heavily infected shoots/branches from the lower canopy and remove severely infected trees to prevent spread
In Christmas tree plantations, remove and destroy any infected trees
Avoid overhead watering while new foliage is growing
Do not plant in areas with poor air drainage / low-lying areas; if the location is exposed to shade during the day, do not plant Douglas-fir
Space trees properly and prune the lowest canopy branches to promote air flow and good air circulation
Remove weeds around the base of trees, thin canopy, and avoid establishing ground cover plantings to reduce humidity and lingering moisture
Avoid using east-side and Rocky Mountain seed sources; in disease-prone or marginal sites use seed sources with partial resistance (among the most resistant: Shuswap and Pillar Lake)

Apply fungicides with thorough coverage of all needles; make first application when new growth is 1 to 2 inches long (or once 50% of buds have broken and new growth reaches 0.5 inch) and an additional application 3 weeks later â€” three applications are usually required for good control

Fungicides include: chlorothalonil, copper-based products (copper hydroxide, copper sulfate, copper salts of fatty and/or rosin acids), mancozeb-based products, thiophanate-methyl, azoxystrobin (Heritage/Quadris), and thiophanate-methyl + chlorothalonil mixtures (Spectro 90 WDG), Tourney EZ

canonical.summary: Browning, stunting, and twisting of new shoots and needles are the first symptoms, with a brown discoloration starting at the base of needles and growing toward the tip; needles die by the time they are one half to three fourths normal length. Resinous cankers may appear on stems and small black fruiting bodies form at the base of needles.
diagnostic_features: During the summer and fall, black fungal fruiting bodies called pycnidia appear at the base of the needles under the fascicle sheath; identification is only reliable when the characteristic pycnidia are recovered or via molecular methods.
look_alikes: diebacks caused by pine shoot moth
treatments: Remove all affected twigs and cones (sanitation), and remove dead twigs, branches, cones, litter, and dead trees; when possible burn infested material to keep the fungus from spreading

Apply fungicide sprays in conjunction with cultural controls at bud break — spray when buds begin to elongate/swell, again just before new needles emerge from the fascicle sheath (candles half elongated, needles ~2-5 cm), and again 10-14 days later; labeled products include chlorothalonil plus thiophanate-methyl, thiophanate-methyl, mancozeb, and copper hydroxide plus mancozeb
Select tree species adapted to site conditions and more drought-tolerant species (e.g., Pinus echinata, Pinus palustris) to reduce tree stress
Reduce stress by mulching (drip line to 3-4 inch depth) and watering as needed; keep weeds and grasses from competing with young trees

Avoid wounding trees, do not prune or shear in wet weather when spores are being released, and avoid activities that damage the root system (do not cut roots or drive heavy equipment within the drip line)
Do not plant susceptible trees near mature, infected pines and consider avoiding the most susceptible pines in landscape plantings
Manage fertilization: Illinois recommends fertilizing stunted trees to stimulate growth, while Alabama advises not fertilizing until a nutritional deficit is proven
Consider beneficial endophytes (yeasts, filamentous fungi, bacteria) as biocontrol agents against S. sapinea as a component of integrated pest management (IPM)

treatments.value: Remove all affected twigs and cones (sanitation), and remove dead twigs, branches, cones, litter, and dead trees; when possible burn infested material to keep the fungus from spreading; Apply fungicide sprays in conjunction with cultural controls at bud break — spray when buds begin to elongate/swell, again just before new needles emerge from the fascicle sheath (candles half elongated, needles ~2-5 cm), and again 10-14 days later; labeled products include chlorothalonil plus thiophanate-methyl, thiophanate-methyl, mancozeb, and copper hydroxide plus mancozeb; Select tree species adapted to site conditions and more drought-tolerant species (e.g., Pinus echinata, Pinus palustris) to reduce tree stress; Reduce stress by mulching (drip line to 3-4 inch depth) and watering as needed; keep weeds and grasses from competing with young trees; Avoid wounding trees, do not prune or shear in wet weather when spores are being released, and avoid activities that damage the root system (do not cut roots or drive heavy equipment within the drip line); Do not plant susceptible trees near mature, infected pines and consider avoiding the most susceptible pines in landscape plantings; Manage fertilization: Illinois recommends fertilizing stunted trees to stimulate growth, while Alabama advises not fertilizing until a nutritional deficit is proven; Consider beneficial endophytes (yeasts, filamentous fungi, bacteria) as biocontrol agents against S. sapinea as a component of integrated pest management (IPM)
treatments.quote: Cultural Techniques Select tree species that are adapted to site conditions to reduce tree stress. ... sanitation practices, such as removing dead twigs, branches, cones, litter, and dead trees, can slow the progression of the disease. When possible, consider burning infested material to keep the fungus from spreading. The application of fungicide treatments is effective for long-term disease management. ... Fungicide applications should be made at bud break when candles are half elongated and newly emerging needles are 2 to 5 centimeters long.

canonical.summary: Early season symptoms include seed rot and pre- and postemergence damping off. At seedling and later vegetative stages, infected stems appear bruised and soft with a dark chocolate-brown discoloration extending from below the soil line upward into lower parts of the plant, often reaching several nodes and girdling the stem; secondary roots rot, leaves turn yellow and wilt, plants may be stunted and chlorotic, and are often killed in patches or in sections of rows with wilted leaves typically staying attached after plant death.
diagnostic_features: A dark chocolate-brown lesion on the lower stem extending from below the soil line upward from the taproot, often reaching several nodes and girdling the stem; wilted leaves typically remain attached after plant death; plants killed in patches or sections of rows.
treatments: Plant resistant cultivars; widely effective Rps resistance genes include Rps 1c and 1k, with Rps 1a, Rps 3 and others also effective in some regions
Where Rps genes are overcome by local pathogen races, plant cultivars with high levels of field tolerance (partial resistance, polygenic)
Create field environment that reduces the likelihood of saturated soil by improving drainage where possible
Use seed treatments or soil-applied fungicides targeting oomycetes; mefenoxam (Apron XL) or metalaxyl (Apron) at the highest labeled rates are effective
Crop rotation and tillage may be of some benefit

treatments.value: Plant resistant cultivars; widely effective Rps resistance genes include Rps 1c and 1k, with Rps 1a, Rps 3 and others also effective in some regions; Where Rps genes are overcome by local pathogen races, plant cultivars with high levels of field tolerance (partial resistance, polygenic); Create field environment that reduces the likelihood of saturated soil by improving drainage where possible; Use seed treatments or soil-applied fungicides targeting oomycetes; mefenoxam (Apron XL) or metalaxyl (Apron) at the highest labeled rates are effective; Crop rotation and tillage may be of some benefit
treatments.quote: Try to create a field environment that reduces the likelihood of saturated soil by taking steps to increase drainage where possible. Treatment of seed with the highest labeled rates of fungicidal compounds such as mefenoxam (Apron XL®) or metalaxyl (Apron®) can be beneficial. In all areas where Phytophthora root and stem rot has been a problem, resistant cultivars should be planted. The most common resistance genes that are widely effective are Rps 1c and 1k. Rps1a can be effective, but is not as effective in many areas as the other genes. Rps 3 and other genes can also be effective. For areas where the Rps genes are not working well due to the presence of pathogen races that overcome the resistance, cultivars with high levels of field tolerance (or partial resistance) should be planted. Crop rotation and tillage may be of some benefit.

canonical.summary: Common rust produces rust-colored to dark brown, elongated pustules on both leaf surfaces; the pustules contain cinnamon brown rust spores (urediniospores) and darken as they age, with leaf chlorosis and death possible under severe conditions.
diagnostic_features: Brown pustules occur on both the top and bottom leaf surfaces, which differentiates common rust from Southern rust.
treatments: Plant resistant or moderately resistant corn hybrids/cultivars — the best and most cost-effective management practice; use moderately resistant cultivars for late-season plantings.
Apply fungicides, especially early when few pustules have appeared on the leaves; in sweet corn, fungicides are typically applied at V7-V8 and tassel.
Use fungicides containing strobilurins (FRAC Group 11) and demethylation inhibitors (FRAC Group 3) for adequate control.
For common rust, spray fungicide when 80% of observed leaves have one or more pustules.
Scout fields early and frequently when corn rust is found nearby to prepare for potential fungicide applications.
If irrigation is used, apply it at midday to minimize the time leaves are wet, reducing infection and disease spread.
Use crop rotation of at least three years between field or sweet corn crops (manages other foliar diseases, though it will not influence common rust severity).

canonical.summary: Initial gray to white lesions develop at the nodes (R3 to R6), rapidly progressing above and below the nodes and sometimes girdling the stem; white, fluffy mold soon covers the infected area, especially during periods of high relative humidity. Leaf tissue between major veins turns a gray-green cast and eventually leaves die and turn completely brown while remaining attached to the stem.
diagnostic_features: Fluffy white mold growth on stems with characteristic black sclerotia (hard, irregular, with a pink to white center, resembling rodent droppings) embedded in the mold on stem lesions and inside the stem; wilted dead leaves remain attached to stems; affected pods contain smaller, lighter, white, cottony seeds that may be replaced by sclerotia.
look_alikes: Bird's nest fungi (can be confused with white mold apothecia)
treatments: Select cultivars with high levels of partial resistance and an open canopy of upright leaves (no soybean variety is completely resistant)
Long-term crop rotation (2-3+ years) with non-host crops such as corn and wheat to minimize inoculum build-up; avoid rotation with beans, peas, sunflowers, and cole crops (Brassicaceae)
Tillage (moldboard plowing) to bury sclerotia at least 10 cm for fields with first occurrence; reduced tillage for fields with a long history of the disease
Reduce seeding rate and increase row spacing (e.g., 30-inch rows) to improve air circulation and avoid complete canopy closure
Where irrigation is used, reduce irrigation frequency during flowering
Weed control, as many broadleaf weeds are hosts of the pathogen

Foliar fungicides applied immediately before infection (timing is critical); boscalid has shown good efficacy; avoid thiophanate methyl and strobilurin fungicides such as pyraclostrobin; rotate active ingredients
Herbicides such as lactofen to modify soybean canopy, delay flowering, and induce systemic acquired resistance; some herbicides may also suppress the fungus or disrupt germination of sclerotia
Biological control with the fungus Coniothyrium minitans, incorporated to a depth of about 2 inches (5 cm)

Use Sclerotinia-free seed; clean seed lots with spiral separators and gravity tables; apply seed treatments with fungicides for infected seed; avoid harvesting heavily infested fields until end of season

affected_parts.quote: Lesions usually develop first at stem nodes during or after flowering. The lesions expand and the tops of the plants become grayish-green and then wilt and die. Infected stems often become soft and watery, and become covered with white moldy growth in moist conditions. Dry, dead stems can develop a bleached, white appearance. Hard, black sclerotia that look similar to rodent droppings develop on or inside infected stems and pods. ... Seed lots can be contaminated with sclerotia, and seeds can be infected with the pathogen.

canonical.summary: Causes leaf spots, blotches, marginal leaf blight, and total collapse of infected foliage, with tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) within necrotic tissue; when severe there can be significant foliar dieback and premature leaf shedding.

treatments: On evergreens like rhododendron and holly, prune out foliage damaged by winter injury by early spring to reduce opportunistic colonization
On deciduous hosts like hydrangea and witchhazel, prune out badly infected leaves from the canopy and remove all prematurely shed foliage during the early growing season
Pruning to improve air flow and reduce the volume of foliage in deep shade within the interior canopy can also help to reduce disease severity

The following fungicides may have some utility against Phyllosticta when applied early in the season as new leaves are developing: copper salts of fatty and/or rosin acids, copper hydroxide, mancozeb, metconazole and propiconazole
Avoid fungicide application during periods of bloom when pollinating insects may have contact

canonical.summary: Irregularly shaped, water-soaked leaf spots that appear angular because they are bounded by the leaf veins; bacteria may ooze from the spots in droplets that dry to a white residue, the area later turns gray and dies, and dead tissue often tears away leaving large irregular holes. Fruit lesions are smaller, circular, and superficial.
diagnostic_features: The spots expand until limited by larger veins, which gives them an angular appearance; under humid conditions the water-soaked spots are covered by a white exudate (bacterial ooze) that dries to a thin, white crust on or adjacent to the spot on the underleaf surface; as spots dry they tear away leaving large, irregular holes.
treatments: Plant certified, pathogen-free (clean, bacteria-free) seed; if saving seed, do not collect seed from infected plants.
Plant resistant/tolerant varieties (many resistant cucumber varieties are available).
Hot water seed treatment can remove some, but not all, bacteria (not fully effective alone).
Rotate out of cucurbits for 2 or more years (do not grow cucurbits in the same field more than once every three or four years) and avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers; if watering by hand, water at the base of the plant.
Do not cultivate, harvest, or work in plants when leaves are wet, and stay out of wet, infected fields.
Remove and destroy infected fruit and vines at the end of the season; in large fields till in or plow under infected debris to speed decomposition.
Apply copper-based bactericides early (e.g., fixed-copper products, Badge SC, Cueva, Kocide, Previsto) at first sign of disease; sprays are not effective once disease is severe.
Apply Actigard 50WG (Group P1) at 0.5 to 1 oz/A on 7-day intervals.
Tank-mix the recommended bactericide with effective fungicides to also protect against fungal diseases.

treatments: Rotate soybean with non-hosts such as wheat or corn

Foliar fungicide applications between R3 (beginning pod) and R5 (beginning seed) may reduce stem and seed infection, especially in seed production fields

canonical.summary: Irregularly shaped pale green to light yellow spots appear on upper leaf surfaces, enlarging into pale to bright yellow spots; older lesions turn brown with yellow-green margins and eventually become necrotic spots; fuzzy, gray tufts may be visible on the leaf underside.
diagnostic_features: Fuzzy, gray tufts (sporulation) growing from lesions on the leaf underside, particularly when humidity is high or leaves are wet (e.g., early in the morning); infected seeds may be smaller, dull white, with cracks in the seed coat, and the inside of the pod can be covered with a dried, whitish crusty fungal mass.
treatments: Plant resistant varieties — many sources of resistance are available
Crop rotation
Burial of infested crop residue to reduce pathogen levels
Typically no fungicide management is warranted; most foliar fungicides available for soybeans are not labeled for downy mildew and have very limited effect

canonical.summary: Round, tan lesions with dark purple to brown margins appear on leaves, bearing small black pycnidia; infected berries turn brown and soft then become hard, black, shriveled mummies dotted with pycnidia.
diagnostic_features: Tiny black dots (pycnidia) appear in the lesion, usually in a ring pattern near the border of the lesion; lesions on shoots, cluster stems, rachises and tendrils are oval, sunken and purple to black; infected berries shrivel into hard raisin-like mummies that remain attached to the cluster.
treatments: Sanitation is the most important element of management; remove infected canes, spurs, and fruit clusters remaining on the vines
Rake up and dispose of fallen leaves and mummies
Use mulch or cultivate beneath the vines prior to bud break to bury mummies and reduce initial inoculum
Drop mummies remaining in the canopy to the ground and bury them at the end of the season
Prune out diseased/infected canes and tendrils during the dormant season; remove leaf lesions and diseased fruit when first observed
Reduce humidity in the canopy by removing canes or leaves and managing weeds
Select a sunny planting site with good air movement and orient rows with the prevailing winds so plants dry quickly
Provide proper vine spacing, maintain an open canopy, and maintain good weed control
Plant resistant or less susceptible varieties, hybrids, and Vitis species
Apply protectant fungicides (sulfur/Bordeaux mix, copper, mancozeb, or ferbam) beginning shortly before bloom and repeat through approximately 4-6 weeks post bloom with thorough coverage
Use systemic fungicides (strobilurins, sterol inhibitors) for later infections and kickback activity, rotating among chemical classes
Time fungicides from early bloom through three to four weeks after bloom, targeting the pre-bloom peak in spore production
Use disease forecasting models to predict periods of high disease pressure

treatments.quote: Sanitation is the most important element of a successful black rot management program. Remove infected canes, spurs, and fruit clusters remaining on the vines. Rake up and dispose of fallen leaves and mummies. Alternatively, mulch may be used to bury mummies... Applications of protectant fungicides such as sulfur (Bordeaux mix), copper, or mancozeb should begin shortly before bloom and be repeated at the intervals recommended on the label until approximately 4-6 weeks post bloom. Thorough coverage is important. Later infections may also be managed by systemic fungicides.

canonical.summary: Characteristic mosaic pattern of chlorosis and necrosis on the upper surfaces of cucurbit leaves, with gray sporangia giving a fuzzy or downy appearance on the underside of leaves.
diagnostic_features: Leaf spots are angular and bounded by leaf veins (most distinct in cucumbers). Dark purplish-grey fuzz forms on the underside of the leaf in high humidity. On watermelons, an exaggerated upward leaf curling is common.
treatments: Early planting so fruit can be harvested before the pathogen arrives (downy mildew arrives in New York between July 4 and August 31).
Plant resistant cultivars; newer cucumber varieties with some resistance to cucurbit downy mildew are commercially available.
Track the spread of cucurbit downy mildew through the IPM Pest Information Platform for Extension and Education (ipmPIPE) at cdm.ipmpipe.org to time fungicide applications.

Apply chemical treatments per current recommendations (e.g., Cornell Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; Midwest Vegetable Production Guide). Rotate products to manage resistance.
Use drip irrigation and wide row spacing to dry the leaves and encourage good air movement around the plants.
Trellis plants to improve air circulation.
Remove plants with symptoms of disease.
Monitor plants for symptoms of disease, especially from August through harvest.

summary.value: Characteristic mosaic pattern of chlorosis and necrosis on the upper surfaces of cucurbit leaves, with gray sporangia giving a fuzzy or downy appearance on the underside of leaves.
summary.quote: Cucurbit downy mildew is easily recognized by its characteristic mosaic pattern of chlorosis and necrosis (dead cells) on the upper surfaces of cucurbit leaves, but leaf symptoms vary between cucurbit species. The name 'downy' is attributed to the development of gray spores called sporangia that result in a fuzzy or downy appearance on lesions located on the underside of leaves.

diagnostic_features.value: Leaf spots are angular and bounded by leaf veins (most distinct in cucumbers). Dark purplish-grey fuzz forms on the underside of the leaf in high humidity. On watermelons, an exaggerated upward leaf curling is common.
diagnostic_features.quote: Leaf spots are angular and bounded by leaf veins. This is most distinct in cucumbers. Dark purplish-grey fuzz forms on the underside of the leaf in high humidity. In wet or very humid conditions, the disease develops rapidly. Leaf spots grow together, and entire leaves turn brown. The leaves appear as if frost had killed them. On watermelons, an exaggerated upward leaf curling is common.

canonical.summary: Mild symptoms may include yellowish leaf streaks and stiff, dark green leaves before heading; affected plants head out early producing sterile heads with clumped, sooty olive-black spores in place of healthy glumes and kernels, with only a bare rachis remaining after spore dispersal.
diagnostic_features: Spores are not enclosed by the seed coat, so are quickly dispersed by rain or wind, leaving only a bare rachis with a few fragments of glumes or awns; loose smut spores will NOT have a fishy odor.
treatments: Less susceptible varieties of wheat are available.
Plant certified seed to reduce disease risk.
Do not save seed from fields with loose smut.
Fungicide seed treatments can effectively manage loose smut.

canonical.summary: Brown lesions develop on leaves with concentric, target-like rings and a yellow surrounding halo; fruit lesions begin as sunken brown spots that can become dark and fuzzy with sporulation.
diagnostic_features: Brown leaf lesions with concentric, target-like rings and a yellow surrounding halo; with significant progression whole leaves become brown and dry.
treatments: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties when possible
Plant certified disease-free seed; do not save seed from infected plants
Rotate away from susceptible cucurbit crops for at least 2 years
Destroy or deep-plow infested plant debris after harvest
Maximize distance between susceptible cucurbit fields to limit spread
Avoid overhead irrigation
Avoid working in fields when plants are wet
Maintain proper nutrition, especially nitrogen
Scout regularly to identify the disease early
Keep plants growing vigorously until harvest
Initiate protective fungicide applications when vines begin to run
Alternate Mancozeb 75DF and Chlorothalonil 6F with tank-mix Chlorothalonil + a fungicide of a different FRAC code every 14 days
Chlorothalonil (Group M5) formulations (e.g., Bravo Ultrex, Echo 720, Bonide Fung-onil for home gardens)
Mancozeb (Group M3) products such as Dithane F-45 (do not apply within 5 days of harvest; some varieties sensitive)
Carboxamide (Group 7) fungicides (e.g., Endura, Fontelis); do not exceed two sequential applications before rotating mode of action
Strobilurin (Group 11) fungicides (e.g., Cabrio EG, Quadris Flowable, Evito 480 SC, Reason 500 SC, azoxystrobin 2.08F); do not make more than one application before alternating
Group 3 fungicides such as Mettle 125 ME
Omega 500F (Group 29); 30-day preharvest interval
OSO 500F (Group 19)
Regalia Fungicide (Group P5)

Copper formulations (Group M1) offer limited control (e.g., Champ WG, Cueva, Cuprofix Ultra 40 Disperss, Kocide 2000-O/3000-O, Liqui-Cop, Previsto, Bonide Liquid Copper for home gardens)
Vacres (potassium bicarbonate) at 2.5 to 5 lb/A on 7- to 14-day intervals
Trilogy at 0.5% to 1% (not labeled in Oregon)
Biological control: Actinovate AG at 3 to 12 oz/A as foliar spray on 7- to 14-day intervals

canonical.summary: Black rot causes large brown rotten areas on fruit (often with concentric rings), 'frog-eye' leaf spots with purplish/reddish edges and tan interiors, and sunken reddish-brown cankers on branches.
diagnostic_features: There is usually one spot per fruit (distinguishing it from bitter rot); leaf lesions show purple margins with brown/tan centers giving a 'frogeye' appearance; decayed flesh is not cone-shaped (unlike bitter rot); concentric bands of mahogany brown to black alternating with brown bands form on rotted fruit; small black pycnidia appear in the centers of leaf lesions.
treatments: Practice good sanitation: prune out dead or diseased branches, pick all dried and shriveled (mummified) fruit remaining on the trees, and remove infected plant material from the area (burn, bury, or send to municipal composting).
Prune correctly during dormancy (below 32 F; Feb-Mar in Minnesota); first prune out all dead branches, then prune to shape the tree.
Prune and remove cankers at least 15 inches below the basal end; properly dispose of prunings by burial or burning.
Take good care of trees: choose an appropriate site, plant only hardy cultivars, provide adequate water, and maintain tree health to prevent stress.
Control fire blight by pruning out infected wood or controlling insect vectors; remove limbs or trees killed by fire blight to discourage black rot.
Fungicide sprays are usually not needed in Minnesota; Captan and sulfur products labeled for scab also control black rot.
Captan and fungicides containing a strobilurin (FRAC Group 11) as an active ingredient are effective in controlling black rot on fruit.

canonical.summary: In high humidity, a dense velvety gray-brown spore mass covers infected plant parts and releases a cloud of spores when disturbed; leaves develop irregular to V-shaped tan to brown blotches starting at margins, stems develop brown oval girdling lesions, and fruit develop a pale soft watery rot or whitish 'ghost spot' rings.
diagnostic_features: Dense velvety gray-brown spore mass that releases a cloud of spores when disturbed; light brown-gray spores on black stalks; V-shaped brown blotches starting at leaf margins; brown oval stem lesions that may expand in concentric rings to girdle the entire stem; small 3-8 mm whitish rings (ghost spots) on the fruit surface from aborted infections.
treatments: Keep humidity and leaf wetness low by rolling up high tunnel sides, increasing ventilation and avoiding overhead irrigation

Space plants well (20-24 inches between plants and 4-5 feet between rows) to avoid excess humidity in dense canopies
Remove infected stems, leaves, and fruit; place in a plastic bag and remove from the field
Clean up leaf debris on the ground; remove all plant debris at the end of the season
Prune plants in the early afternoon when dew has dried so wounds can dry quickly
Do not work on wet plants
Maintain consistent and adequate soil moisture and adequate calcium for healthy tissue
Practice good greenhouse sanitation; scout, bag, and remove infected plants
Apply fungicides preventatively prior to dense canopy growth; rotate fungicide groups or tank mix to manage resistance

canonical.summary: Early-season shoot blight produces patches of soft brown tissue and death of infected plant parts, with infections in leaf axils causing shoots to wilt or break off. At veraison, individually infected berries turn brown on white cultivars or reddish in red and black cultivars, and epidermal cracks develop fungal growth with a characteristic gray, velvety appearance.
diagnostic_features: Epidermal cracks form in which fungal growth produces mycelium and spores, resulting in the characteristic gray, velvety appearance of infected berries; under high humidity infected berries become covered with a gray growth of fungus mycelium.
treatments: Promote good air circulation and light penetration by proper pruning, controlling weeds and suckers, and positioning or removing shoots for uniform leaf development.
Where possible, rows should be planted in the direction of the prevailing wind.
Removal of leaves around clusters (or basal leaves immediately after berry set) before bunch closing reduces losses caused by Botrytis.
Canopy management practices such as shoot thinning, hedging, and leaf removal can be used to manage canopy density when appropriate.
Design vineyards to the anticipated vigor of the site to produce balanced canopies with moderate shoot vigor that optimize leaf and cluster exposure.
Prevent wounding by controlling insects, birds, and other grape diseases; manage insect populations that produce entry wounds.
Avoid unnecessary irrigation or nitrogen fertilization that may promote excessive canopy growth.

Apply effective fungicides at appropriate times: between bloom and pea-size berries if the canopy interior remains dry, otherwise before rainfall at bloom or after veraison; treat late-harvest grapes prior to bunch closure and as needed before harvest.
Alternate fungicides with different modes of action within and between seasons to prevent fungicide resistance.
Use resistant cultivars when practical.
Organically acceptable methods: canopy/cultural management plus sprays of Organic JMS Stylet Oil and Serenade.

Conventional fungicide options include CYPRODINIL (Vangard WG), FENHEXAMID (Elevate 50WDG), PYRIMETHANIL (Scala SC), FLUOPYRAM + TEBUCONAZOLE (Luna Experience), CYPRODINIL + FLUDIOXONIL (Switch 62.5WG), DIFENOCONAZOLE + CYPRODINIL (Inspire Super), IPRODIONE (Rovral 4F), PYRACLOSTROBIN + BOSCALID (Pristine), NARROW RANGE OIL (JMS Stylet), BACILLUS SUBTILIS (Serenade Max), ISOFETAMID (Kenja 400SC).

canonical.summary: Circular to angular leaf spots about 1/8 to 1/4 inch (3-6 mm) in diameter, brown to gray with dark reddish brown, purplish, or nearly black borders, which may converge to cover much of the leaf surface. On Bigleaf and panicle hydrangea the spots first appear on the bottom leaves; on oakleaf hydrangea the infected areas are more angular and dark brown to purple.
diagnostic_features: Spots roughly 1/8 to 1/4 inch in diameter with a pale or light brown center and dark margins (a frogeye pattern); the disease progresses from the bottom foliage to the top, and spores may eventually become visible as dark specks within the leaf spots.
treatments: Remove any diseased leaves that have fallen from the plant and hand-pick highly infected leaves from the plant.
Discard diseased leaves in the trash; do not put them in the compost bin.
Practice good sanitation to remove overwintering fungal inoculum; dispose of plant debris and infected leaves in the autumn.
Provide adequate plant spacing to increase air movement and sunlight penetration so leaves dry quickly.
Avoid practices that prevent leaves from drying quickly, such as overhead and excess watering; if foliage must be wetted, irrigate in the early morning.
Placement of hydrangeas in areas of lower light intensity may reduce infection.
Fertilize lightly with a nitrogen fertilizer to encourage new disease-free growth.

Apply labeled fungicides at the first onset of symptoms, e.g. chlorothalonil (Bonide Fung-onil, Ortho MAX, Daconil), azoxystrobin, mancozeb, myclobutanil, or thiophanate-methyl, strictly according to the label.

canonical.summary: Lesions and cankers appear on all aboveground parts of the peony. Stem cankers are elongate and gray, often causing severe twisting or curling of the stem, while foliar leaf spots and infections of flowers and flower buds are similarly gray.
diagnostic_features: Elongate gray stem cankers that often cause severe twisting or curling of the stem, with pink-colored fruiting structures (acervulus) sometimes observable in the cankers.
treatments: Increase air movement by wide plant spacing to avoid overcrowding of plants.
Avoid overhead irrigation that keeps plants wet for extended periods of time.
Remove all infected plant parts during the growing season.
Cut and remove or destroy all plants at the end of the year to reduce overwintering inoculum.

Mancozeb-based products can be used to provide some protection. Group M3 fungicides. 24-hr reentry.
Fore 80WP Rainshield at 1.5 lb/100 gal water plus a spreader-sticker.

canonical.summary: Foliar blight causes yellowing to reddish brown discoloration of leaves and general thinning of the turf, with leaves dying from their tips down; basal rot causes scattered plants or small patches to turn yellow and die, with a water-soaked black rot of the crown tissue. On annual bluegrass putting greens, symptoms typically appear as bright yellowing of turf in irregular patterns, with patches an inch or two to more than a foot across.
diagnostic_features: The most reliable diagnostic features are the dark/black coloration at the base of the plant (crowns, roots, and lower stem bases) and the presence of fungal spore-producing structures (acervuli) on stems and leaves, which look like small pin cushions and bear protruding, black, hairlike structures (setae) observable with a hand lens.
treatments: Alleviate conditions that cause turf stress (aeration, redirecting traffic, reduced watering, and tree pruning or removal)
Adequate / light, frequent nitrogen fertilization (~3.0 lb/1,000 ft2/year) to reduce anthracnose severity on annual bluegrass putting greens, without overstimulating turf during heat stress
Do not apply nitrogen at high rates during periods of high temperature stress or drought
Fertilize with complete fertilizers, avoiding deficiencies of potassium and phosphorous; soil test to avoid potassium deficiencies
Water deeply and infrequently; irrigation at 60-80% of ET is preferred
Increase mowing height (cutting heights of 0.141 inch) and reduce mowing frequency; avoid mowing below 0.125 inch and scalping
Lightweight rolling with smooth rollers to maintain green speed
Light and frequent sand topdressing
Reduce soil compaction by core aeration in spring and fall; manage thatch
Modify traffic patterns and move cups frequently
Minimize leaf wetness by improving air circulation, watering early in the day, and/or dew removal
Wash mowers thoroughly after mowing areas where disease is active
Renovate greens with newer, less susceptible bentgrass cultivars

Preventive fungicide programs (beginning 2-4 weeks before symptoms appear) using penetrant fungicides or penetrant/contact combinations at label rates; preventive applications are more effective than curative
For basal rot, apply and water in a systemic fungicide to reach the crown, followed by a separate protectant application
Avoid Group 3 fungicides (DMIs) during the summer stress period to avoid growth regulator effects
Alternate active ingredients / fungicide classes and mix contact with penetrant fungicides to delay resistance

canonical.summary: On cucumber leaves, symptoms begin as water-soaked areas that expand into roughly circular brown spots (1/4 to 1/2 inch in diameter); on watermelon, lesions are circular at first but coalesce into irregular black necrotic areas, with stem/petiole lesions shallow, elongate and tan, and fruit lesions sunken with pinkish spore masses in moist weather.
diagnostic_features: Presence of a pinkish to salmon mass of spores, black stroma, and black setae (bristle-like fungal structures visible with a hand lens); conidia are hyaline, nonseptate, oblong and 4-6 x 13-19 micrometers; whisker-like setae can be seen in the pink spore masses under a hand lens or microscope.
look_alikes: Angular leaf spot (Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans)
Powdery mildew (Podosphaera xanthii or Erysiphe cichoracearum)
treatments: Use disease-free seed and consider seed treatments to ensure no pathogens are present
Inspect each seedling for freedom from leaf spots before taking from nursery to field; destroy seedlings with leaf spots
Do not plant near older crops of cucumber, melon, or watermelon, especially those with signs of anthracnose
Practice at least a one-year, preferably two or three-year, rotation away from cucurbit crops (leave a 2-3 year gap with no cucurbit family crops)
Avoid overhead irrigation since water splash spreads the fungus; if used, irrigate in the early morning so foliage dries before nightfall
Avoid working in or moving machinery through crops when leaves and vines are wet, since people and equipment can spread spores
Control weeds, especially wild or volunteer cucurbits
Plough in or remove crop residues in infected fields; 'flip plow' the field with a modified moldboard plow; practice fall tillage
Use resistant cultivars of watermelon and pickling/slicing cucumbers (resistant varieties are not available for melon)
Do not save seeds from fields where anthracnose has been observed
Use fungicides to prevent disease at or before the time vines begin to touch within the row; begin spraying at first appearance of disease, then every 5 to 10 days (shorter interval in rainy weather)
Fungicide options include mancozeb, chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stick 6SC), or a copper product
Prothioconazole (Proline 480 SC)
Thiophanate-methyl (Topsin)
Fluxapyroxad + Pyraclostrobin (Merivon)
Pyraclostrobin + Boscalid (Pristine)
Pyraclostrobin (Cabrio EG)
Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole (Quadris Top)

Lesions on fruit are roughly circular, sunken and contain pinkish spore masses in moist weather.

treatments.value: Use disease-free seed and consider seed treatments to ensure no pathogens are present; Inspect each seedling for freedom from leaf spots before taking from nursery to field; destroy seedlings with leaf spots; Do not plant near older crops of cucumber, melon, or watermelon, especially those with signs of anthracnose; Practice at least a one-year, preferably two or three-year, rotation away from cucurbit crops (leave a 2-3 year gap with no cucurbit family crops); Avoid overhead irrigation since water splash spreads the fungus; if used, irrigate in the early morning so foliage dries before nightfall; Avoid working in or moving machinery through crops when leaves and vines are wet, since people and equipment can spread spores; Control weeds, especially wild or volunteer cucurbits; Plough in or remove crop residues in infected fields; 'flip plow' the field with a modified moldboard plow; practice fall tillage; Use resistant cultivars of watermelon and pickling/slicing cucumbers (resistant varieties are not available for melon); Do not save seeds from fields where anthracnose has been observed; Use fungicides to prevent disease at or before the time vines begin to touch within the row; begin spraying at first appearance of disease, then every 5 to 10 days (shorter interval in rainy weather); Fungicide options include mancozeb, chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stick 6SC), or a copper product; Prothioconazole (Proline 480 SC); Thiophanate-methyl (Topsin); Fluxapyroxad + Pyraclostrobin (Merivon); Pyraclostrobin + Boscalid (Pristine); Pyraclostrobin (Cabrio EG); Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole (Quadris Top)
treatments.quote: Disease-free seed is desirable, consider seed treatments to ensure no pathogens are present. Practice at least a one year, preferably two or three, rotation away from cucurbit crops. Avoid moving machinery or workers in the fields when the foliage is wet. If overhead irrigation is necessary, irrigate in the early morning so the foliage will dry before nightfall. Resistant cultivars of watermelon, pickling and slicing cucumbers are available with desirable horticultural characteristics.

canonical.summary: Common leaf spot first appears as small, deep purple spots on the upper surface of leaves that enlarge to 0.125 to 0.25 inch (3-6 mm) in diameter, with the lesion center turning brown then gray to white; numerous spots may coalesce to kill the leaf.

treatments: Reduce inoculum on planting stock to greatly reduce the likelihood of disease development; ensure planting stock is clean and certified disease-free
Use drip irrigation and remove infected leaves when practical
Choose a growing area with environmental conditions not conducive to disease development
Cultural controls are acceptable on organically certified crops; use fungicides only when monitoring indicates they are necessary
Apply labeled fungicides such as chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stik) or myclobutanil (Rally 40W); products containing captan, myclobutanil or copper are also effective
Use copper-containing fungicides only prior to flowering
Alternate myclobutanil applications with a fungicide of a different active ingredient
Plant resistant varieties such as 'Crimson King', 'Earliglow', 'Glooscap', 'Ogallala', and 'Ozark Beauty'
Plant in full sunlight, in well-drained soils, with proper spacing to optimize air circulation
Avoid overhead watering; use a drip or soaker hose
Do not work in the strawberry patch when it is wet; wait until the patch is dry
For June-bearing strawberries, use bed renovation techniques (particularly mowing) to help manage common leaf spot
At the end of the season, remove plant debris and deep bury, burn (where allowed), or hot compost it to minimize overwintering sites

canonical.summary: Symptoms include abnormal red coloring of shoots and foliage, thick succulent stems, rapid elongation of new shoots followed by witches' brooms (clustering of small branches with shortened internodes), distorted or dwarfed leaves that may show conspicuous red pigmentation, an overabundance of unusually soft and pliable red or green thorns on canes, and deformed buds and flowers.
diagnostic_features: Excessive growth of unusually soft and pliable red or green thorns on canes is diagnostic for RRD when present; on RRD-diseased plants the reddish leaf color does not go away, whereas on healthy plants it disappears as the leaf matures.
treatments: Host resistance / research to breed RRD-resistant roses (no resistant cultivars currently available)
Start by purchasing disease-free plant material; inspect at the nursery and avoid buying roses showing symptoms
Early detection; remove and destroy suspect/diseased roses immediately (infected plants are not curable)
Where permitted, burn diseased plants; otherwise bag and remove them, including roots
Do not allow uprooted diseased plants to remain in the vicinity of healthy roses
Eliminate wild R. multiflora within a 100-meter (100-yard) radius of rose nurseries and gardens; monitor and remove regrowth
Avoid planting cultivated roses downwind of known multiflora rose plantings
Space plants so canes and leaves do not touch; consider mixed plantings with non-rose plants
Avoid using leaf blowers near roses
Promote plant health and vigor by irrigating during drought, maintaining fertility, and controlling other diseases
Control mites with miticides (e.g., abamectin registered for eriophyid and spider mites; carbaryl or bifenthrin insecticides); spray surrounding roses every two weeks from April until September
Disinfect pruners used on infected roses before use on other roses to prevent spreading the virus
Thoroughly remove symptomatic plants and prevent regrowth from infected root pieces

canonical.summary: Typical symptoms are rotting stems at or near the soil line and root decay (post-emerging damping-off), with affected seed-bed areas a foot or more in diameter showing shriveled brown, collapsed or stunted seedlings; young seedlings develop a sunken, necrotic lesion near the soil line that, if it girdles the stem, causes the seedling to collapse and die.
diagnostic_features: Plants affected by damping-off will be scattered or occur in patches whereas plants affected by abiotic issues will be more consistently affected and at or near 100% incidence; affected seedlings show a sunken, necrotic lesion near the soil line that can girdle the stem.
look_alikes: plant injury caused by excessive fertilization
death of seedlings from excessive heat, cold, fuel fumes, or chemical injury
treatments: Sanitize all seed trays, flats, pots and containers; use new ones or thoroughly wash and disinfect old containers
Use new, pasteurized soil mix or treat media with heat (e.g. 158Â°F/70Â°C for 30 min with aerated steam) to reduce damping-off fungi
Proper soil preparation for good drainage, structure, aeration, water-holding capacity and nutrition
Use fungicide-treated seed with high germination
Use proper seeding rates to avoid thick stands, poor air movement and low light
Use proper planting depth and soil temperature for rapid emergence and growth

Provide drier conditions: increase greenhouse temperature, increase air circulation/ventilation and light, reduce watering frequency, improve drainage; if damping-off appears, stop watering and let soil dry

canonical.summary: On redcedar/juniper, dark brown swollen galls (up to two inches diameter) with circular dimples form on branches and produce bright orange gelatinous telial horns in spring. On apple/crabapple, small chlorotic yellow spots develop on leaves that turn orange with red rings, bearing orange pustules above and hairy tube-like aecia below; fruit develops yellow/orange lesions that turn brown with tube-like aecia.
diagnostic_features: Galls on juniper/redcedar always have small circular dimples across the surface, from which bright orange gelatinous telial horns (1/2 to 3/4 inch long) erupt in spring. On apple/crabapple leaves, yellow spots develop red rings around the edge, small raised black dots in the center on the upper surface, and produce hairy, finger-like aecia (less than 1/10 inch) on the leaf underside; on crabapple fruits the aecia give the fruits a spiky appearance.
treatments: Plant disease-resistant varieties of crabapple, apple, and juniper
Avoid planting eastern red cedar and juniper within several miles / a few hundred yards of susceptible Rosaceae plants
Inspect nearby juniper/red cedar trees in late winter or early spring and remove brown, woody galls before orange gelatinous structures form
Prune and remove infected twigs or branches on Rosaceae plants
Apply fungicides on the primary (juniper) host every 14 days from June to September

Apply fungicides on apple/crabapple beginning around flowering and continuing on a seven-day interval until telial horns dry up; sterol inhibitors (e.g., Myclobutanil) are most effective; copper and sulfur products can also be used
Spray trees/shrubs when flower buds first emerge until spring weather becomes consistently warm and dry
For organic apple production: bloom thinning combined with lime sulfur or a labelled biofungicide
Tolerate leaf spots and fruit infection on apples, hawthorns, serviceberry, and other Rosaceae
Avoid planting highly susceptible varieties such as Beacon and Wealthy apple where cedar-apple rust is a problem

canonical.summary: Phytophthora capsici causes seedling damping-off, leaf spots, foliar blight, root and crown rot, stem lesions, and fruit rot, with infected tissue initially appearing water-soaked and often producing a white yeast-like growth of sporangia.
diagnostic_features: Seeing sporangia (white, yeast-like growth containing many lemon-shaped sporangia) on affected tissue is diagnostic for Phytophthora capsici; sporangia can be induced by putting affected plant tissue on wet paper towel in a closed plastic bag overnight.
treatments: Long rotations between susceptible crops and selecting fields where Phytophthora blight has never occurred
Manage resistance by using a diversity of chemistry, based on FRAC code, in alternation and combination
Grow a mustard biofumigant cover crop before a crop susceptible to Phytophthora blight, preferably during spring rather than previous fall
Use deep-zone reduced tillage to produce pumpkin, winter squash, or another crop like corn grown in rotation
Select well-drained fields
Use a land plane to level the field as much as possible
Physically separate plantings of susceptible crops (cucurbits, pepper, eggplant, and tomato)
When growing small-fruited pumpkins, select varieties producing hard, gourd-like rinds (such as Lil' Ironsides)
Minimize hardpans and plowpans by subsoiling or chisel plowing before planting
Do not plant the crop in areas of the field with poor drainage. Plant a cover crop in place of the crop in these areas
Prepare raised dome-shaped beds for summer squash and other bush-type crops. Ideally beds should be a minimum of 9 inches high
Use a transplanter that doesn't leave a depression around the base of the plant. Fill in any depressions
Covering raised and flat beds with plastic mulch provides a good barrier between crop and pathogen in the soil
Seed driveways between vining crops like pumpkin, to avoid driving over plants when applying pesticides
Clean farm equipment, shoes, etc. of soil between fields
Subsoiling between rows after planting and before vining can improve drainage
Avoid over-irrigating
Do not irrigate at night time when temperatures are above 70 F
Drip irrigation is a good way to provide water to a crop while avoiding creating potentially favorable conditions
Lay the drip tape a couple inches from the crown of plants because drip too close can create conditions favorable for crown rot
Do not irrigate from a pond that could contain water that drained from an infested field
Several fungicides have been developed with targeted activity for P. capsici and other oomycetes
There also are several biopesticides labeled for application to soil before or at planting and to foliage
Scout fields for symptoms routinely, especially after major rain storms
When symptoms are localized in a small area of a field, disking the area is worthwhile
Do not discard cull fruit in the field

Do not save seed from a field where Phytophthora blight occurred

canonical.summary: White, powdery fungal growth develops on both leaf surfaces, petioles, and stems (primarily asexual conidia), usually first on crown leaves, shaded lower leaves and leaf undersurfaces; yellow spots may form on upper leaf surfaces opposite the colonies, infected leaves shrivel and die, and plants may senesce prematurely.
diagnostic_features: White, powdery fungal growth (conidia) on both leaf surfaces, petioles and stems, developing first on crown leaves, shaded lower leaves and leaf undersurfaces, with yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces opposite the colonies; older plants are affected first. The first sign is often pale yellow leaf spots.
treatments: Plant varieties with complete or partial resistance to powdery mildew; select varieties with resistance from both parents (homozygous resistance) when possible.
Provide good air movement around plants through proper spacing, staking, and weed control; choose planting sites free of shade.
Apply fertilizer based on soil test results and avoid over-applying nitrogen.

Inspect/scout crops routinely (particularly lower leaf surfaces) beginning at the start of crop development; the action threshold for starting applications is one leaf with symptoms out of 50 older leaves examined.
Physically separate successive cucurbit plantings (or plant up-wind of older plantings) to prevent older plants serving as an inoculum source for the main crop.
Before disease appears / early in disease development, apply fungicides on a 7 to 10-day interval following detection through an IPM scouting program.
Alternate products with different modes of action / FRAC groups to avoid generating fungicide-resistant strains, and include a protectant fungicide in every application.

Use mobile (systemic or translaminar) fungicides tank-mixed with a contact fungicide, applied only when needed at the highest labeled rates, alternating among as many different mobile fungicides as possible.
Recommended protectant fungicides include chlorothalonil, sulfur, copper, mineral oil, and several biopesticides; sulfur is one of the most effective and least expensive products.
Remove debris, weeds, and volunteers that may harbor the pathogen.
Organic growers: fixed copper formulations are the only OMRI-labeled active ingredients with some efficacy against cucurbit powdery mildew.
Home gardeners: products containing copper or chlorothalonil are the best effective products available, combined with growing tolerant varieties.

diagnostic_features: Expanded lesions first become light green, almost transparent, with irregular margins and then form large circular spots of concentric rings, taking on a characteristic 'bullseye' appearance; tissue in the center of the lesions is thin and may drop out, giving a shot-hole appearance to the leaf.

Steam treatment for used pots and trays (center of stack held at 75 to 80Â°C for one hour)
Practices that open the plant canopy, increase air circulation, and reduce leaf wetness
Early harvesting of lower leaves from infected plants
Isolates of T. harzianum can reduce the growth of R. solani and enhance disease control
Fungicides containing Azoxystrobin and Mancozeb applied preventatively as a foliar spray

canonical.summary: Small, roughly circular bleached/white-to-tan patches of dead turf, silver-dollar sized on closely mowed greens and 1-5 inches (occasionally exceeding 6 inches) on fairways, athletic fields, and lawns; numerous spots may coalesce into large, irregular dead areas.
diagnostic_features: On individual leaves, initial symptoms appear as yellow-green blotches that progress to tan-colored lesions with reddish-brown borders; lesions occur near the middle of the leaf and extend completely across the blade, often with a classic 'hourglass' shape. White mycelia can be observed on diseased leaves in early morning following rainy/dewy periods.
treatments: Late spring nitrogen fertilizer applications to minimize dollar spot severity; maintain adequate nitrogen in a balanced nutritional program
On athletic fields and lawns use slow-release nitrogen; on golf courses quick-release nitrogen can be applied in liquid form at low rates frequently
Avoid light, frequent waterings; irrigate to apply more water less frequently and wet the entire rootzone
Water in the morning so turf dries before night
Remove dew and guttation fluid from foliage (dragging fairways with weighted hoses, dew whips, rollers, or early-morning mowing)
Daily/lightweight rolling of putting greens, particularly coupled with increased mowing height, to reduce dollar spot activity
Collect and remove plant debris
Use resistant cultivars (e.g., creeping bentgrass: Proclamation, Declaration, 007, Barracuda, Luminary, Pin-Up, V8, Memorial, Benchmark DSR)
Focus on cultural control tactics first; implement a broad-based cultural program to reduce the number of fungicide applications
Apply fungicides on irrigated turf with persistent dollar spot; early-season applications just before symptoms appear reduce later outbreaks
Alternate modes of action / tank-mix fungicides from different groups, mix contact and penetrant fungicides, or use only contact fungicides; limit use of any one group

Specific products (PNW): Group 3 (BioAdvanced Fungus Control, Bonide Infuse, Densicor, Eagle 20 EW, propiconazole products such as Banner MAXX/PropiMax EC), Group 2 (Chipco 26019 FLO), Group M5 (Daconil Weather Stik), Group M3 (Mancozeb - Fore, Manzate, Protect DF), Group 11 (Disarm 480 SC, Fame SC), Group 7 (Emerald, Velista), plus combination fungicides (Armada 50 WDG, Briskway, Concert, Encartis, Exteris Stressgard, Headway, Honor, Interface, Lexicon, Navicon, Pillar G, Premion, Renown, Tartan Stressgard)

canonical.summary: Symptoms begin as small whitish or yellowish flecks or blotches on the upper leaf surface that enlarge with black specks inside; these specks merge into irregular black stomata 0.5 to 3.0 mm in diameter surrounded by a yellow-white band of dead tissue.
diagnostic_features: Raised black fungal fruiting bodies (stromata) form within the leaf spots, giving the leaf a bumpy texture as if dotted with tar; black specks merge into single irregular stomata 0.5 to 3.0 mm in diameter surrounded by a yellow-white band of dead tissue, and successive seasons of twig blighting can cause witches' broom.
treatments: Remove infected leaf debris and dead shoots; rake up leaf litter and prune out infected stems to remove inoculum for the following season.
Avoid overhead irrigation and close spacing of cuttings and young trees.
Chemical control / fungicides are generally not warranted for large, mature trees in landscapes since full foliage coverage is impractical and damage is not usually severe.

For small nursery trees, preventive fungicide applications (e.g. mancozeb, copper, or chlorothalonil) may be made starting at budbreak in spring and continued at regular intervals until leaves are fully developed, especially where overhead irrigation is used.

canonical.summary: Initial symptoms are yellowish or chlorotic flecks on leaves (especially those in contact with soil) that enlarge into elliptical, tan-brown lesions, often with yellowish halos. Lesion centers die, becoming bleached gray or ash-white, and produce small, dark brown to black pycnidia, giving the lesion a characteristic speckled appearance. Subsequent lesions on higher leaves generally follow leaf veins, with straight edges and no yellow margins.
diagnostic_features: The presence of small, black pycnidia in lesions is the most reliable in-field character for identifying the disease. Lesions generally do not have pronounced chlorotic halos like Stagonospora leaf and glume blotch and tan spot, and lesions are more elongated with rougher edges. When humid, a translucent, curling thread of whitish (or pinkish-brown, column-shaped, jellylike) ooze of spores (conidia) may exude from the pycnidia and is visible with a hand lens.
treatments: Plant varieties less susceptible / resistant to Septoria tritici blotch
Avoid early plantings (October); later plantings (November to December) are less likely to be severely affected
Practices that encourage residue decomposition
Crop rotation â€” a rotation where wheat is planted in only 1 of 3 years is recommended
Destroy volunteer wheat, rye, barley, and wild grasses in the field before planting
Plant certified, disease-free seed treated with a recommended seed-protectant fungicide
Sow winter wheat after the Hessian fly-safe date recommended for the county
Fertilize wheat based on a soil test; avoid high rates of nitrogen that would increase lodging potential
Foliar fungicides labeled for management of Septoria tritici blotch (e.g., MANCOZEB / Dithane M45 2 lb; PROPICONAZOLE / Tilt 4 fl oz)
Apply between tillering and heading (single full-rate application at flag leaf emergence or at heading) to protect the flag leaf
Scout and consider varietal susceptibility, forecasted weather, length of rotation away from wheat, and yield potential prior to fungicide application

canonical.summary: Causes sudden wilt, death of sprouts and melt down of storage roots, with damage ranging from small tire-size dead spots to the loss of entire beds.
diagnostic_features: Characterized by the production of rapidly growing white mycelium and the yellow to brown mustard seed-like sclerotia that serve as survival structures and are produced on the mycelium.
treatments: Site selection: Choose a well-drained site for the plant bed that has not had sweetpotatoes for at least 3 to 4 years.
Plant handling: Cut plants in beds 1 inch above the soil line. Do not pull plants. Use disease-free planting stock.
Removal of bed covers: bed covers should be removed as soon as the sprouts emerge from seed roots.
Deep plowing: The sclerotia do not survive when buried at least 8 inches into soil with a breaking plow.
Solarization: the soil may be covered with black polyethylene sheets for a 6 week period during the hottest months of the year.

Chemical control: Dipping roots prior to bedding, or to a lesser extent, spraying roots laid out in beds with a protectant fungicide such as dichloran (Botran) can reduce the incidence of Southern blight.

canonical.summary: Infected seedlings appear light to reddish brown in color and may be covered with a mass of pink or whitish mold; surviving seedlings lack vigor and produce few tillers with small heads.
diagnostic_features: Light to reddish brown discoloration with pink or whitish mold mass on seedlings; later a light to reddish brown root or crown rot develops as plants mature.
treatments: Avoid using grain from scab-affected fields for seed
If scabby grain is used, thoroughly clean the seed to remove lightweight kernels
Use seed treatment fungicides to improve germination and control seedling blights
Delay planting of winter cereals until the soil temperature is 60Â°F (16Â°C) or below
Planting should always be after the Hessian fly free date
Spring-seeded grains should be sown as early as possible when soil temperatures are relatively cool
Sow seed in a well prepared seed bed with adequate fertilizer to ensure good root growth and vigorous plant development
Rotate small grains and corn with legumes, and leave at least one year between cereals, grass or corn before planting small grains

canonical.summary: Infected spikelets prematurely die, becoming bleached (brown or straw-colored) while non-infected spikelets on the same head remain green; entire heads may be killed prematurely, and infected kernels become shriveled, wrinkled, and discolored.
diagnostic_features: Pinkish to salmon (orange) spore masses and mycelium (sporodochia) form on the margin of the glumes of individual spikelets, especially near the base, at the attachment to the stem, or along the awns; severely infected kernels are lightweight, chalky, pink to red ('tombstones'); later, dark purplish-black perithecia may appear on heads.
look_alikes: Root and foot rots (common root rot, Fusarium root, crown and foot rot, eyespot, take-all)
Abiotic disorders (salinity, frost, herbicide injury, water stress, hail, rodent feeding)
treatments: Plant moderately resistant varieties
Plant cereals as far away as possible from old corn fields if stalk residues are left on the soil surface
Use clean, deep plowing of all infested stubble and straw of cereals and weed grasses, corn stalks and rotted ears when conventional tillage is used

When possible, plant wheat following a legume crop (soybean) and maintain a rotation with 2 to 3 years between wheat crops; longer rotations between small grain and corn crops to promote residue decomposition

Apply fungicides directed to the head at flowering (anthesis) in wheat (Feekes 10.51; Zadoks 61) up to about 7 days after start of flowering, and at complete head emergence in barley (or up to 7 days after full head)
Use DMI (triazole; FRAC group 3) or SDHI (FRAC group 7) fungicides; avoid QoI (strobilurin; FRAC group 11) at boot stage or beyond as they can increase DON
Use the scab prediction/forecasting system (www.wheatscab.psu.edu) as a guide to determine if the risk of scab warrants a fungicide application
Use a fungicide seed treatment if seed-lot was confirmed to be infected with F. graminearum
At harvest, use a properly adjusted combine with fan speed adjusted to remove moldy and lightweight kernels
Segregate poor quality grain from good quality grain
Store grain cool and dry: less than 50Â°F (10Â°C) and less than 15% moisture for short-term storage; below 13% moisture for long-term storage
Test moldy grain for mycotoxins before being used for food products or fed to animals

canonical.summary: On leaves, yellow spots or purple ring spots may appear, with feathery patterns along the veins that may be yellow or purple; in many cases there are no symptoms or they are faint and short-lived. On roots, strain RC causes external cracking in rings around the storage roots and internal cork (small brown to black corky spots).
diagnostic_features: Purple feathery-like patterns along veins typical of infection; strain RC causes external cracking in rings around storage roots and internal cork (small brown to black corky spots).
treatments: Use virus-tested planting material
Plants are tested for virus and, if infected, given heat treatment before removing the meristem and growing it into a healthy plant in tissue culture
Use planting material, produced through a healthy 'seed' scheme
Remove wild Ipomoea species if they are present around the sweet potato plantings
Remove old, harvested, vines and, if possible, plant new crops away from older ones that might be a source of aphids and viruses
Use resistant varieties
Chemical control is not a method that can be used to control this virus

summary.value: On leaves, yellow spots or purple ring spots may appear, with feathery patterns along the veins that may be yellow or purple; in many cases there are no symptoms or they are faint and short-lived. On roots, strain RC causes external cracking in rings around the storage roots and internal cork (small brown to black corky spots).
summary.quote: On its own, there may be yellow spots (Photo 1), or purple ring spots (Photo 2). Feathery patterns may appear along the veins, and these too may be yellow or purple (Photos 3&4). In many cases, there are no symptoms, or they are faint and short-lived, with the new leaves looking healthy. On the roots, the symptoms, depend on the strain and the variety. Strain O does not produce symptoms, whereas strain RC causes external cracking in rings around the storage roots (Photo 5), and internal cork – small brown to black corky spots, seen after harvest and during storage.

canonical.summary: Angular chlorotic lesions bound by leaf veins on the foliage of cucumber, with a 'downy' appearance on the lower leaf surface caused by sporulation.
diagnostic_features: Chlorotic lesions on the adaxial leaf surface, sometimes with necrotic centres, restricted by the leaf vein giving them an angular appearance in cucumber; on the lower leaf surface a 'downy' appearance from sporulation (masses of sporangia visible with a 20X hand lens); in melon and watermelon, foliar lesions are less defined and not always bound by leaf veins.
look_alikes: Angular leaf spot (Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans)
Powdery mildew (Podosphaera xanthii or Erysiphe cichoracearum)
treatments: Use tolerant/resistant cucurbit cultivars (e.g., pickling cucumber 'Citadel' and 'Peacemaker'; slicing cucumber 'SV3462CS' and 'SV4142CL' tolerant to clade 2 isolates)
Aggressive fungicide programme with sprays every 5-7 days for cucumber and every 7-10 days for other cucurbits to control outbreaks

Before disease appears, apply fungicides at 7-day intervals for cucumbers and 10-day intervals for other cucurbits; after detection in your area, tighten to 5-day (cucumber) and 7-day (other cucurbits) intervals
Alternate fungicide products and tank-mix with mancozeb or chlorothalonil to avoid generating fungicide-resistant strains

Example fungicides for cucumber/cantaloupe: Cyazofamid (Ranman 400 SC), Fluazinam (Omega 500 F), Chlorothalonil + oxathiapiprolin (Orondis Opti), Mandipropamid + oxathiapiprolin (Orondis Ultra), Propamocarb (Previcur Flex 6F), Ethaboxam (Elumin 4SC), Mancozeb + zoxamide (Gavel 75DF), Chlorothalonil + zoxamide (Zing!), Mancozeb (Dithane 75DF Rainshield), Chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stik 6SC)

Example fungicides for watermelon, squash, pumpkin: Cyazofamid (Ranman 400 SC), Fluazinam (Omega 500 F), Chlorothalonil + oxathiapiprolin (Orondis Opti), Mandipropamid + oxathiapiprolin (Orondis Ultra), Propamocarb (Previcur Flex 6F), Ametoctradin + dimethomorph (Zampro 4.38 SC), Ethaboxam (Elumin 4SC), Mancozeb + zoxamide (Gavel 75DF), Chlorothalonil + zoxamide (Zing!), Fluopicolide (Presidio 4F), Famoxadone + cymoxanil (Tanos 50WG), Mancozeb (Dithane 75DF Rainshield), Chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stik 6SC)
Use sporangia trapping and forecasts (e.g., Cucurbit Downy Mildew IPM Pipe) to time the first fungicide application
Plant early in the season to escape high disease pressure
Do not allow water to remain on leaves for long periods of time
Scout plants often and remove infected plants
Report outbreaks via the Cucurbit Downy Mildew IPM Pipe alert system
For organic growers: fixed copper formulations are the only OMRI labeled active ingredients with some efficacy
For home gardeners: plant early, destroy infected plants, plant tolerant varieties, use products containing copper or chlorothalonil (e.g. 'Daconil')

canonical.summary: Greenish-gray water-soaked lesions appear on the leaf sheath near the water level, circular to oblong or ellipsoid and about 1 cm long. Lesions enlarge to irregular shape with gray-white centers and brown margins, and can spread to upper sheaths, leaf blades and panicles causing rotting, leaf drying and seed discoloration.
diagnostic_features: Greenish-gray water-soaked lesions on the leaf sheath near the water level, circular/oblong/ellipsoid ~1 cm long, enlarging with gray-white centers and brown margins; at field level the infection affects plants in a circular pattern referred to as 'bird's nest'.
treatments: Use resistant rice varieties / develop resistant genotypes

Use a reasonable level of fertilizer adapted to the cropping season; apply balanced K, Zn, S, Fe; use slow-release nitrogenous fertilizer (e.g., Crotonylidene diurea, Guanyl urea phosphate) with silica, phosphorus and potash
Use reasoned density of crop establishment (direct seeding or transplanting); improve canopy architecture by reducing seeding rate or providing wider plant spacing
Carefully control weeds, especially on the levees
Drain rice fields relatively early in the cropping season to reduce sheath blight epidemics
Use fungicide to treat seeds; apply chemical fungicides as needed
Apply soil amendments including neem cake, farm yard manure (FYM), vermicompost and rice husk
Spray Ganoderma diethyl ester biological formulation
Use resistance-linked molecular markers in breeding programs; use non-host plants as a genetic resource for developing resistant rice varieties
Use novel biotechnological approaches such as RNAi, transgenics and genome-editing (e.g., transgenic rice overexpressing oxalate oxidase)

Plow under / promptly incorporate crop debris soon after harvest
Irrigate so that carrots are dry by nightfall
Plant tolerant cultivars (e.g. Improved Half Long Chantenay, K-2043)

canonical.summary: Symptoms include marginal yellowing and browning of leaves beginning with the lower leaves, progressing to entire discoloration, wilting, and collapse, with rotted petiole bases and mushy crowns; a white mat of fungus and tiny spherical sclerotia appear at the crown and soil surface.
diagnostic_features: Because the bases of the petioles are rotted, the leaves can be easily pulled away from the crown; a white mat of fungus (mycelium) fans out from the infected crown across the soil surface, and thousands of tiny, spherical sclerotia (BB to pepper grounds in size, white to brick red) are present in the rotted crown.
look_alikes: Other basal stem rots such as those caused by Rhizoctonia or other fungi
treatments: Dig up/dig and burn or remove hostas showing crown rot symptoms.
Thoroughly scrape and/or wash soil from all tools used in infested soil, then sterilize tools in a 10% solution of household bleach.
Buy disease-free plants / use only pathogen free stock.
Plant nonhost species into holes from which sick hostas have been excavated.
Follow good Integrated Pest Management practices to avoid fungicide applications.
Solarize or otherwise pasteurize soil before planting.
Remove soil from affected area and replace with new or sterilized soil.
Avoid overwatering and provide good soil drainage, for example, by planting in raised beds.
Rhizomes or bulbs can be treated with hot water to eliminate the fungus.
Soil drenches of fungicides (Cleary's 3336, Terraclor) around the base of plants before infection can prevent disease development (but will not cure affected plants).
Amendment of the soil with biological control agents such as MycoStop, PlantShield, SoilGard, or YieldShield may offer some control.

canonical.summary: Disease often begins as tiny, almost translucent spots that turn brown and water-soaked; infected fruit, leaves, petals, and succulent stems become dark, soft, and wilted and die. On flowers, water-soaked petal spots develop reddish-brown blotches and buds may die before opening. Under high humidity a thin to thick grayish web of mycelium develops on diseased tissue, hence the name gray mold.
diagnostic_features: A fuzz of grayish-brown fungal sporulation (a thin to thick grayish web of mycelium) develops on dead/diseased tissue under humid conditions, giving rotted tissue a fuzzy or woolly appearance. When inner or middle petals develop brown lesions first, gray mold is the likely cause; on thin leaves (e.g. redbud) lesions are light brown to brown and irregular, while on fleshier leaves (e.g. rhododendron) concentric rings of different shades of brown may be visible.
treatments: Control the environment and keep plants healthy by avoiding stresses such as plants staying too wet or too dry, chemical or mechanical injury, and too little or too much fertilizer.
Improve air circulation and sunlight; adequately space plants and prune canopies, and cut back nearby and overhead vegetation.
Avoid overhead or late-evening watering; use drip or microsprinkler irrigation and avoid wetting foliage.
Especially keep open flowers with many petals dry.
Maintain low humidity in the greenhouse and avoid sunburn by planting in shadier locations.
Avoid wounding leaves or shoots.

Use good sanitation: dead-head dying flowers, remove and dispose of old blossoms, infected plant tissue, crop debris (especially spent blooms), fallen leaves, and weeds; do not practice sanitation when plants are wet.
Destroy infected tissue by burning where permitted, or bury it under at least a foot of soil.
Apply fungicides to help prevent or reduce leaf, fruit, and stem infections; chlorothalonil, thiophanate-methyl, or triforine can be applied before disease develops.
Tank-mix and/or alternate products from different groups with different modes of action to prevent buildup of resistant fungi.

Labeled chemical products include Astun (Group 7), Bonide Fung-onil Multi-purpose Fungicide, Broadform (Group 7+11), Chipco 26019 FLO (Group 2), Daconil Weather Stik (Group M5), Decree 50 WDG (Group 17), mancozeb-based Fore 80WP/Protect DF (Group M3), OHP 6672 4.5 F (Group 1), Orkestra (Group 7+11), Pageant (Group 7+11), Palladium (Group 9+12), Phyton 27 (Group M1), Postiva (Group 3+7), Spectro 90 WDG (Group 1+M5), and Terraguard SC (Group 3).
Biological control: BotryStop (Ulocladium oudemansii U3 strain) at 2 to 4 lb/A, kept refrigerated before use.
