canonical.summary: Infected plants are stunted with dead or dying outer leaves, showing water-soaked lesions at the soil line on the neck that progress up the leaves and down the neck; a gray mold develops on or between the scales and large distinct black sclerotia form around the rotting neck.
diagnostic_features: Large, distinct black sclerotia (rough black masses of hardened fungal mycelium) as large as Â¾ inch but typically Â¼ inch in diameter form around the rotting neck, with gray mold on or between the garlic scales.
treatments: Use disease-free seed stock.
Use adequate plant spacing and good weed control to encourage air movement.
Remove infected plants from the area and do not compost.
Try to harvest mature plants with a minimum of injury.
Properly cure garlic bulbs with good air movement; if normal dry weather prevails, cure garlic on the ground for 6 to 10 days.
Practice proper crop rotation.
Do not plant garlic or other alliums in a field where the pathogen is present.
Allow the tops to mature well, then lift or undercut the garlic.
When topping, keep bruising and mechanical injury to a minimum.
Store garlic in well-ventilated houses at temperatures of 32Â°F, or just slightly higher.
Avoid frequent and excessive irrigation.
Visual inspection of seed garlic with a hand lens may help; examine the basal plate or bottom of garlic for gray mold.
Treat seed (cloves) to reduce incidence of fungi in the seed.
Cueva (Group M1) at 0.5 to 2 gal/100 gal water on 7- to 10-day intervals.
Fontelis (Group 7) at 16 to 24 fl oz/A on 7- to 14-day intervals.
Inspire Super (Group 3 + 9) at 16 to 20 fl oz/A prior to disease onset on 7- to 10-day intervals.

canonical.summary: Peach scab causes small, slightly raised reddish-grey lesions on green shoots that expand and develop dark brown borders, and sunken lesions on fruit that grow into large dark, grey to olive, circular well-defined spots often concentrated at the stem end.
diagnostic_features: Sunken (not raised) lesions that are grey to olive, circular, and well-defined, sometimes with a yellowish halo; a corky cell layer beneath the lesion does not expand as the fruit grows, causing cracks in the skin.
treatments: Planning during the orchard establishment phase should include proper site selection. Avoid low-lying areas with poor air circulation and soil drainage.
Implementation of a monitoring program based on the presence of lesions on the bark of the previous years' growth

Cultural controls are limited to ensuring that proper pruning practices keep the tree canopy open in order to facilitate fungicide spray penetration.
Fungicide sprays must be applied just before peak infection periods to provide maximum protection on developing fruit.
During spring seasons with frequent precipitation, spray intervals should be shortened, and fungicides should be rotated to avoid development of fungicide resistance.

canonical.summary: On fruit, symptoms appear as flat to sunken necrotic lesions (0.5 to 6 cm), light to dark brown, progressing toward the core in a V-shaped pattern; lesions begin as small, slightly sunken circular spots that may be surrounded by a red halo on mature fruit and can develop concentric rings with pink or orange spore masses. On leaves, Glomerella Leaf Spot appears as brown angular spots that may merge into irregular blotches.
diagnostic_features: After making a cross-section of the infected fruit a V-shaped, brown, watery lesion that extends toward the core can be observed, distinguishing it from other summer fruit rots (white rot and black rot).
treatments: Integrate good sanitation, cultural practices, and chemical control
Prune trees to remove and destroy dead or diseased wood, including shoots infected with fire blight, and burn it to reduce inoculum
Chopping/flail-mowing dead wood on the ground to remove bark and increase decomposition
Remove and burn (eliminate) mummified fruit from trees and the orchard floor throughout the growing season
Maintain tree vigor with a balanced fertility program (based on soil/foliar analyses), proper watering, and annual pruning
Do not use susceptible cultivars; select resistant cultivars and prune canopies open and well-ventilated to reduce surface wetness
Apply fungicides from fruit set / first cover until harvest where a good sanitation program is in place

Rotate FRAC groups to reduce fungicide-resistance risk (FRAC M multisite: captan, ziram, ferbam; FRAC 7 benzovindiflupyr; FRAC 11 pyraclostrobin/trifloxystrobin/picoxystrobin; FRAC 29 fluazinam; FRAC 12 fludioxonil postharvest)
Use drip/under-canopy irrigation to prevent spore dispersal by water splash
Select a good planting site (plant on hilltops instead of valleys)
Biological control: Serenade ASO (Bacillus subtilis QST713), DoubleNickel55 (B. amyloliquefaciens D747), Theia (B. subtilis AFS032321), Howler (Pseudomonas chlororaphis AFS009)
Consult the New England Tree Fruit Management Guide for current fungicide recommendations

profiles.profile_id: Eastern White Pine::White Pine Blister Rust

canonical.summary: On Eastern white pine, needles on infected branches turn yellow then rusty red, and branches develop swollen cankers with discolored, cracked bark that ooze sticky sap and form white-to-yellow blisters releasing orange spores. On Ribes plants (currant and gooseberry), angular yellow leaf spots appear on the upper leaf surface with raised orange pustules on the underside.
diagnostic_features: On pine: cankers on the main trunk are oval or diamond-shaped, often with a dead branch in the center, oozing sticky clear-to-white sap, with white-to-yellow blisters releasing powdery orange spores and gummy orange spore droplets. On Ribes: angular yellow leaf spots contained by leaf veins with raised orange pustules and orange or brown hair-like tendrils on the leaf underside.
treatments: Diseased pine branches should be pruned out of the tree before the infection comes within 4 inches of the main trunk.
Prune off branches with cankers at a branch union or where the branch meets the trunk. Remove at least 4 inches of healthy wood beyond the visible symptoms of disease.
Remove lower branches gradually as the trees mature; never remove more than 1/3 of the canopy at a time.
When planting white pine trees, space plants to promote good air movement around the trees. Redirect lawn sprinklers or irrigation systems to avoid wetting pine needles.
Don't plant eastern white pine and currants or gooseberry together in the landscape unless resistant cultivars are used. Avoid planting white pine in low lying areas or cold pockets.
Plant resistant varieties â€” 'Paton's Silver Splendor' eastern white pine and resistant gooseberry and currant cultivars are available.
Eradicating Ribes plants has not worked to eliminate the disease but may help slow the disease spread.

Pruning off the lower branches can help if done before rust symptoms on the branches get within six inches of the trunk; pruned branches can be left since the pathogen cannot survive in dried out tissue.
If symptoms develop within six inches of the trunk, removal of the tree is suggested to help reduce spread of disease.

canonical.summary: The primary symptom is browning and dieback of new shoot tips in the spring; blighted twigs first turn pale green then brown by early summer, with shoots killed back to the previous season's wood and sunken dark cankers forming at the junction of live and dead wood.
diagnostic_features: Attacks new, immature growth at branch tips while mature foliage remains resistant; sunken dark lesions called cankers form at the junction of live and dead wood, and scraping the bark reveals a sharp line between discolored dead wood and healthy wood.
treatments: Closely inspect the entire plant, since tip/twig blight symptoms can be caused by other problems such as drought, overwatering, or root injury

Purchase and select disease-resistant juniper varieties/cultivars with no dead or dying twigs (e.g. Juniperus chinensis 'Pfitzeriana Aurea', 'Iowa', var. sargentii; J. sabina 'Broadmoor', 'Skandia'; J. scopulorum 'Silver King')
Do not stress junipers by planting in shaded or poorly drained locations; plant in areas with good air circulation for rapid drying of needles
Do not crowd plants; avoid sprinkler/overhead irrigation and keep plants as dry as possible, watering only when foliage can dry quickly
Avoid wounding plants and do not overfertilize
Prune and destroy/remove diseased, dead, or browning twigs and branches, especially early in spring before new growth begins

Apply registered fungicides before new growth starts in spring and continue as new growth is produced (at 2-week intervals); options include mancozeb, thiophanate-methyl, or copper fungicides (e.g. Bonide Infuse Systemic Disease Control, active ingredient thiophanate methyl)

canonical.summary: Small, bleached light-brown to tan spots appear first on the upper surface of one-year-old leaves; one or several brown to black fruiting structures (apothecia) form in the center of the spots in late spring; leaves turn brown and drop in fall, while infected leaves remaining on the tree turn ashy gray.
diagnostic_features: Apothecia are embedded in the leaf tissues and the entire structure drops out, leaving deep pits; the disease progression gives the appearance of having been scorched by fire.
treatments: Application of fungicides to manage the disease is rarely necessary
A copper fungicide (Bordeaux Mix) or mancozeb (Dithane) should be effective if applied early in the season, when susceptible foliage is developing
Propagate from disease-free stock plants
Use seed from British Columbia coastal, low-elevation populations
Space nursery plants and time irrigation to promote rapid drying of foliage
Do not grow susceptible cultivars downwind of infected hedges, windbreaks, or nearby stands of native western red cedar
Pruning out and burning affected twigs is of limited use
Remove plant debris from seed before seeding
Apply fungicides during wet periods in spring and fall to protect healthy foliage
Banner MAXX at 5 to 8 fl oz/100 gal water can be used if not phytotoxic to plants
Topas (propiconazole) registered in British Columbia for use every 4 weeks during the growing season to a maximum of six applications (Group 3 fungicide, 12-hr reentry)
Bordeaux or fixed-copper sprays (such as CuPRO 5000 at 1.5 to 2 lb/A) in spring and early summer (48-hr reentry)
Mancozeb-based products applied as regular sprays late March through May and late August through October (Group M3, 24-hr reentry)
Tebuject 16 registered for tree injections, number of capsules based on tree size

canonical.summary: The most conspicuous symptom is brown, stunted new shoots with short, brown needles; needles become discolored while still encased in their fascicle sheaths, with a brown discoloration starting at the base of the needle and growing toward the tip. Small drops of resin ooze from shoot buds in early spring and the shoots die.
diagnostic_features: Small black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) of the fungus can be seen with the unaided eye at the base of needles, just under the fascicle or sheath tissue, and on second-year cone scales; dead needles are held on the shoot and resin flows from shoots and branches. Needles die by the time they are one half to three fourths normal length.
treatments: Apply fungicide to the entire crown (especially lower branches) as buds begin to swell at bud break and again about 2 weeks later; some sources recommend a third application 10-14 days after that. Sprays at other times are not effective.
Remove all affected twigs and cones; if infected branches are pruned out, disinfest pruning tools between cuts.
Do not plant healthy/susceptible 2- or 3-needled pines near older infected pines, and consider avoiding the most susceptible pines in landscape plantings.

Promote tree vigor and reduce stress by protecting from environmental stress, insect attack, and injuries, mulching and watering as needed; fertilize stunted trees to stimulate growth but do not use high-nitrogen fertilizers.
Avoid wounding trees; do not prune or shear in the spring or in wet weather when spores are being released.

canonical.summary: Foliar symptoms range from angular-shaped leaf spots and blotches, marginal leaf scorch, and a complete blight of infected foliage; leaf spots are round to blotchy with tan centers and reddish-purple margins. Leaf dieback first occurs in the lower crown and works up the tree. Infection moves from leaves to twigs, where cankers develop causing twig dieback, and succulent shoots and small stems can be killed while perennial cankers develop on larger branches.
diagnostic_features: Tan leaf spots with distinctive purple borders; dead twigs appear tan and are often covered with black, pin-point fruiting bodies (conidiomata) that produce masses of orange spores in wet weather; the leaf blotch often spreads down the midvein giving a wedge-shaped appearance; vascular cambium infected with the disease is chocolate brown in contrast to the pale tan color of healthy sapwood; and prolific epicormic/water sprouts develop on the trunk and adjacent to large branch cankers.
treatments: Plant resistant species/cultivars: Cornus kousa (e.g. Milky Way, Steeple) is tolerant; C. kousa x C. florida hybrids (Celestial, StarDust, Stellar Pink, and several 'stellar' crosses) and disease-resistant C. florida cultivars greatly reduce the need for management
Practice early detection; trees with extensive dieback and only a few active branches cannot be saved and should be removed
Trees showing only initial signs (leaf spots and twig canker) can be pruned and treated with fungicides
Prune out and destroy infected/blighted twigs, shoots, and stems as they develop, and remove epicormic/water sprouts that form
Rake and remove fallen leaves from spring through fall, and remove dead twigs and leaves remaining attached to the tree
Plant in full sun with good air circulation, in well-ventilated areas where plants dry quickly after wetting, with no surrounding plantings
Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers that produce lush succulent shoots more susceptible to the fungus
Do not let irrigation wet the tree canopy; provide a soaking root-zone irrigation during droughts and maintain a 2-3 inch layer of composted mulch over the root zone
Limit additional stresses such as string trimmer and mower damage

Apply protective fungicide sprays beginning at bud break/budbreak, repeating every 10-14 days until leaves are fully open / until dry weather, with an additional application in late summer when flower buds form
Alternate or tank-mix fungicide products from different groups (modes of action) to prevent resistance; limit use of any one group during the growing season

canonical.summary: Fusarium dry rot appears as an internal light to dark brown or black rot of the potato tuber that is usually dry, often rotting out the center and leaving a dark sunken area on the tuber surface with internal cavities.
diagnostic_features: Lesions from F. solani var. coeruleum progress in a fairly uniform manner and turn yellow to brown with age, whereas lesions caused by F. sambucinum tend to be very dark brown to black and progress irregularly, sometimes called "tunneling"; yellow, white, or pink mold may be present on affected tissue.
treatments: Purchase seed that has as little dry rot as possible.
Warm seed tubers to at least 50° F before handling and cutting to minimize injury and promote rapid growth.
Clean and disinfect the seed storage area before receiving seed.
Keep knives on the cutter sharp to make a smooth cut that heals easily.
Disinfect seed cutting and handling equipment often and clean up well between seed lots.
Grade out obviously rotted tubers before they reach the cutter.
Treat seed pieces with fungicide to help control decay and other seedborne diseases.
Do not precut seed.
Use antibruise practices when harvesting and piling potatoes; avoid wounding and bruising tubers by handling carefully.
Allow a period for wounds to heal before dropping the temperature in storage.
Monitor storages often for dry rot.
Be sure tubers mature and skins are well "set" before harvest; harvest during dry, cool weather.
Apply fungicides as tubers enter storage.

canonical.summary: Roughly circular or sometimes angular, ¼ to ½ inch diameter dead spots on affected leaves, often with a purple-red border, and centers that may eventually fall out.
diagnostic_features: Within the spots, a diffuse ring of black dots (reproductive structures of the fungus) is typically visible; young leaves are more susceptible than mature leaves, and early infections can cause puckered, distorted leaves.
treatments: Remove and burn (where allowed by local ordinance), bury or hot compost fallen, infected leaves.
Thin plants to increase airflow and promote rapid drying of foliage.
Water plants at the base using a soaker or drip hose to minimize wetting of leaves and reduce the movement of spores.

Do not use the same active ingredient for all treatments (particularly if you are using thiophanate-methyl). Instead, alternate the use of at least two active ingredients.

treatments: Maintain good air circulation around trees; don't overcrowd plants; use the mature size of the tree as a spacing guide when planting

Provide supplemental water for newly planted and young trees

canonical.summary: Signs and symptoms include white woolly scale insects on the bark, orange cankers with rough callous edges that may exude a red-brown fluid, and small bright red fungal fruiting bodies (perithecia) on the bark in fall; severe infection causes girdling, stem breakage, and death.
diagnostic_features: Adult beech scale insects are round, soft-bodied, and yellow, often noticed due to the white, woolly substance they create; cankers may appear orange with rough edges and may exude a red-brown fluid; fungal perithecia are small and bright red, produced in clusters as superficial perithecia (each about 0.25 mm diameter), while irregular, blocky bark indicates a host resistance response.
treatments: Insecticides may be used to prevent infection, more effective if timed for the crawler stage before it develops a protective waxy covering

Promote and breed/plant resistant beech trees in forests
Report suspected cases of BBD to the North Carolina Forest Service - Forest Health Branch
Silvicultural selective harvesting of larger beech (about 45% basal area reduction) to improve overstory growth of sugar maple and birch

profiles.profile_id: Japanese Maple::Phomopsis Cankers And Twig Blights

canonical.summary: Infected woody plants show thinning canopies, browning and prematurely shedding foliage, scattered branch dieback, and eruptive cankers on the bark, sometimes with sunken sap-stained lesions and oozing sap; in many cases the only symptoms are leaf wilting and canopy dieback.
diagnostic_features: After establishing in the canopy, the pathogen produces an abundance of small, black-colored pads of fungal tissue (pycnidia) that erupt through the bark to release cream-colored spore tendrils (cirrhi).
treatments: Minimize stresses that predispose woody plants to infection and maintain high plant vigor
Irrigate susceptible trees and shrubs at regular intervals during extended dry periods to minimize drought stress
Fertilize if soil nutrients are lacking and mulch the root zone to retain soil moisture
Limit mechanical wounds (e.g. string trimmers) and avoid needless damage to canopy and roots
Avoid excessive pruning, especially on recently transplanted plants, and avoid pruning during wet spring periods
Perform regular sanitation pruning to remove dead twigs; prune cankered stems/branches at least 6-12 inches away from blighted tissue and remove diseased material from the site
Sanitize pruning tools after working with infected or suspected plants

Apply registered fungicides in spring to protect newly developing tissues (azoxystrobin, captan, copper salts of fatty and rosin acids, copper hydroxide, mancozeb, metconazole, phosphites, propiconazole, tebuconazole, thiophanate-methyl); avoid application on actively flowering plants to protect pollinators

canonical.summary: White, powdery fungal growth develops on both leaf surfaces, petioles, and stems, usually developing first on crown leaves, shaded lower leaves, and leaf undersurfaces; affected leaves senesce early and fruit yield and quality can be reduced.
diagnostic_features: Yellow spots may form on upper leaf surfaces opposite the powdery mildew colonies; older plants are affected first; late in the season dark brown, very small (about 0.003 inches) chasmothecia that are barely discernable without a hand lens may develop.
treatments: Manage with resistant varieties/cultivars; an integrated program using both resistant varieties and fungicides is the best approach for effective control
Apply fungicides on a 7 to 10-day interval beginning very early in disease development (before disease appears / following IPM-based detection)
Initiate a weekly spray program when symptoms are found; action threshold is one leaf with symptoms out of 50 older leaves examined
Alternate products with different modes of action / FRAC groups and include a protectant fungicide in every application to manage fungicide resistance
Apply mobile (systemic) fungicides together with a contact/protectant fungicide as a tank mix, at highest labeled rates, only when needed to protect yield
Provide adequate plant spacing; choose planting sites with good air movement and free of shade
Physically separate successive cucurbit plantings or plant up-wind of older plantings, which can serve as a source of conidia
Remove debris, weeds, and volunteers that may harbor the pathogen
Scout fields regularly, particularly lower leaf surfaces, beginning at the start of crop development

Example conventional products: Chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stik), Myclobutanil (Rally 40WSP), Pyraclostrobin + boscalid (Pristine), Quinoxyfen (Quintec), Metrafenone (Vivando), Cyflufenamid (Torino), Azoxystrobin + difenoconazole (Quadris Top)
Organic growers: fixed copper formulations are the only OMRI-labeled active ingredients with some efficacy; several biopesticides approved for organic production are registered
Home gardeners: products containing copper or chlorothalonil (e.g., 'Daconil') are the best effective options; also grow tolerant varieties

canonical.summary: Symptoms include bleeding of color out from the leaf veins, blue or dark green mottling on the leaves, leaf distortion (puckering and twisting), ring spots, flecks, zipper marks, stunted growth, and occasionally necrotic lesions.
diagnostic_features: Bleeding of color out from the veins of the leaves and blue or dark green mottling, along with zipper marks, ring spots, and flecks; symptoms are easier to distinguish in gold-colored cultivars, and holding an infected leaf up to the light versus a healthy leaf aids identification.
treatments: Carefully inspect any plants for color bleeding and leaf mottling before purchasing; avoid buying plants with symptoms of HVX.
When purchasing hostas (especially expensive ones), consider requesting that the seller provide proof that the plants are HVX-free.
Send samples to a diagnostic lab when HVX is suspected; virus testing kits are available and relatively inexpensive.
Before planting new plants, isolate them from any other hostas for at least 1 week (up to several weeks) and watch for symptom development.
Remove and destroy all plants that test positive or show symptoms â€” burn (where allowed) or landfill/throw away in their own trash bags. Do NOT compost.
Disinfest tools that may have contacted infected plants; for home gardeners, thoroughly scrubbing tools in hot soapy water is generally sufficient.

Professionals may use disinfectants such as Zerotol, KleenGrow, Physan, or Virkon after removing all organic matter from tools; or treat items for at least one minute with Alconox plus SLS/SDS, or trisodium phosphate solution.
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water (for at least one minute) before and after working with the plants.
Minimize wounding that could release sap and provide an entry point for HVX.
Note: normal sterilization with 70% rubbing alcohol is NOT effective for HVX management.

treatments: Disease control on seedlings is especially important

Fungicide applications at regular intervals are necessary when disease is severe; fungicides labeled for control of rusts on ornamental plants can be used preventatively, with the first application made when the first leaves are expanding and treatments repeated according to label directions throughout the growing season
Plants should be cut back as soon as flowering is done
Plant debris should be removed and destroyed (bury, burn or bag and dispose in the landfill), not composted
Control weeds in the mallow family (e.g., common mallow) in the growing area to limit inoculum
Plant hollyhock in full sun in locations with good air circulation and soil drainage
Space plants to promote foliar drying and avoid overhead irrigation
Remove diseased leaves as soon as symptoms appear to reduce inoculum, and remove severely diseased plants; remove any diseased plants at the end of the growing season since hollyhock rust is systemic
Start new plants from seed or purchase disease-free transplants each year
Use resistant varieties where appropriate (A. rugosa and A. ficifolia have some resistance), recognizing that different races of the pathogen exist and resistance is not effective against all races
Use a wetting agent with fungicide applications since hollyhock leaves are hairy and good coverage is necessary for fungicide efficacy

canonical.summary: Needles become discolored â€” new needles at branch tips stay green while older needles turn brown to purple (yellow in July, reddish-purple in August), eventually turning brown and falling off; infected trees look thin or see-through with many bare branches, and damage starts on the lower branches and moves up the tree.
diagnostic_features: Tiny brown to black spots called pycnidia (fruiting bodies) emerge from the stomata on the needles, arranged in neat rows/lines and visible with a hand lens (10X); the disease attacks the oldest needles in the lower canopy first and progresses upward, giving the appearance of death from the bottom up and inside out.

treatments: Do not plant Colorado blue spruce (Picea pungens) or other spruce not well adapted to local conditions; plant more resistant Norway (P. abies) or white spruce (P. glauca)
Plant spruce trees on sites with acidic, moist, well drained soils and full sun, preferably grown from local seed sources
Do not overcrowd plants; use the mature size of the tree as a spacing guide, and remove the bottom-most branches to increase air circulation around the canopy
Do not shear spruce, as shearing creates dense, compact growth that stays wet longer
Remove weeds under trees and maintain a 3-4 inch wood chip mulch layer (leaving a 2 inch gap from the trunk); avoid wetting needles with sprinkler irrigation
Plant only healthy trees and avoid planting new trees next to established trees

summary.quote: Sirococcus causes disease of young, succulent shoots in the spring, shortly after budbreak. Infected shoots can die rapidly, and the stunted, wilted needles first appear pale green to yellow-brown while the shoots can be irregularly curved. Over time, the needles become darker brown and desiccated. After symptoms appear, the fungus produces small black pads of tissue on the diseased needles and shoots.

diagnostic_features.value: Small black pads of fungal tissue on diseased needles and shoots that rupture under humid conditions to release spore masses; small purple lesions with a drop of resin at the point of infection; hook-shaped tip growth when infection occurs in the region of shoot elongation; shoots killed by Sirococcus are scattered rather than uniform; affects only young current-year shoots while older shoots (>1 year old) remain unaffected.
diagnostic_features.quote: After symptoms appear, the fungus produces small black pads of tissue on the diseased needles and shoots. When moisture and humidity are abundant, the pads rupture to release large masses of spores, which may be splashed or blown onto nearby shoots or trees, where new infections are initiated. Older shoots (>1 year old) remain unaffected

treatments.value: Prune dead shoot tips and remove diseased material from the site to reduce inoculum; Apply fungicide early in the growing season as new shoots are flushing to protect sensitive tissues; Chemicals labeled for use against Sirococcus include thiophanate-methyl, mancozeb, and copper hydroxide; Once tissues are fully hardened off, a locally systemic fungicide may be required for mid-season applications; Provide supplemental irrigation during extended dry periods to avoid drought stress; Preventative fungicides such as chlorothalonil (Bravo) and Bayleton 25wp may be effective on nursery stock and young trees
treatments.quote: Pruning dead shoot tips and removing the diseased material from the site is the first step in controlling the disease. For large and mature trees with significant outbreaks, this can be a daunting task, but inoculum reduction is important. Fungicide application early in the growing season as new shoots are flushing can help to protect these sensitive tissues. Chemicals labeled for use against Sirococcus include: thiophanate-methyl, mancozeb and copper hydroxide. Chemical control can be challenging with shoot blight pathogens since they live within woody tissues and can be difficult to contact. Therefore, once the tissues are fully hardened off, a locally systemic fungicide may be required if applications occur mid-season. Keeping trees healthy and robust is important, so provide supplemental irrigation (if possible) during extended dry periods to avoid drought stress.

canonical.summary: Needles on new shoots turn brown as they grow from the fascicle sheath and the shoots die; infected buds ooze small drops of resin and stop growing, new shoots curl and die, and whole branches may be killed while dead needles remain attached.
diagnostic_features: Small black spore-forming fruiting bodies (pycnidia) erupt through infected needles, especially below the sheath at the needle base, and appear as black dots; they also develop on the scales of second-year cones and on shoots. treatments: Promote tree vigor by protecting from environmental stresses, insect attack, and injuries

Avoid planting too close to other plants that can limit airflow
Do not plant healthy 2 or 3-needled pines near older infected pines
Prune diseased branches to limit the spread of the disease
Avoid pruning during wet weather and disinfest/sanitize pruning tools between cuts (e.g., 70% rubbing alcohol)
Treat the entire crown, especially the lower branches, with a fungicide as the buds begin to swell during bud break and again 2 weeks later; sprays at other times are not effective

canonical.summary: Symptoms include yellowing of leaf margins (chlorosis), light- to dark-brown necrotic spots on cotyledons, water-soaked stem tissue, stem lesions that girdle the stem, cracking with gummy ooze, red/brown/black cankers exuding red to amber gummy substance, and brownish-black depressed fruit lesions (black rot).
diagnostic_features: Black fruiting bodies of the fungus (pycnidia, perithecia, or pseudothecia) on infected leaves, stems, and fruits; pycnidia swell and release tendrils of spores when wetted, observable with a hand lens or microscope; large brown irregularly shaped lesions with concentric ring pattern on leaf margins and interveinal areas; stem lesions often exude a gummy, reddish-brown liquid.
treatments: Purchase seeds from reputable companies with a good history of GSB-free seed production
Seed treatment is necessary if not previously treated, and disinfectants as solutions are more effective than dry-dust treatments
Regularly inspect transplant seedlings in the greenhouses; avoid using healthy-looking seedlings from trays with infected plants
Decaying debris from that crop should be disked and deep plowed into the soil if it is to be followed by a long-term crop rotation practice
Wild citrons, balsam pear, or volunteer cucurbits are other sources of inoculum and should be eradicated before planting cucurbits
A two- to three-year rotation with non-hosts is an effective way to reduce incidence of GSB
Routine scouting of the fields helps in timely application of fungicides that can prevent major crop losses
Apply fungicides in a preventative manner. Chlorothalonil and Mancozeb are effective contact fungicides, and there are many effective systemic fungicides for management of GSB
To prevent development of fungicide resistance, various chemistries should be alternated during the spray program
Avoid wounding fruits during harvest, and store fruits at 45°F–50°F to prevent postharvest black rot
Chlorothalonil mixed with another product such as prothioconazole or tebuconazole
Mixing chlorothalonil with Luna Experience (tebuconazole and fluopyram)

canonical.summary: Symptoms include brown, stunted new shoots with short, brown needles, with resin droplets forming early and dead needles at branch ends; entire new shoots may be killed rapidly and the fungus can also cause resinous cankers on stems and branches.
diagnostic_features: Tiny black fungal fruiting bodies (pycnidia) formed on the surface of infected needles and infected cones are a telltale sign of the pathogen.
treatments: Avoid planting susceptible pines in areas prone to cool and wet weather in spring followed by drought or dry soil conditions.
Keep trees in good vigor with regular maintenance, deep watering during droughts, and control of insects (promote tree vigor by protecting from environmental stresses, insect attack, and injuries).
Do not use high-nitrogen fertilizers on pines.
Build organic soil fertility with adequate mulching, especially with composted material.
Do not plant healthy 2- or 3-needled pines near older infected pines; ensure no nearby sources of inoculum for nurseries or plantations.
Prune infected branches on lightly diseased trees, making the cut at least two feet below visible symptoms; prune only as needed.
Disinfect/disinfest pruning tools between cuts, e.g. with bleach or alcohol.
Follow pruning with sanitation: removal and destruction of infected needles and cones to lower disease pressure.
Avoid pruning or shearing in the spring.
Protect new spring growth with fungicide from bud swell/bud break to full candle elongation, with additional applications at 10-14 day intervals.
Fungicide options include thiophanate methyl (e.g. Cleary's 3336, OHP 6672), propiconazole (e.g. Banner MAXX), and azoxystrobin (Heritage).
Follow good Integrated Pest Management practices, which may allow fungicide applications to be avoided.

treatments: Plants diagnosed with TRV should be removed to avoid spread to other susceptible plant hosts.

canonical.summary: Seedling infection appears as blackening along the cotyledon margin; leaves develop small, wilted, V-shaped (wedge-shaped) chlorotic areas extending inward from the leaf edge toward the midrib that turn yellow to brown and dry out, and the veins of leaves, stems, and roots turn black; the disease eventually becomes systemic, producing leaf drop and head rot.
diagnostic_features: The presence of black veins in yellowish, V-shaped (wedge-shaped) diseased areas along the leaf margins is diagnostic of black rot; a crosswise cut of the stem, leaf petiole or veins will reveal a darkened ring of vascular tissue.
treatments: Purchase only certified, pathogen-free seed and disease-free transplants; grow your own transplants or source them locally
Use hot water seed treatment to reduce or eliminate the seedborne pathogen
Grow transplants in a soilless mix or a new, pasteurized or fumigated seedbed
Practice a 3-year rotation between cole crop plantings (grow where a crucifer crop has not been grown for at least three consecutive years)
Use black rot resistant varieties (some cabbage, rutabaga, turnip, kale, and black mustard varieties have varying degrees of resistance)
Avoid planting in low, wet sites with poor soil drainage; plant on raised beds for better drainage and use plastic mulch to reduce water splashing
Avoid planting in fields infested with crucifer-family weeds; manage weeds such as mustard and shepherdspurse
Inspect seedlings frequently and rogue infected and surrounding plants immediately
Avoid working in fields when the foliage is wet
Plow cole crop fields after harvest to hasten decomposition of crop residues
Apply recommended bactericides when conditions favor disease; fixed copper or copper hydroxide applications every 7 to 10 days may slow spread in dry seasons

canonical.summary: Pink rot appears as a decay of tubers beginning at or near the stem end (or through the eyes in storage); infected tissue becomes rubbery but not discolored, and when cut the rotted portion is delineated by a dark line at its margin and turns salmon pink on exposure to air before darkening to brown and then black.
diagnostic_features: The cut surface of the decay turns salmon pink on exposure to air (later brown then black), the rotted portion is delineated by a dark line at its margin, infected tissue is rubbery but not discolored, and a cut tuber gives off a characteristic ammonia-like odor after 20-30 minutes.
treatments: Scout regularly, especially in waterlogged parts of a field
Destroy infested plant debris and rogue volunteer plants
Maintain proper soil moisture; avoid prolonged saturation of soils during irrigation and provide good drainage
Rotate away from susceptible crops (4 years)
Avoid bruising and wounding during harvest; minimize wounding
Avoid harvesting in hot conditions / wet tubers or tubers with pulp temperatures above 65°F
Store tubers in cold, well-ventilated storage with good airflow; maintain low temperatures because the fungus is inactive below 40°F
Do not bring infected tubers into storage; remove wet tubers from storage
Be aware of the risk of pathogen resistance to phenylamide fungicides (metalaxyl and mefenoxam)
In problem areas apply fungicide 2 and 4 weeks before harvest
MEFENOXAM/MANCOZEB (Ridomil Gold MZ) — first application at flowering and another 14 days later
MEFENOXAM/CHLOROTHALONIL (Ridomil Gold Bravo SC) — first application at flowering and another 14 days later
POSTHARVEST stored tubers: PHOSPHITES (Phostrol)
In-furrow options: Elumin (Group 22), Orondis Gold (Group 49+4), Quadris Ridomil Gold (Group 11+4), Ranman (Group 21, Idaho SLN only)
Ridomil Gold SL (Group 4) broadcast or band, preplant or at planting
Ridomil Gold Copper (Group 4 + M1) at nickel-size tubers, second application two weeks later under high pressure
Biological/seed options: Amplitude ST, Bexfond, Stargus

canonical.summary: The leading edge of infection in sweetpotato storage root tissue is somewhat firm and light-brown, tinged red, with the area behind becoming darker as black sclerotia form; symptoms may present as wet or dry rot, often at the stem end.

Maintain a balanced fertilization program.
Maintain grass height at recommended levels (between 2.5 and 3 inches for Kentucky bluegrass).

Avoid mowing during wet weather, and reduce mowing frequency / increase mowing height during outbreaks.
Maintain uniform soil moisture and verify irrigation uniformity to avoid drought stress.

canonical.summary: The first symptoms on fruit are a slight water-soaked area on or near the blossom end of the fruit; the affected area darkens and enlarges, becoming dark, shrunken, with a dry, leathery appearance.
diagnostic_features: Spot located at the blossom end of the fruit; starts water-soaked and light tan, enlarges and becomes dark brown or black with a leathery look; typically dry; affected fruit ripen faster than normal.
treatments: Do not plant watermelon where drainage is poor, surface water accumulates, or soil is droughty.
Use a soil test to determine if there is a calcium shortage. If so, add lime, preferably in fall, to adjust soil pH to 6.8 to 7. Mix lime thoroughly in top 8 to 12 inches of soil.
Mulch plants with black plastic or loose organic material to help maintain more even soil moisture levels.
Ensure uniform soil moisture. Wet all soil in the root zone at least every 7 to 10 days. About 24 hours after watering, dig a small hole one foot deep to be certain that water penetrated that far.
Home gardeners should provide even moisture levels throughout the fruiting period if possible by controlled watering and mulching.

Ensure good air movement by plant spacing and pruning practices. By reducing relative humidity, plant transpiration increases, aiding in the uptake of calcium when sufficient amounts are present in soil.
Fertilize only moderately to keep plants normally green and vigorous but not luxuriant. Side-dress with nitrogen fertilizer only if required to maintain green color and moderate growth.

Foliar applications of calcium nitrate fertilizers or calcium chloride dihydrate (1.5 teaspoons per gal water plus 0.5 teaspoon of a surfactant such as CapSil) on a weekly basis during fruiting can provide necessary calcium to developing fruit when needed.
Making applications in early morning can help avoid spray injury.
Application of lime to fields known to be low in calcium; soil should be limed according to recommendations of soil analysis report, usually to pH 6.5-6.8.
Use of gypsum (land plaster), at rates of 500 to 1000 pounds per acre (1 to 2 pounds per 100 square feet) as a supplement to liming on calcium deficient soils.
Lime and/or gypsum should be applied several months in advance of planting.
Spraying foliage and stems with anhydrous calcium chloride (4 pounds per 100 gallons of water per acre) four times on a weekly schedule beginning when the second forms, or when symptoms first appear.
Regulate moisture supply in the soil.
Cultivation and hoeing can be avoided if proper weed-control chemicals are used. If cultivation is necessary, it should be shallow to avoid root pruning.
Irrigation supplied via a drip system.
Plants need at least one inch of water per week in the form of rain or supplemental irrigation.
Young plants should not be grown too quickly nor should the plants be subjected to severe "hardening-off" before transplanting.
Removing affected fruits when symptoms are first observed.

treatments: Practice good greenhouse sanitation: use a 10 percent bleach solution or Physan 20 to dip all tools, recycled planting trays, and containers for at least 10 minutes; spray benches and interior with the same solution
Thoroughly clean the greenhouse and treat with a disinfectant before each planting
Remove weeds growing in the greenhouse
Plant only tested bacteria-free seed (negative in a seedling grow-out test for BFB) from fields where no fruit blotch has been found before
Water plants evenly in early morning or by afternoon; bottom watering of transplants will help control BFB
Separate trays by lots to prevent bacterial movement between lots; segregate triploid seedless varieties and seed lots from diploid seeded varieties in the greenhouse
Reduce physical contact with seedlings; rogue diseased plants without touching healthy plants
Monitor transplants for symptoms; if suspicious symptoms are observed, remove infected plants and have them diagnosed immediately

Do not transplant infected plants

Do not irrigate from overhead; use drip tube and plastic mulch
Fields should not be cultivated or sprayed when the foliage is wet

canonical.summary: Symptoms begin as wilting followed by plant death, with a reddish-brown, dry canker at the base of infected stems near the soil line; as the stem rots the entire plant wilts and turns yellow. White fungal growth and small, round, tan-to-reddish/brown sclerotia develop at the crown, and fruit in contact with soil becomes soft, water-soaked, and covered with a dense mat of white, fan-like fungal growth.
diagnostic_features: Coarse, thick white mycelium/mold on stem cankers and fruit, and numerous small, round sclerotia that are white at first and turn tan-to-reddish/brown as they mature; symptoms are usually found at the soil line.
treatments: Space plants for air circulation and rapid drying.
Promptly remove and destroy diseased plant material during the growing season.
Manage weeds and potential alternative hosts.
Avoid movement of infested soil to clean fields; avoid fields with a history of host crops.
Promptly destroy crop residues after harvest.
Deep plow / deep turning to bury residual inoculum and sclerotia (depriving them of oxygen).
Rotate with nonhost crops with long rotations (at least 3 years); wait twelve months before planting another susceptible crop where southern blight developed.
Maintain soil pH at the level recommended for each crop, as the disease is worse in low-pH soils.
Plant crops early so fruit set and harvest begin before southern blight appears.
Avoid damaging fruit and depositing soil over runners.
Apply fungicides before symptoms appear (e.g., Priaxor, Fontelis, Cabrio for tomato and pepper); fungicidal control is often limited, variable, or rarely practical.

canonical.summary: Coarse white strands of mycelium grow in a fan-shaped pattern on lower stems, leaf litter, and soil, followed by tan-to-brown mustard-seed-sized sclerotia. A brown to black lesion develops on the lower stem near the soil line and can girdle the stem, causing sudden permanent wilt and complete collapse; infected fruit develops soft, water-soaked, sunken star-shaped spots.
diagnostic_features: Coarse white mycelium in a distinctive fan-shaped pattern on lower stems/crown â€” at least a trace evident even under dry conditions â€” plus tan-to-reddish-brown, spherical, mustard-seed-sized sclerotia (0.5 to 2 mm) on the mycelial mat; on fruit, sunken water-soaked star-shaped spots with no offensive odor.
treatments: Avoid planting in fields with a history of southern blight; selecting fields free of S. rolfsii is the most successful method of control.
Rotate host crops for two years or more with non-hosts such as corn, wheat, barley, or small grains to reduce inoculum; avoid rotations with peanuts, soybeans, cabbage, and carrots.
Maintain weed control during rotations and reduce or eliminate weed populations.
Modify planting dates to avoid conditions favorable to disease.
Bury infected plant debris and sclerotia via deep plowing to invert the soil.
Ensure the previous crop is decomposed prior to planting (may require disking several times in fall and spring).
Remove symptomatic plants.
Maintain adequate soil pH; lower soil pH encourages disease. Certain fertilization regimes (high calcium, ammonium-type, and non-acidifying fertilizers such as calcium nitrate) may suppress disease.
Avoid close plant spacing and over-irrigation; avoid injury during cultivation.
Use black plastic mulch, row covers, or staking to keep fruit from touching the soil.

Use resistant/grafted material: tomato rootstocks 'Maxifort', 'Big Power', 'Beaufort'; resistant tomato breeding lines (5635M, 5707M, 5719M, 5737M, 5876M, 5913M); pepper cultivar 'Golden California Wonder'; grafting onto interspecific hybrid rootstocks.
Apply labeled fungicides for tomato and pepper.
Fumigate soil with broad-spectrum chemicals such as chloropicrin and metam sodium, applied days to weeks prior to planting (toxic to sclerotia and mycelium).
Use organic amendments (cotton gin trash, swine manure) to improve colonization by antagonistic Trichoderma spp.
Apply biological control agents such as Gliocladium virens, Bacillus subtilis, Penicillium spp., and an isolate of Streptomyces philanthi.

treatments.quote: Sweet potato rot is introduced through wounds, so minimizing wounding of the roots will help to curtail the incidence of the disease. Handle the sweet potatoes carefully as they are being harvested and stored, and work around them gently when weeding or the like. Wounding may be caused by mechanical means but also by insect feeding, so controlling insects will also help to control the spread of the disease. Also, some varieties of sweet potato are more susceptible to the disease. For example, 'Beauregard' is very susceptible to root rot. Use cultivars with a tolerance to bacterial sweet potato rot and select only certified disease-free propagating materials. For transplanting , only use vines that have been cut above the soil's surface. Lastly, immediately remove and destroy any infected roots found during storage to prevent the spread of sweet potato rot.

canonical.summary: Plants wilt during the heat of the day and often recover overnight but continue to wilt each day; leaves first appear dull green, then yellow and brown at the margins, completely wither and die. Wilt progresses down the vine until the entire vine wilts or dies, beginning on a single runner and ultimately killing the whole plant.
diagnostic_features: Cut a wilted vine close to the crown, press the cross-sections together, then slowly pull them apart: thread-like strands of sticky bacterial ooze form between the two cut sections, which is diagnostic (works best for cucumbers and melon, less well for squash and pumpkins).
look_alikes: wilting from insufficient water / heat of the day
treatments: Bacterial wilt cannot be controlled once a plant is infected; immediately remove infected plants and dispose of them by burning (where allowed by law) or burying them
DO NOT compost infected plants
If disease appears in a few plants, rogue and bury these plants to prevent further spread
Managing cucumber beetles is the most effective way to prevent bacterial wilt; remove wilted plants to keep beetles from moving bacteria to other cucurbits
Target non-chemical and chemical control of cucumber beetles at the beginning of the season when plants are most attractive to beetles
Use mechanical barriers such as floating row covers placed as seedlings emerge, removing them as flowers appear to allow pollination
In hoop houses/greenhouses, use insect exclusion screens (0.8 x 1.0 mm) to keep beetles out while allowing ventilation
Inspect cucurbits regularly for cucumber beetles and their damage (two to three times per week early, then weekly)
When cucumber beetle numbers are high (more than 20 per plant), spray with an appropriate insecticide
Use trap crops such as blue hubbard squash to reduce feeding on the main crop
Remove or destroy crop residue to reduce overwintering sites for cucumber beetles
Surround (kaolin clay) can reduce beetle numbers and defoliation
Plant resistant cucurbit varieties where available (check seed catalogues / Disease Resistant Vegetable Varieties lists)
Use less-attractive crops such as watermelons and pickling cucumbers as alternatives to more susceptible cucurbit species

canonical.summary: Roots and stems near the soil line appear water-soaked, dark brown and soft, and whole plants or vines collapse quickly; in peppers distinctive black lesions form on rigid stems while foliage and fruit wilt and wither yet remain attached; infected fruit shows water-soaked areas that enlarge and become covered in gray to white sporangia. On eggplant symptoms also include large leaf spots, fruit rot, crown rot, and dieback of the growing tip.
diagnostic_features: In peppers, distinctive black lesions form on stems which remain rigid while foliage and fruit wilt, wither and remain attached; on fruit, sporangia-covered lesions have a yeast-like, gray to white appearance.
treatments: Manage water so that there is never standing water for longer than 24 hours anywhere in the field
Avoid planting susceptible crops in Phytophthora-infested soil and keep records of contaminated fields
Rotate with corn, small grains, brassicas, alliums, or other non-hosts (minimum 3-4 year rotation)
Plant in raised, dome-shaped beds (at least 9 inches for non-vining cucurbits and peppers) in well-drained areas of the field
Practice light irrigation or sub-surface drip irrigation to keep the soil surface dry; improve drainage, break up hardpan with a V-ripper, and avoid soil compaction
After working in infested soil wash soil from equipment, and always work in clean fields before infested fields
Mulch between rows with straw or leave cover crop stubble to reduce splash dispersal of inoculum
Biofumigation with brassica (especially mustard) cover crops
Practice good sanitation and do not discard cull fruit in the field
Avoid introducing the pathogen into a field and promptly destroy affected plants at the start of an outbreak to limit spread
Plant resistant varieties where available (e.g. hard-rinded pumpkins 'Lil' Ironsides', 'Apprentice', 'IronMan', 'Rockafellow', 'CannonBall'; bell peppers 'Conquest', 'Paladin', 'Emerald Isle')
Apply fungicides preventively starting before disease onset
Preventive fungicide programs: mefenoxam/mancozeb (Ridomil, Apron), copper compounds (Kocide, Basic Copper 53, Champ 2F), phosphorous acid fungicides (Prophyt, K-phite, Agri-fos)

Targeted preventive fungicides: in cucurbits Presidio, Ranman, Zing!, Gavel, Zampro, Revus, Curzate, Tanos; for pepper Omega 500 and Reason 500; Presidio, Revus, Forum and phosphorous acid fungicides labeled on eggplant
Soil-applied products: Orondis Gold (in-furrow/banded), Ridomil Gold SL (directed base spray), Regalia Biofungicide, Warhammer (chitosan)
Biofungicides/biologicals: Serenade, Double Nickel, Taegro, RootShield/Rootshield Plus, Actinovate, Mycostop, Stargus, Bexfond, BioTam (soil drench)

canonical.summary: The most characteristic symptoms are root distortion and galling (swelling) that give roots a club-like appearance; aboveground, infected plants are stunted, wilt easily (especially on warm days, often recovering at night) and may show yellowing leaves and blue-green foliage. Clubroot may develop extensively on roots before aboveground symptoms are noticed.
diagnostic_features: Roots are swollen and distorted into large club-shaped malformations ranging from very small swellings on tap and lateral roots to large spindle-shaped clubs; galls are firm with a white interior at the beginning of infection (light-colored early in the season) and eventually turn brown and decay. Clubbing symptoms are unique to members of the Cruciferae.
treatments: Prevent introduction of the pathogen into a field (prevention is the primary control, as the pathogen is long-lived in soil)
Use disease-free, certified transplants; inspect roots for symptoms before planting; reject the entire lot if even a trace of clubroot is present
Sanitize tools and equipment: remove all soil, then apply a surface disinfectant or 1% bleach solution (or a 1:9 household bleach solution / undiluted Lysol), keeping surfaces wet for 15-20 minutes
Only add soil or compost heated to kill pathogens (compost should reach 148 F)
Crop rotation away from susceptible crucifers for a minimum of 4-7 years (Cornell advises at least 7 years; UMN 5-7 years); planting corn or alfalfa can reduce inoculum
Manage weeds and eliminate weedy hosts and brassica crop volunteers during rotation
Raise soil pH by liming to 7.1-7.5 (adjust to ~6.8-7.5 with ground limestone; calcitic lime preferred over dolomitic unless soil magnesium is low; hydrated lime may be added)
Reduce soil moisture: avoid planting in saturated/wet fields, improve drainage, deep-plow, break up hard pan, or use raised beds
Avoid water run-off and irrigation from contaminated fields/ponds into clean areas
Use green manure, organic soil amendments, and soil solarization
Plant clubroot-resistant varieties whenever available
Bury or compost infected plants on site

Fungicides are limited and have not provided adequate or consistent control: e.g., Blocker (PCNB), Omega 500F (fluazinam), Ranman (cyazofamid); see current Cornell/Midwest vegetable production guides for labeled options

Avoid dryness of soil with timely irrigation

canonical.summary: Symptoms vary widely: yellow, brown or black ringspots on leaves (sometimes forming a target-like pattern), distorted leaf growth, and necrotic areas with or without yellow haloes; on tomato the uppermost leaves appear bronzed with small brown lesions and on pepper small brown necrotic spots and/or chlorotic ring spots, with heavily infected leaves browning, rolling and wilting; black streaks on petioles/stems with branch tip dieback; infected seedlings form a 'shepherd's crook' and die; and tuber symptoms include surface rings, dark patches and internal discolored patches, rings, spots or flecks.
diagnostic_features: Lesions caused by TSWV have blurred margins, whereas lesions caused by early blight and other leaf spot diseases have definite margins; spots are smaller than early blight and tend to be clustered, and symptomless plants often occur right next to affected plants.
treatments: Remove and destroy infected plants to eliminate a virus reservoir; burn (where allowed), deep bury, or hot compost them
Deploy TSWV resistant or tolerant varieties (select tomatoes with the Sw-5 gene and peppers with the Tsw gene)
Control thrips vectors with chemical and/or biological insecticides; treating transplants with imidacloprid just before field setting is one of the most effective ways to suppress primary spread
Use biological control agents such as minute pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus) and big-eyed bugs (Geocoris punctipes)
Plant on reflective mulch to disorient thrips and prevent them from landing on plants
Control weeds in and outside greenhouses/fields (e.g., dandelions, sow thistle, chickweed, buttercup, plantain) to eliminate TSWV and thrips reservoirs
Inspect, segregate and quarantine newly purchased/externally sourced plant material and discard symptomatic plants
Install thrips-proof screening (e.g., 400-mesh screens) on greenhouse vents and air intakes as a physical barrier
Monitor thrips with blue and yellow sticky cards placed above plants and near doors and vents
Routinely decontaminate tools and surfaces (pruners, knives, pots, work surfaces) for a minimum of one minute with a disinfecting solution
Limit thrips movement on clothing by avoiding colors (pink, blue, yellow, white or green) that attract thrips
Avoid growing ornamentals and vegetables in the same greenhouse
For home gardeners, neem oil or other botanical insecticides, summer oil, or insecticidal soap may help control thrips

canonical.summary: Older/lower leaves yellow (often on one side) with V-shaped areas narrowing from the leaf margin; plants wilt during the hot part of the day but recover in the evening, eventually leaves shrivel, turn brown, and die; light tan discoloration develops in the vascular tissue near the base of the plant; growth is retarded and yields are low.
diagnostic_features: V-shaped leaf lesions are distinctive of Verticillium wilt; vascular streaking can also be observed in the leaves, which is a characteristic symptom.
treatments: Use resistant cultivars effective against Race 1 (marked with V for Verticillium resistance)
Sanitation, especially washing equipment to prevent movement of infested soil
Rotation to nonsusceptible crops such as small grains and corn
Incorporate crop rotations to non-host plants at 4-5 year intervals (4-6 years for tomatoes)
Remove and destroy all infected plant material, including roots
Soil solarization — heating the top six inches of soil to high temperatures
Sanitize pots and tools with water and treat for at least 30 seconds in a 10% bleach solution or 70% alcohol
Grow early-maturing varieties
Control weeds
Use mulch from resistant trees (conifers, beech, hickory, white oak, and poplar)
Soil fumigants such as chloropicrin and metam sodium applied before planting (conventional growers)
Provide ample amounts of nutrients and water (organic growers)
Regalia Biofungicide (Group P5) at 1 to 3 quarts/100 gal water for soil drenches on 10- to 14-day intervals or 1 to 4 quarts/A for in-furrow spray applications
Bexfond at 7 to 28 fl oz/A
Stargus at 6 to 8 fl oz per 1,000 ft row as in-furrow treatment, or 3 to 4 quarts/A as a soil drench on 10- to 21-day intervals

canonical.summary: New shoots can be entirely covered with the fungus and appear white ("flagshoots"); secondary infections on leaves appear as whitish, powdery spots on upper or lower leaf surfaces, sometimes preceded by a small blister. Infected cones are stunted, malformed, and mature rapidly, and infected areas on cones become red to blackish if chasmothecia are produced.
diagnostic_features: White, circular powdery colonies on leaves; entire white shoots (flagshoots) typical in spring; infected cones are stunted, malformed, and mature rapidly, leading to cone shatter, with infected areas becoming red to blackish if chasmothecia are produced.
treatments: Reduce or eliminate infected buds and flag shoots by crowning, harrowing, burning, etc. Treating before shoots emerge reduces early-season spread within a field.
Completely removing green tissue during preparation for training reduces spore load and subsequent secondary spread.
Maintain adequate nitrogen levels but do not over-apply because more succulent tissue is more susceptible.
Scout yards regularly for signs of powdery mildew.
Control bottom growth after training, mechanically or with burn-back herbicides, etc., in order to reduce active colonies.
Strip lower leaves up to about 4 ft in order to break the "green bridge" that facilitates powdery mildew's climb up in the canopy.
Early harvest can reduce powdery mildew losses in fields with high disease pressure.
Remove seedlings from around harvesting shed and hop dryer. Remove pole plants. Eliminate feral hops.
Protect regrowth against infection or remove shoot regrowth (mow, desiccate, flail, flame, etc.).
Replace highly susceptible varieties.
Thorough spray coverage is essential to protect hop plants; spray every row. Apply protective fungicides before disease is reproducing and spreading.
Bicarbonates are registered to control powdery mildew (Bi-Carb Old Fashioned Fungicide, HO Carb-O-Nator, Kaligreen, MilStop SP, Vacres).

Demethylation-inhibiting (DMI) Fungicides (Group 3) are labeled for use. Alternate or tank-mix with a non-Group 3 fungicide for resistance management (Procure 480SC, Rally 40WSP, Rhyme, Sonoma 40WSP, Tebustar 3.6L, Tebuzol 3.6F, Topguard).
Luna Experience (Group 7 + 3), Luna Sensation (Group 7 + 11), Magister SC (Group 39).
Oils are labeled to control hop powdery mildew (IAP Organic 440 Spray Oil, JMS Stylet Oil, 440 Superior Spray Oil, Trilogy).
Quintec (Group 13).
Regalia Biofungicide (Group P5).
Strobilurin fungicides (Group 11) are labeled for use (Flint Extra, Pristine).
Sulfur formulations are registered for hop (Microthiol Disperss, Proganic Micronized Sulfur); primarily a protectant and must be applied before infection.
Torino (Group U6).
Biological control (Actinovate AG, Double Nickel LC, Ecoswing, Romeo, Sonata) â€” efficacy unknown in the Pacific Northwest.

canonical.summary: Fruit lesions are the most common symptom, initially small, depressed, and circular; as the disease progresses they enlarge and develop mats of salmon to pink-colored spores that appear wet and gelatinous, eventually rotting the entire fruit. Lesions are often circular and sunken and the pathogen can infect immature fruit.
diagnostic_features: Characteristic salmon-to-pink spore mats on the fruit, with lesion centers ranging tan/orange to brown/black and concentric circles commonly surrounding the lesions; spiked black spore masses called acervuli can be seen in the center of lesions.
treatments: Use certified pathogen-free seed
Rotate to non-solanaceous crops for 2-3 years; avoid strawberry (an alternative host)
Inspect transplants and discard any with water-soaked lesions or soft stem decay; disinfect trays and greenhouse tools between uses
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation to limit splash dispersal; limit field operations when plants are wet
Control weeds and remove solanaceous volunteers near transplants
Choose well-drained planting sites and ensure adequate field drainage
Use black plastic or other barrier material between the soil-borne pathogen and the plants
Scout fields frequently (especially during wet weather) and remove infected fruit immediately
